introduction:
A major goal of modern robot learning is to perform complex and varied tasks to high precision. As a result, the community has devoted significant study to the question of how to parametrize the actions predicted by robotic policies and foundation models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025) and world action models (WAMs) (Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026b; Kim et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). The common consensus is that robot models should predict continuous-valued actions during deployment, as these are lossless and therefore support high-precision behavior. For example, most of today’s VLAs predict actions using continuous-space generative models, such as flow (Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence and others, 2025) or diffusion models (Chi et al., 2023), which are believed to better capture training data diversity whilst enhancing the precision of action predictions.

At the same time, modern robot learning is adopting increasingly more features from other AI domains, notably language modeling. These include test-time reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), on-task self-correction (Huang et al., 2022), future goal prediction (Du et al., 2023), and long-term memory (Wang et al., 2023). In fact, recent work has showcased the possibility that frontier language models can directly control robot embodiments through text generation (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Yet, today’s frontier AI models, even ones that process multiple modalities such as text, images, and audio, both take as input and produce discretely quantized tokens. Whether robot actions should follow the same discrete format therefore raises a key question:

In this work, we undertake a systematic comparison between the performance of continuous and discrete action parameterizations for both single-task robot policies and multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) models. In short, we show that discrete action parametrization can be competitive with, and even uniformly outperform, continuous action prediction, provided that correct design decisions are made. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the performance of recent discrete diffusion/flow VLA policies (Liang et al., 2026b; Wen et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2026a).

In greater detail, we consider parametrizations of the action head, or part of a robot model responsible for action prediction. Our comparison builds on classical supervised control and imitation learning (Pomerleau, 1988; Ross et al., 2011; Osa et al., 2018). We focus our study on 4 representative parametrizations: (1) continuous regression (CR), which predicts continuous-valued actions in a single forward pass and is trained with a regression objective (Bojarski et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2025) (2) continuous flow (CF), which generates continuous actions using flow matching, a family applied to robot control and motion planning (Hu et al., 2024; Chisari et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2025) (3) discrete regression (DR), which predicts a quantized action via cross-entropy classification (Brohan et al., 2022) and (4) discrete flow (DF), which predicts quantized actions in multiple steps via the discrete flow matching objective (Gat et al., 2024). Hybrid methods such as Behavior Transformer (Shafiullah et al., 2022) combine discrete action-bin prediction with a continuous offset; in contrast, we study purely discrete and continuous action heads separately to isolate the effect of action representation. Recent work compares regression and flow policies under architecture-matched settings (Pan et al., 2026). We evaluate these parametrizations from single-task policies on RoboMimic (Mandlekar et al., 2021) to multi-task VLA-scale policies using RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2026), DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), as well as real-world robot experiments. All are evaluated using closed-loop task success, action prediction accuracy, and within-chunk temporal variation.
We identify 3 key findings that upend prior beliefs about the relative performance of discrete and continuous action modalities, challenging the prevailing view that precise robot control requires predicting continuous action prediction:

Finding 1: Control Precision Contrary to prior belief, discrete action parametrizations, even discrete regression (DR) with the simplest bin discretization, can exhibit greater control precision than their continuous counterparts, despite the possibly lossy quantization of actions! We support this claim in both sim and real settings in Section 3. We show that this arises from greater policy reactivity, both to the action-chunk time index and the conditioning observation.

Finding 1: Control Precision Contrary to prior belief, discrete action parametrizations, even discrete regression (DR) with the simplest bin discretization, can exhibit greater control precision than their continuous counterparts, despite the possibly lossy quantization of actions! We support this claim in both sim and real settings in Section 3. We show that this arises from greater policy reactivity, both to the action-chunk time index and the conditioning observation.

Finding 2: Iterative Refinement and Guidance Mitigate Factorization Error (Section 4). Independently predicted tokens can combine incompatible choices across time and action dimensions, even when individual token distributions are accurate. DF solves this by iterative computation, while classifier-free guidance reduces ambiguity by changing token preferences. Both improve control significantly, supporting joint consistency as main explanation for their gains. In the RoboCasa comparison, guidance raises DR success from 27.1% to 49.2%, approaching DF’s 53.9% and CF’s 52.7%, largely ahead of CR’s 38.8%.

Finding 3: Explicit Geometry and Structured Tokenization Provide Limited Additional Gains (Section 5).
Encoding action distances or using alternative tokenizers improves some configurations, but none exceeds our best DF result with uniform bins and the standard mixture path. Adjacent bins also acquire similar output embeddings, suggesting that discrete heads can learn local geometry without encoding it explicitly.

abstract:
Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining
vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for
target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment
of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A
human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a
mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs
in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made
possible not by retargeting the hand’s motion but the object’s. A capture
yields a body-free record: the object’s pose over time, its contact
intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation
against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the
human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured
per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a
named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs

introduction:
A human demonstration records what an object did, and a great deal about
the body that did it. Any robot can use the first, but only a body built
like the demonstrator’s can use the second. Today, robot learning uses
human demonstrations mostly for
pretraining, where human video at internet scale is retargeted in bulk to
teach a vision-language-action model what manipulation looks
like [25, 42].
Deployment depends on the step after that (Fig. 3), in
which a specific robot is
post-trained on a specific task from tens to a few hundred episodes of its
own body. Human demonstrations are hard to use there, because the robot’s
body decides which of them it can execute at all. Systems that do transfer
a demonstration to a robot target one robot at a
time [21, 15, 54, 50],
and they drop the demonstrations that robot cannot use.

This paper turns a demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device,
such as a mobile phone with nothing attached to it, into post-training data
for any robot (Fig. 1). It does so by retargeting the object’s motion. Throughout, the data is post-training data: a target-embodiment
training set, the tens to a few hundred episodes of one robot on one task on
which a pretrained policy is post-trained, or at that scale a task policy is
trained from scratch. Nothing here is pretraining data. We write
post-training set for short.

Fig. 2 shows the design, and Table 1
collects the terms. A capture is reduced to a body-free record: the
object’s pose over time in metres, the intervals over which it was held,
and one reconstructed 3D object whose observed surface is kept apart from the completed one.
The hand is treated as a witness to contact rather than copied: when and
where it held the object are kept on the object, as the contact intervals
and as a contact map on the mesh. Any robot, given as a
URDF and the short descriptor of Table 4, is solved
against that record without rescaling it. Its kinematic replay is then
scored against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth. This
measures, for each robot, the human-to-simulation leg of
human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer (§2). Each (robot,
episode) pair receives one outcome. The pair passes at the declared
tolerance or fails with a named mode, or the robot refuses the episode
before any motion is generated. A refusal carries a reason from a fixed
list and the measured quantity behind it. Every outcome goes to an
append-only ledger in which the latest entry for a run supersedes the
earlier ones. A pass that cannot meet a later check is therefore retracted
by a dated entry, and the earlier row stays in the ledger.

Every pipeline we know of that retargets human demonstrations already makes the
refusal decision. A feasibility filter drops motions a humanoid cannot
track [12, 16]. A grasp planner discards a
trajectory when none of its sampled grasps survives a simulator
check [54], and a curation stage removes
whatever a quality model dislikes [42, 48].
The decision stays inside the pipeline, and only what survives it is
released. A reader then cannot tell whether an episode is missing because
it was never captured, because one body could not reach it, or because a
filter that no longer exists once rejected it. We keep the decision, with
its reason, beside the record.

The set analysed here holds 42 captures solved on
8 robots from 4 body classes, 157 (robot, episode)
pairs in all, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail,
14.0% are refused and 2.5% are
unauditable. Every refused pair that
ran anyway failed (13 of
13, §6.3). A robot’s
description predicts its outcomes barely better than guessing does
(§6.4). Ranking grasps by sweep coverage passed
33% of pairs where ranking by grasp quality
passed 13% (§6.2).

Human2Sim2Robot [24] names the human-to-robot embodiment gap. It and Video2Sim2Real [11] cross that gap for one robot. They use the demonstrated
object motion as a reward for reinforcement learning in simulation, then
transfer the policy. We use the same object motion as ground truth, not as a
reward. We measure the human-to-simulation leg for every robot,
kinematically and with no learning in the loop, and we keep the
measurement. The simulation-to-robot leg belongs to the policy post-trained
on the result and is measured downstream.

title: AutoRSR: Automated Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Generation for Scalable Robot Learning
authors: Jiawei Zhang,Chang Liu,Litao Deng,Tao Zhang,Qin Jin
abstract:
Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets,
but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and
robot time. Simulation provides a scalable alternative,
yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still
requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing,
coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification. We present
AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data. Given multi-view observations, robot states,
and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace,
extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base
frame at metric scale. Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization.After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation. Across three
real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated
episodes per task achieve 73.3–86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to π0.5\pi_{0.5} trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by
an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that real-world observations
can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation
data with substantially reduced human effort.
introduction:
A major bottleneck in embodied robot learning is the lack of scalable and diverse manipulation data. Real-world teleoperation provides high-fidelity demonstrations but requires substantial human effort and robot time, whereas simulation can generate large-scale data at much lower cost. The challenge, however, is not simply to create a visually realistic simulation.
For simulation to serve as a practical data engine, a real workspace must be converted into a robot-learning-ready embodied environment: its objects should be individually reusable, its geometry should remain metrically consistent with the physical workspace, and its manipulation trajectories should be executable and scalable without repeatedly involving a human operator.

Existing approaches for constructing robot-learning simulations can be broadly categorized into generative and reconstruction-based methods. Generative
approaches [1, 2] offer flexible scene and asset synthesis, but the generated environments may differ from the geometry and appearance of a target workspace.
Reconstruction-based approaches [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
, in contrast, preserve the visual and spatial characteristics of real environments and are therefore attractive for sim-to-real robot learning.
However, when reconstruction is used as a data generation engine, substantial human intervention remains between scene reconstruction and executable robot learning data. In particular, the remaining effort arises from two coupled challenges: preparing reusable simulation assets and making the reconstructed environment executable by a robot.

On reusable asset construction:
Obtaining simulation-ready objects from a real workspace typically involves separate object and scene scanning [3], manual object segmentation [4], or additional per-object processing for extraction and completion [7].
Such operations introduce object-level human effort that grows with scene complexity and must be repeated
when the workspace changes. More importantly, these pipelines generally treat scene reconstruction and object preparation as separate stages rather than
providing a unified mechanism for turning a scanned workspace into reusable manipulation assets.

On executable trajectory generation: A reconstructed scene alone is also insufficient for robot policy learning. The reconstruction is typically represented in its own coordinate system and must be registered to the robot before trajectories can be executed. This registration often requires explicit scene-to-robot calibration or manual alignment. Moreover, demonstrations used for learning are commonly collected through real-robot teleoperation, or trajectories must be manually specified and adapted to the reconstructed scene. Consequently, even when simulation removes the cost of physically executing thousands of demonstrations, human effort remains embedded in the process of producing the initial executable data. This limits the extent to which reconstruction-based simulation can serve as an automated and reusable data engine.

We address these limitations with AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to-real framework that converts a scanned real workspace into scalable manipulation data. The key idea is to exploit information already
available during workspace scanning to eliminate subsequent manual alignment and annotation. We perform a hybrid scan of the workspace while recording wrist-camera poses and robot joint states. Given open-vocabulary semantic queries, these observations are used to reconstruct the workspace and extract
individual object assets without manually annotated masks. Because the camera is rigidly attached to the robot and its poses are synchronized with the robot
states, the reconstructed scene can be automatically registered to the robot
base frame at metric scale using the recorded geometric relationships. This produces a simulation environment in which reconstructed objects and robot motions are expressed in a physically consistent coordinate system.

Within this aligned environment, we use a human demonstration as motion seeds and automatically recover executable manipulation trajectories. Trajectory interpolation and domain randomization then produce diverse simulation episodes without requiring additional real-robot interaction. The result is a complete data-generation pipeline in which human effort is
concentrated on the initial workspace scan and semantic specification, while object extraction, coordinate registration, trajectory generation, and data
augmentation are automated.

We evaluate AutoRSR on three real-world manipulation tasks. For each task, we
generate 1K simulation episodes and train robot policies using only the automatically generated data. We compare them against policies trained from 150 human teleoperated real-world demonstrations. On the physical robot, AutoRSR-trained policies achieve 73.3–86.7% success, with performance within
10 percentage points of the corresponding real-data baselines. We further measure the human time required by the complete data-generation process and observe an order-of-magnitude reduction compared with collecting an equivalent amount of real-world data. These results suggest that automatically reconstructed real workspaces can provide a practical intermediate representation for scalable robot learning.

In summary, our main contributions are: (i) We present AutoRSR, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that converts scanned real workspaces into reusable, metrically
aligned, and robot-executable simulation environments for manipulation data generation.
(ii) We introduce an automated processing for open-vocabulary object extraction, scene-to-robot registration, and executable trajectory
generation, enabling large-scale simulation data generation without manual object annotation, manual coordinate alignment, or robot teleoperation. (iii) We demonstrate the effectiveness of AutoRSR on three real-world manipulation tasks. Policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes achieve real-robot performance comparable to policies trained on 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while substantially reducing human data-collection effort.

title: VIGOR-MPC: Vision-Guided Objective Regulation MPC
authors: Jelena Trisovic,Rahel Rickenbach,Marek Landert,Panagiotis Minos,Melanie N. Zeilinger
abstract: Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student–teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which addresses reference tracking across navigation tasks by distilling a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a multi-level recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher’s behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.3
introduction:
In vision-based control tasks, an agent acts in an unknown environment that it perceives only through an onboard camera. While this setting allows for operation without previously mapping the environment and thereby enables a broader range of applications, such as hand-eye coordination for robotic grasping from monocular images [20], or general exploration tasks of mobile robots [38], it introduces challenges for control performance and safety: (i) uncertain and noisy perception, leading to imperfect reference and constraint estimates, (ii) a limited and potentially occluded field of view, (iii) the computational overhead of the perception module leaving limited compute for the controller, which can hinder fast reaction times, and (iv) the absence of prior knowledge about the environments encountered at deployment. While challenges (i)–(iii) are inherent to any vision-based controller, challenge (iv) is where end-to-end learning approaches fundamentally struggle, as they tend to generalize poorly to unseen layouts or new information sources.
Inspired by recent progress in combining vision-based with optimization-based control [23, 40], as well as developments in imitation learning exploiting the structure of optimization-based controllers [1, 32, 37], we demonstrate how structured imitation learning can be leveraged to bring the strengths of optimization-based control to the vision-based setting.
Our approach employs a student-teacher framework that addresses these challenges through a privileged, field-of-view-aware model predictive control (MPC) teacher with full state information, that is by construction capable of remaining safely within the field of view, and a computationally efficient student with multi-level memory that, via imitation, learns to adapt the parameters of a predefined control structure from the noisy, partially occluded, variable-length context produced by a perception module. Unlike prior work that learns short-horizon cost parameters under perfect information [32], our setting introduces imperfect, time-varying, partially occluded and missing context, addressed through a field-of-view-aware privileged teacher, a memory-capable parameter mapping, and real-time context-driven reference adjustment mechanisms enabling obstacle avoidance from perceived context alone. The student thereby inherits the teacher’s field-of-view-aware safe and obstacle avoidant behavior while adapting online to perceptual uncertainty, demonstrated in simulation and on hardware on a vision-based racing task with no prior track knowledge.

We organize prior work on vision-based control by how much classical control structure is preserved between perception and action. End-to-end policies map camera observations directly to actions, from early behavior-cloning approaches in driving [4, 9] to recent foundation-model-scale variants [13]. However, they are data-intensive, lack constraint-handling, and require retraining under domain shift. Modular pipelines with a classical controller feed fixed-form perception outputs into a predefined controller, which was applied both in agile flight [15, 22, 23]
and driving [26, 7]. The controller is safe and interpretable but rigid, and cannot adapt to noisy, or variable-length context. A recent line of work designs controllers that handle perception uncertainty explicitly [40, 28, 12] through different variants of constraint tightening rather than learned
adaptation. Modular pipelines with a learned controller either map
perception-derived system and environment states to actions via reinforcement learning or imitation trained policy [14, 43, 19, 44]
or learn only specific ingredients of an otherwise classical
controller, such as the cost or decision variables of an
MPC [37, 33, 32],
dynamics
model [27], its sampling
distribution [36], or a terminal value
function [24]. Fully learned
controllers handle constraints only implicitly; partially learned ones
preserve the optimization scaffolding and inherit its safety and
generalization, but have been developed almost exclusively with clean
state-based context, hence neglecting perception. Building on [32],
our work fills the gap in this last category by adapting cost
parameters to the noisy, occluded, variable-length context produced
by a perception module.

title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Fucai Zhu,Xidong Zhang,Yichi Zhang,Yipan Wang,Fubo Wang,Zibin Wu,Kaiqi Li,Jianhao Jiao,Shihan Lu,Di Hu,Mengdi Xu,Siyu Zhu,Xiaoxiao Long,Yao Yao,Xun Cao,Zhuo Xu,Koichi Hashimoto,Qifeng Chen,Zhe Li,Jianfei Yang,Haofei Lu,Danica Kragic,Shuicheng Yan,Jianghua Duan,Michael Yu Wang,Weihao Yuan
abstract:
Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision.
We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection.
TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators.
Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types.
We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding.
We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
introduction:
Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations to support generalizable manipulation across tasks, objects, and environments. While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale multimodal data, contact-rich manipulation additionally requires tactile information that is difficult to infer from vision alone, especially under occlusion, sustained contact, or fine-grained interaction. However, tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale because collection is often tied to robot-specific sensor integration, calibration, and teleoperation. Moreover, large-scale multimodal demonstrations can vary substantially in quality and typically provide limited structured supervision for contact, task progress, and interaction targets.

To address these challenges, we introduce TacClaw-Infinity,
a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset
for contact-rich manipulation, as illustrated in
Fig. id1. The dataset is collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that synchronously records visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. This robot-independent design enables scalable acquisition across different operators and environments while preserving rich physical interaction signals.

To achieve both scale and diversity, TacClaw-Infinity is collected at more than 50 physical locations spanning homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, outdoor environments, and other everyday settings around the world. Leveraging the portability of TacClaw, we combine protocol-driven recordings of common skills from a shared task catalog with open-ended tasks chosen by collectors.
Worldwide academic and industrial collaborating organizations further contribute tasks according to their own research and application interests. Together, these efforts yield data of over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types.

To make the heterogeneous corpus reliable and learning-ready, we develop a scalable processing pipeline covering trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, and embodiment-aware feasibility filtering based on the reachability and manipulability of multiple robot embodiments. We further provide automatic temporal, semantic, and spatial annotations, including contact-centric subtask segmentation, segment-level language descriptions, and contact-anchored target-object localization and mask tracking. These annotations transform raw multimodal streams into structured supervision for downstream policy learning.

We validate TacClaw-Infinity from both data and model perspectives. At the data level, we evaluate the haptic fidelity of the TacClaw interface, characterize the cross-embodiment action-space compatibility of the collected demonstrations, and assess the quality of the structured annotations. At the model level, we evaluate two representative policy families across three heterogeneous robot embodiments and demonstrate that policies trained solely on TacClaw-Infinity can transfer without embodiment-specific demonstrations. Controlled comparisons further isolate the contributions of tactile observations to downstream policy learning.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured VTLA dataset spanning more than 1,000 task types, collected in a distributed manner across 50+ locations and 20+ organizations around the world.

We develop a scalable robot-independent collection and processing pipeline with trajectory reconstruction, embodiment-aware feasibility assessment, and automatic temporal, semantic, and spatial annotations.
We further evaluate the collection interface, action-space compatibility, and annotation quality.

We validate the dataset across three robot embodiments and two policy families, demonstrating both cross-embodiment transferability and the effectiveness of tactile sensing.

1. We introduce TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured VTLA dataset spanning more than 1,000 task types, collected in a distributed manner across 50+ locations and 20+ organizations around the world.

2. We develop a scalable robot-independent collection and processing pipeline with trajectory reconstruction, embodiment-aware feasibility assessment, and automatic temporal, semantic, and spatial annotations.
We further evaluate the collection interface, action-space compatibility, and annotation quality.

3. We validate the dataset across three robot embodiments and two policy families, demonstrating both cross-embodiment transferability and the effectiveness of tactile sensing.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation For Robot Policies
authors: Motasem Alfarra,Pietro Mazzaglia,Markus Peschl,Daniel Dijkman,Christos Louizos
abstract:
Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints.
We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and self-supervised during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.
Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic’s predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value (“hard”) observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions.
Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
introduction:
Robots deployed in the real world must contend with operating conditions that can diverge sharply from those encountered during training (Kumar et al., 2021).
These discrepancies arise from multiple sources: terrain variability (e.g., rocks, low-friction surfaces) (Sun et al., 2025), hardware changes (e.g., localized payloads or partial actuator degradation) (Pouroullis et al., 2025), emergent situations (e.g., a weight stuck on one arm/calf) (Zhang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2023), and the broader sim-to-real gap between simulated and physical environments (Peng et al., 2018).
In practice, such factors rarely occur in isolation: a deployed robot may simultaneously experience altered contact dynamics, sensor noise, actuator wear, and previously unseen environmental configurations.
These distribution shifts can substantially degrade policies that perform well under nominal conditions (refer to Figure 1 left), making online adaptation central to robust autonomy.

A common response to combat this problem is to apply large-scale domain randomization during reinforcement learning to improve zero-shot generalization (Tobin et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018).
While effective in some cases, this approach is fundamentally constrained by what can be specified in advance: it presumes one can enumerate relevant sources of variability, model them with sufficient fidelity in simulation, and collect enough data to cover their interactions.
When robots encounter truly novel conditions, adaptation is performed offline. This interrupts operation to gather new data and fine-tune from scratch, which is misaligned with real-time, on-device compute and reliability constraints.
Architectural add-ons for adaptation can help but often increase system complexity and reduce portability across tasks, embodiments, and deployment settings (Kumar et al., 2021).

We study Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) (Wang et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020) as a practical alternative for robotic control under distribution shift.
TTA is well-suited for tackling this problem as it adapts the pretrained model at test time in an online and self-supervised manner, alleviating the need to disrupt the inference stream for retraining and requiring no labeled data.
Thus, our starting point is a simple, general baseline: we update only the actor (policy) parameters at deployment while freezing the critic, using a compact on-device memory of recent observations.
At periodic intervals during execution, the actor is adapted by maximizing the critic’s estimated action value on stored observations—treating the critic as a learned performance surrogate and requiring no online rewards.
Unlike standard deployments where the critic is used primarily for training and often discarded at inference, here we actively leverage the pretrained critic during runtime.
While distribution shift also affects the critic, we find it still provides a sufficiently informative signal to guide test-time actor updates (Chen et al., 2023); nonetheless, naive value maximization can overfit to spurious, overconfident estimates (Kumar et al., 2020) and under-explore the loss landscape.

In this work, and to address these limitations, we introduce an enhanced framework with two complementary elements.
First, we add an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic’s predictive distribution during adaptation, which tempers overconfidence under shift and biases updates toward regions that are simultaneously high-value and high-uncertainty. This
yields more informative gradients due to the stability and exploration benefits of maximum-entropy objectives in RL (Eysenbach and Levine, 2021), which we adapt to the critic’s uncertainty at test time.
Second, and in the spirit of prioritized experience replay (Schaul et al., 2016), we employ a score-based memory that prioritizes observations inversely proportional to the critic’s predicted value, coupled with importance sampling to focus updates on the most informative deployment conditions under tight memory and latency budgets.
We evaluate on Go1, Go2, and G1 in Mujoco Playground simulation (Zakka et al., 2025), spanning quadruped and humanoid morphologies under four representative shifts (mass on torso, mass on calf, rocky terrain, slippery terrain) and three different architectures, and observe up to 50% performance gains very efficiently in a single-device setting.
We further validate our approach on a physical Unitree Go2 robot by attaching a {3,2}​kg\{3,2\}\,\mathrm{kg} calf payload and performing fully on-device TTA
, observing trends consistent with simulation.
We can summarize our contributions in four folds:

A lightweight, on-device TTA framework for RL control. We adapt only the actor parameters while freezing the critic, maintain a compact memory of recent observations, and perform periodic, self-supervised updates that fit strict control-loop latency and compute budgets.

A lightweight, on-device TTA framework for RL control. We adapt only the actor parameters while freezing the critic, maintain a compact memory of recent observations, and perform periodic, self-supervised updates that fit strict control-loop latency and compute budgets.

Entropy-regularized critic-driven adaptation. We introduce an objective that maximizes the critic’s estimated action value while promoting higher-entropy critic outputs during test-time updates—mitigating overconfident value extrapolation and preserving local action coverage; the procedure is architecture-agnostic and supervision-free.

Score-based memory with importance sampling. We propose a memory mechanism that assigns each observation a score inversely proportional to the critic’s predicted value, stores harder samples, and employs importance sampling to focus on more informative samples under memory constraints.

Comprehensive validation in simulation and on-device. We show consistent gains on Go1/Go2/G1 embodiments and on four deployment shifts, and confirm the same trends on a physical Unitree Go2 via fully on-device adaptation with a {3,2}​kg\{3,2\}\,\mathrm{kg} calf payload.

1. A lightweight, on-device TTA framework for RL control. We adapt only the actor parameters while freezing the critic, maintain a compact memory of recent observations, and perform periodic, self-supervised updates that fit strict control-loop latency and compute budgets.

2. Entropy-regularized critic-driven adaptation. We introduce an objective that maximizes the critic’s estimated action value while promoting higher-entropy critic outputs during test-time updates—mitigating overconfident value extrapolation and preserving local action coverage; the procedure is architecture-agnostic and supervision-free.

3. Score-based memory with importance sampling. We propose a memory mechanism that assigns each observation a score inversely proportional to the critic’s predicted value, stores harder samples, and employs importance sampling to focus on more informative samples under memory constraints.

4. Comprehensive validation in simulation and on-device. We show consistent gains on Go1/Go2/G1 embodiments and on four deployment shifts, and confirm the same trends on a physical Unitree Go2 via fully on-device adaptation with a {3,2}​kg\{3,2\}\,\mathrm{kg} calf payload.

title: Learning-Based Adaptive MPC for Magnetorquer-Only Satellite Attitude Control
authors: Patrick Schwartz,Abhishek Cauligi
comment: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo) 2026
abstract:
Nanosatellites (e.g., CubeSats) have the potential to carry out useful science and exploration activities for outer solar system exploration, but their small size leads to trade-offs between attitude control and science capabilities.
Magnetorquers offer a unique compromise as compact actuators that enable three-axis attitude control, but suffer from a loss of control authority and require full knowledge of the planetary magnetic field.
In this work, we present a learning-based adaptive model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans rotational trajectories for the satellite while accounting for this loss of control authority.
Key to our approach is the inclusion of a learned magnetic field model that is trained in simulation using low-fidelity magnetic field data.
Using measurements collected online, our proposed algorithm adapts this learned magnetic field model using a simple last-layer update scheme, allowing the MPC controller to quickly adapt to the true planetary magnetic field model and more effectively plan attitude trajectories.
We demonstrate the results of our proposed approach for two use cases, (1) Earth-orbit and (2) Uranus-orbit, and show that our learning-based adaptive MPC algorithm improves controller success for these system simulations by 5% and 61%, respectively.
introduction:
In recent years, NASA has expressed an increased interest in robotic exploration of the outer solar system [1].
In the most recent planetary decadal survey, the Uranus flagship mission was highlighted to study its unique and largely unexplored characteristics such as its low-internal energy and active atmospheric dynamics [2].
The magnetic field of Uranus in particular has garnered significant scientific interest, yet existing measurements are drawn from sparse Voyager II mission data when the field may have been in an anomalous state, so there is high uncertainty around the current models [3, 4].
Concurrently, nanosatellites (e.g., CubeSats) have emerged as a promising and affordable means of carrying out useful planetary science and augmenting the exploration capabilities of flagship science missions.

Yet, the small size of nanosatellites imposes constraints on their scientific capabilities, chief among them the difficulty of using large actuators such as reaction wheel assemblies (RWAs) for precise attitude control.
As an alternative to RWAs, magnetorquers have been explored as a more compact and mechanically simple means of three-axis pointing control, but these require full knowledge of the planetary magnetic field and experience a loss of torque authority in the direction parallel to the local magnetic field.
These limitations preclude the use of magnetorquers as primary means of attitude control for Uranus exploration, where the magnetic field is poorly understood, and render simple feedback control strategies such as PID control ineffective.
As such, the development of a three-axis magnetorquer-only attitude controller for Uranus exploration would pave the way for more capable nanosatellite science and exploration for future Uranus missions.

Related Work: 
There have been numerous attempts at designing magnetorquer-only attitude control algorithms.
The works in [5, 6] tackle the problem of underactuated control via optimal control, wherein the attitude control problem is modeled as an optimization problem and solved in a receding horizon fashion to compute the torque commands.
Although flight tests demonstrated promising results for such MPC strategies in Earth orbit [7], MPC presumes an accurate model of the planetary magnetic field and a limited understanding of the Uranus planetary magnetic field precludes the direct use of such strategies.
An alternate line of research has pursued tackling spacecraft attitude control under uncertainty using model-free reinforcement learning [8, 9] and synthesized an attitude control policy through trial-and-error in simulation.
However, such purely model-free methods prove brittle in the face of out-of-distribution scenarios encountered in flight.

In recent years, learning-based adaptive MPC has emerged as an effective way to use online measurements to quickly adapt the model used within optimal control [10] and thereby provide a sample-efficient means of accomplishing online adaptation without forgoing interpretability.
One strategy of nonparametric learning approaches trains a Gaussian process (GP) regression model online to quickly learn the unmodeled dynamics [11], but GP regression scales with cubic complexity as the number of training samples increases.
In such cases, neural networks provide a more expressive capability to handle large amounts of data and a host of approaches have explored adapting neural networks online for the purpose of learning-based MPC.
To facilitate stable adaptation of the network parameters online without risking catastrophic forgetting, a common approach is to only update the last-layer of the network.
The authors in [12] leverage Bayesian meta-learning with last-layer adaptation to learn the dynamics model for a spacecraft control task.
For drone trajectory tracking, [13] learns an approximate dynamics model offline using a neural network and then performs last-layer network updates to adapt the dynamics to unknown disturbances.
As such, many approaches have demonstrated the efficacy of learning an approximate neural network dynamics model offline and then performing last-layer network updates to improve downstream control performance.

Statement of Contributions: 
Our work presents a framework for magnetorquer-only attitude control for nanosatellites using learning-based MPC with online adaptation.
Our approach, shown in Fig. 1, leverages a learned neural network model of the planetary magnetic field within an MPC-based attitude controller and uses magnetometer data collected online to update the network model at test time.
Our proposed approach has the following key properties:

We use a “grey-box” dynamics model that uses a learned magnetic field model within an analytical dynamics model to balance model expressivity with controller interpretability.

Our controller makes minimal assumptions on the orbit and operates across inclinations spanning from polar orbits to more challenging equatorial ones.

Our MPC formulation carefully considers the geometric structure of quaternions to improve controller performance.

1. We use a “grey-box” dynamics model that uses a learned magnetic field model within an analytical dynamics model to balance model expressivity with controller interpretability.

2. Our controller makes minimal assumptions on the orbit and operates across inclinations spanning from polar orbits to more challenging equatorial ones.

3. Our MPC formulation carefully considers the geometric structure of quaternions to improve controller performance.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Receding-Horizon Safety Critic and Differentiable Action Shields
authors: Siwei Ju,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz
abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy–filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled increasingly agile legged locomotion, yet safety remains a central obstacle to deploying learned controllers beyond narrow training conditions. In practice, many locomotion failures are delayed: a destabilizing contact, a slight foot scuff, or a suboptimal recovery step may not cause an immediate violation, but can drive the robot into an unrecoverable state several steps later. This makes safety inherently horizon-dependent in locomotion, especially under disturbances and terrain-induced contact variability.

A common approach to safety in continuous control is to enforce state constraints using control barrier functions (CBFs) [3] and differentiable safety layers that project actions through constrained optimization [1, 31]. Data-driven CBF variants often learn uncertainty or residual terms to compensate modeling error [27, 9], while neural CBFs (NCBFs) parameterize the certificate itself to reduce manual design effort [37, 24, 20, 25, 36, 17, 2]. In safe RL, CBF-style shields are frequently combined with actor–critic training [10, 7, 8, 32, 34] or treated as part of the environment dynamics [6]. Despite their success, these methods face persistent challenges in locomotion: (i) computational overhead from per-step optimization and the associated training-time scalability limits, (ii) myopia from one-step constraints on the safety layer that may not anticipate multi-step failures, and (iii) policy–filter mismatch, where the executed (filtered) actions induce a distribution shift that is not always accounted for during policy optimization.

Predictive safety filters address myopia by enforcing safety over a horizon, typically relying on known or nominal dynamics models and uncertainty representations [28, 29, 30]. In parallel, safe RL has explored learning feasibility or long-horizon safety signals that resemble critics/value functions [13, 26] and structured safety enforcement that avoids generic QPs when dynamics are known [15]. For robot control, complementary approaches predict failure and switch to recovery behaviors (e.g., safe-fall policies) [19, 14], or deploy CBF shields on complex platforms such as humanoids [33, 34]. These strands collectively indicate the need for safety mechanisms that are horizon-aware, computationally lightweight, and compatible with end-to-end policy learning under distribution shift.

We propose a receding-horizon safety critic that directly predicts whether the system will remain non-terminated over the next HH steps from a state. The critic is trained from rollouts using horizon-wise binary labels, shaped by a temporal consistency prior inspired by discrete-time CBF conditions, and regularized for smoothness to improve robustness under distribution shift. To make the safety signal actionable for control, we derive a differentiable safety layer that minimally corrects the policy action via a single-constraint projection with a closed-form solution, and we use a slack variable scaled by the ensemble uncertainty. Because the safety layer is differentiable, we integrate it into PPO and introduce a safety anticipation loss so the policy learns to reduce interventions and align with the horizon-safety objective.

We evaluate the approach on quadruped locomotion under controlled domain shifts, including stochastic action noise and external perturbations on both flat and heightfield terrains. Across disturbance intensities, the proposed method substantially improves success rates while maintaining competitive returns compared to PPO with domain randomization and PPO augmented with an NCBF-style safety layer. An ablation on the horizon length reveals a clear trade-off: longer horizons better mitigate myopic failures but are harder to train and can become over-conservative under shift.

We summarize our contribution as follows:

Receding-horizon safety critic.
We learn a safety critic that predicts whether the system remains safe over the next HH steps from horizon-labeled rollouts.

Structured horizon-safety training.
We propose a training objective combining horizon classification, temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization with balanced sampling of rare failures.

Closed-form differentiable safety shield.
We derive a one-constraint projection that minimally corrects the policy action to prevent decreases in predicted safety, enabling end-to-end optimization.

Robust safe locomotion under shift.
Integrated with PPO via a safety-anticipation loss, our method reduces catastrophic failures and improves robustness under domain shift, outperforming PPO baselines and an NCBF safety layer without hand-designed CBFs.

1. Receding-horizon safety critic.
We learn a safety critic that predicts whether the system remains safe over the next HH steps from horizon-labeled rollouts.

2. Structured horizon-safety training.
We propose a training objective combining horizon classification, temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization with balanced sampling of rare failures.

3. Closed-form differentiable safety shield.
We derive a one-constraint projection that minimally corrects the policy action to prevent decreases in predicted safety, enabling end-to-end optimization.

4. Robust safe locomotion under shift.
Integrated with PPO via a safety-anticipation loss, our method reduces catastrophic failures and improves robustness under domain shift, outperforming PPO baselines and an NCBF safety layer without hand-designed CBFs.

title: Learning Navigation from Multimodal Demonstrations with Geometric Candidate Modes
authors: Chengyang Peng,Zhihao Zhang,Upama Pant,Yiming Wang,Keith A. Redmill,Ayonga Hereid
abstract:
Offline navigation demonstrations are multimodal, because one observation often allows several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on either side. Behavior cloning averages these actions, potentially leading to unsafe routes. Multimodal policies must discover the alternatives from the data, but similar states can lead to different routes whose current actions overlap. In navigation, the alternatives have a geometric cause and can be computed from one observation. We propose a hierarchical neural-network policy that computes candidate modes from local geometry and learns from demonstrations which mode to follow and how. A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and its previous choice among a set of candidate modes, and a low-level policy turns it into an action.
In simulation, the policy succeeds in over 95% of seen and unseen test cases, compared with at most 43% and 20% for four offline learning baselines and 79% and 67% for a heuristic that uses the same modes without learning. The simulation-trained policy also transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.
introduction:
Learning navigation policies from offline demonstrations needs neither the online interaction nor the reward design of reinforcement learning (RL) [18, 14], and it lets a policy that sees only a local occupancy map imitate an expert planner that had access to the full map. Its central difficulty is multimodality, because a single observation often admits several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on the left or on the right. Behavior cloning (BC) [15, 3] regresses the demonstrated actions, and offline RL methods such as Decision Transformer (DT) [4, 19] condition this regression on the desired return. Both predict one action per observation, so the regression optimum is the mean of the valid actions [16], and the mean of a left and a right detour points into the obstacle (Fig. 1(a)).

Multimodal policy classes avoid this averaging by modeling the distribution of actions given the observation, so that a sampled action follows one alternative instead of falling between them. Behavior Transformers (BeT) [16, 10] learn a discrete vocabulary of actions from the demonstrations, by kk-means or vector quantization, and predict a distribution over it together with a continuous offset. Diffusion Policy (DP) [5] and its navigation variants [17] generate actions by iterative denoising, and implicit BC [7] selects them by minimizing a learned energy. In all of these, the alternatives are learned from the statistics of the demonstrations. The model must infer from data coverage how many alternatives a scene admits and where they lie, although in navigation both change with every obstacle arrangement. The current actions do not always reveal them either, because routes that differ in navigation demonstrations can have overlapping current actions. Moreover, a sampled action is not tied to a route around an obstacle, so successive predictions can switch routes.

In navigation, however, the alternatives have an identifiable geometric cause. Nearby obstacles split the free space into a few distinct passages (Fig. 1(b)), a local analogue of the homotopy classes that topological planners search over given a map [1]. These passages can be computed from a single observation, without data or search. Computing them does not solve navigation: geometry does not indicate which passage leads to the goal beyond the observed region, it recomputes the passages at every step with no memory of the previous choice, and it gives each passage only a coarse direction rather than an executable command. The demonstrations contain what geometry lacks, because the planner that produced them saw the whole map and followed one route from start to goal.

We therefore propose a hierarchical policy in which geometry supplies the alternatives and learning selects and executes them (Fig. 2). Choosing a mode before acting has precedent: conditional imitation learning takes the mode from an external command [6], and latent-plan methods learn it as a latent variable [12]. In our policy the modes are computed from geometry, and only the choice among them and their execution are learned. Our contributions are:

A geometric module with no learned parameters that intersects tangent lines at the closest points of nearby obstacles, with one another and with the observation-window boundary, to enumerate a variable-size set of candidate modes from a single observation.

A hierarchical policy trained on demonstrations without mode annotations. A high-level policy selects a mode, conditioned on the goal and the previously selected mode; a low-level policy converts it into a continuous action and is also trained toward the mode’s direction.

An evaluation that separates what geometry and learning each contribute. Against four offline learning baselines, success rises from at most 43% and 20% in seen and unseen environments to 96.5% and 95.2%. A heuristic that uses the same modes without learning reaches only 79.2% and 66.7%, so the modes help but are not enough, and learning closes the gap with fewer mode switches and abrupt action changes.

Hardware experiments in which the simulation-trained policy runs on a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot without retraining and without tuning for each environment. The robot computes the modes from the occupancy map that it builds onboard, and navigates indoor environments with different complexities.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Sec. II defines the problem and constructs the candidate modes from local geometry, without learning. Sec. III presents the hierarchical policy and how it is trained from demonstrations. Sec. IV reports simulation and hardware experiments, and Sec. V concludes the paper.

1. A geometric module with no learned parameters that intersects tangent lines at the closest points of nearby obstacles, with one another and with the observation-window boundary, to enumerate a variable-size set of candidate modes from a single observation.

2. A hierarchical policy trained on demonstrations without mode annotations. A high-level policy selects a mode, conditioned on the goal and the previously selected mode; a low-level policy converts it into a continuous action and is also trained toward the mode’s direction.

3. An evaluation that separates what geometry and learning each contribute. Against four offline learning baselines, success rises from at most 43% and 20% in seen and unseen environments to 96.5% and 95.2%. A heuristic that uses the same modes without learning reaches only 79.2% and 66.7%, so the modes help but are not enough, and learning closes the gap with fewer mode switches and abrupt action changes.

4. Hardware experiments in which the simulation-trained policy runs on a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot without retraining and without tuning for each environment. The robot computes the modes from the occupancy map that it builds onboard, and navigates indoor environments with different complexities.

title: Smart Fusion for Adaptive Visual-IMU Weighting in cuVSLAM Sparse Bundle Adjustment
authors: Wonju Lee,Dara Molloy,Abhilash Nand Kumar,Onias Castelo,Petar Trslic,David Adley,Conor Ferguson,Hesam Rabeti
abstract:
In cuVSLAM, visual and inertial measurement unit (IMU) residuals are fused in sparse bundle adjustment (SBA) with a weighting fixed by pre-calibrated noise covariances, leaving no mechanism to adapt the visual-inertial balance at runtime.
We introduce a scalar α≥1\alpha\geq 1 that upscales the visual information matrix relative to the IMU preintegration constraint. Across the candidate set {1.0,2.0,5.0,10.0,20.0}\{1.0,2.0,5.0,10.0,20.0\}, the resulting trajectories form two empirical performance regimes. The imu-trust regime contains α∈{1,2}\alpha\in\{1,2\} near the calibrated baseline, while the vision-trust regime contains α∈{10,20}\alpha\in\{10,20\}. The intermediate value α=5\alpha=5 is treated as a transition case. Differences within each regime are small relative to those observed between the regimes.
This structure motivates reducing α\alpha-selection to a binary decision.
We train a lightweight Visual Quality Estimator (VQE), implemented as a multilayer perceptron with 914 trainable parameters. It maps a 10-dimensional visual quality feature vector assembled from statistics already maintained by the tracker to a per-SBA regime prediction.
The proposed method reduces mean RMSE APE by 27.7%27.7\% and by 14.9%14.9\% under leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) on EuRoC MAV and TUM-VI Room, respectively.
introduction:
Tightly-coupled visual-inertial odometry (VIO) fuses reprojection residuals and IMU preintegration constraints in a joint optimization [1, 2, 3].
The relative weight assigned to the two residual types affects the influence of each sensor modality on the optimized trajectory.
Increasing the visual weight under degraded observations can increase the effect of visual measurement errors. Conversely, a low visual weight may underuse geometric constraints when the observations are reliable.
An appropriate balance can depend on scene and motion conditions, yet most systems determine it during calibration and retain it during operation.

In the original cuVSLAM [1] formulation, visual and IMU residuals are combined under a fixed weighting derived from pre-calibrated noise covariances (corresponding to α=1.0\alpha\!=\!1.0), with no mechanism to adjust this balance at runtime.
This fixed weighting is appropriate when the calibrated noise model remains representative of the measurements. It may be less appropriate when scene conditions such as sparse texture or large depth variation increase reprojection error, or when motion blur and illumination changes temporarily degrade tracking.
Under these conditions, retaining the visual weight near its nominal calibrated level can limit the influence of degraded measurements, but the original formulation does not perform this adaptation.
Fig. 1 illustrates contrasting visual-quality conditions and the corresponding regimes selected by the greedy reference.

We present Smart Fusion, which introduces a global fusion weight α\alpha to scale the visual information matrix relative to the IMU constraint.
Smart Fusion uses a lightweight Visual Quality Estimator (VQE), implemented as an MLP, to map tracker-derived visual quality features to a regime prediction and set α\alpha before each SBA call.
The design is motivated by the empirical grouping observed over 𝒜={1.0,2.0,5.0,10.0,20.0}\mathcal{A}=\{1.0,2.0,5.0,10.0,20.0\}. The imu-trust regime contains α∈{1,2}\alpha\in\{1,2\} and the vision-trust regime contains α∈{10,20}\alpha\in\{10,20\}. On many evaluated sequences, within-regime differences are small relative to between-regime differences.
On EuRoC MH_01, the APE difference between the two regimes is 47%47\%, while the tested values within each regime produce similar APE. This observation motivates the binary formulation used in Smart Fusion (Fig. 3).
The VQE operates on a 10-dimensional visual quality feature vector assembled from statistics already maintained by the tracker.
Training labels are generated by a sequential non-causal greedy reference that evaluates final full-trajectory APE for each sequence segment.

We make two contributions.
First, we characterize the two empirical performance regimes observed when varying α\alpha in cuVSLAM SBA and formulate their selection as binary classification.
Second, we present Smart Fusion, a 914-parameter MLP that predicts a regime at each SBA call from tracker-internal visual quality features. The model is trained on sequential greedy-reference labels derived from trajectory APE.
Smart Fusion reduces mean RMSE APE by 27.7%27.7\% on EuRoC MAV and by 14.9%14.9\% on TUM-VI Room, both under leave-one-out cross-validation.

title: ObjDream: Guiding Vision-Language-Action Models with Object-Level Understanding and Future State Prediction
authors: Huailiang Ma,Yuxuan Li,Ziyi Zhao,Xinkai Wang,Mingyu Li,Xinyu Guo,Lifeng Zhu,Aiguo Song,Cewu Lu,Jianhua Sun
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions.
However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation.
As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations.
To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction.
ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels.
These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens.
In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations.
Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes. Project page.
introduction:
Robust robot policies must reliably manipulate objects in out-of-distribution environments, where their appearance, position, and surrounding context may differ from those in the training data.
VLA models have made rapid progress in generalist robot control by scaling pretrained vision-language backbones, robot data, and action decoders (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b).
To improve generalization, recent work has sought to preserve knowledge acquired during pretraining (Guo et al., 2026; Hancock et al., 2026), use high-level plans to guide low-level control (Li et al., 2025c), or anticipate scene changes through future visual or latent-state prediction (Zhang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026).
Although these approaches improve generalization to some extent, most VLA models still lack fine-grained object-level understanding. Their visual representations, inherited from VLMs, remain largely image-level, leaving the identity and spatial state of task-relevant objects entangled with appearance and surrounding context. This entanglement can weaken out-of-distribution robustness under shifts in object appearance, spatial layout, and background context.

Object-centric approaches offer a natural way to strengthen object-level understanding by explicitly representing individual objects and their properties.
Prior work incorporates object-aware visual representations to help policies focus on task-relevant regions (Zhu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025a; Liang et al., 2026).
Other methods extend object representations to relational reasoning (Hanyu et al., 2025), object-level memory (Chung et al., 2026), and long-horizon manipulation (Yang et al., 2026).
Although these approaches demonstrate the value of object-level representations, they often encode persistent object identity and time-varying object state in the same slot or token. As appearance and geometry change, this coupling can obscure persistent identity cues by mixing them with dynamic object state.
Recent dual-state slot models show that separating identity from dynamic appearance can improve temporal consistency in video perception by keeping identity information distinct from time-varying visual content (Tran et al., 2026).
Building on this insight, we investigate whether persistent identity references can be represented alongside dynamic object states and further used to guide VLM attention for language-conditioned manipulation.

Beyond modeling the current visual observation, predictive models support manipulation by anticipating future observations or object states (Ferraro et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Villar-Corrales and Behnke, 2025).
The choice of prediction target is important: reconstructing complete images requires modeling texture and background details that may be irrelevant to control (Zhang et al., 2025), while goal-image methods such as Goal-VLA introduce an additional synthesis stage before estimating the target object pose (Chen et al., 2025a).
In contrast, object-centric world models show that scene evolution can be modeled using compact object representations (Jeong et al., 2025).
Motivated by this trade-off, we use action-conditioned prediction of compact future object states, including geometry and visibility, as auxiliary supervision for VLA training without requiring future object state prediction at inference.

To this end, as illustrated in Fig. 1, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric vision-language-action framework for improving manipulation generalization. The architecture of ObjDream builds on a pretrained VLM backbone and integrates a spatio-temporal object encoder, an object-level forward dynamics module, and a flow-matching action expert. Specifically, the spatio-temporal object encoder transforms visual observations into structured object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These factorized object representations are mapped into the VLM hidden space and inserted into the token sequence, where identity-guided routing modulates attention to the corresponding object tokens. The forward dynamics module predicts future object states during training, providing auxiliary supervision for future object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. The object encoder is pretrained with automatically generated offline object supervision and frozen during VLA training. We optimize ObjDream with a joint objective combining action imitation with current and future object state supervision. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robot experiments demonstrate competitive manipulation performance across diverse scene perturbations.

The main contributions of this paper are listed below:

We present ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction to improve generalization under perturbations. ObjDream introduces a spatio-temporal object encoder that explicitly represents persistent object identity and dynamic object state through separate channels. The resulting representations are integrated into the VLM hidden space with a novel identity-guided routing mechanism for robust language-conditioned manipulation.

We introduce an action-conditioned object-level forward dynamics module for modeling object evolution during manipulation.
