title: Investigating Behavior Cloning from Few Demonstrations for Autonomous Driving based on Bird's-Eye View in Simulated Cities
authors: Eric Aislan Antonelo,Gustavo Claudio Karl Couto,Christian Möller,Pedro Henrique Fernandes
comment: . Accepted manuscript (author version) of the paper published in the proceedings of BRACIS 2024 (34th Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems, Belém, Brazil, 17-21 November 2024). Project page:this https URL
abstract:
This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird’s-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments.
BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors.
Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance.
Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC.
This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.
introduction:
Autonomous driving has traditionally been implemented using separate modules for perception, planning, and control, organized in a sequential pipeline [13, 21, 15, 16]. However, learning-based approaches have been gaining popularity as they attempt to address the complexities of autonomous driving in various scenarios, whether in simulation or real-world environments.

Most of these learning-based approaches rely on Behavior Cloning (BC), which employs supervised learning on a collection of expert demonstrations gathered offline [3, 19, 2, 6, 7]. For example, a human driver generates a set of input (observations) and corresponding desired output pairs.

Codevilla [6, 7] employed BC for autonomous driving in the CARLA simulator.
He collected a large dataset of human driving and augmented it using image processing techniques to train end-to-end policies conditioned on the desired route.
Further improvements in BC were introduced in [4], where a large deep ResNet network was used for feature extraction.
This approach combined data from cameras, LiDAR, and radar to create comprehensive feature maps.
The work also incorporated a probabilistic motion planner to account for uncertainties in the trajectory.

Couto [11] has shown results on behavior cloning on the CARLA simulator, but the agent did not have to respect traffic lights. In this work, we investigate an approach where the agent is able to navigate the city while respecting traffic lights, i.e., breaking when the light is red, and crossing the traffic light when it is green.
Only relying on regular BC to train an agent is not enough in a scenario with limited amount of training routes and where the agent needs to break at the red light and accelerate from stillness when light turns to green. To solve that, we employ a kernel density estimator [18] to estimate the actions density from the expert dataset. Then, the training samples are weighted in the BC loss function individually by setting the weight equal to the inverse of the actions’ density. In this way, we can account for the underrepresented actions in the expert set, i.e., those happening at traffic light transitions. This weighting is needed because we are considering only eight routes as training data.

Instead of learning directly from raw camera pixels as in [11, 12], the agent in this work has structured image inputs that are more abstract and meaningful to the navigation task.
To decouple feature representation from policy learning [14, 8] has its advantages as potentially easing up the learning task.
In our context, this decoupling is accomplished by using a mid-level representation of the vehicle’s raw camera images.
For example, Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) representations of the road ahead have been used as mid-level inputs for trajectory generation and motor control networks in [2] and [20], respectively.
In BEV representation, the camera scene is projected onto a top-down view, segmenting areas of interest, like vehicle lanes and sidewalks, into different colors [21].
By using BEV as input for the control policy, the learning process can focus on the navigation problem, leveraging a more abstract and simplified view of the road ahead. The policy here is represented by convolutional neural networks, mapping the BEV image to control actuators such as steering and acceleration.

Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC.
This weighted approach proved to be essential in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training.

In Section 2, we present
the bird’s-eye view representation employed as input to the convolutional neural network, the behavior cloning loss for the agent, and the kernel density estimation used to generate the weights per sample for the modified loss function. The agent architecture is presented in Section  3.
Finally, the experiments and conclusions are shown in Sections 4 and 5.

title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
authors: Shijun Shi,Zhe Liu,Zhi Hou,Yinan Chen,Tao Zhang,Kai Hu,Yong Liu,Jiangning Zhang
abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction.
However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection.
To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions.
Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk.
Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success.
Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. 
Project page:
https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) transfer visual and motion priors from video foundation models to robotic control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions [28, 41, 20, 18, 1].
Through video pretraining, these models acquire rich dynamic priors for modeling physically plausible future evolution.
However, robot control further requires determining which local evolution is appropriate under the current task and state. Given a fixed task-level instruction, the object to manipulate, the current interaction phase, and the local motion to execute are often not explicitly specified.
Such task-level conditioning leaves two related requirements to the executor.
First, a semantic grounding gap arises when categories, relations, or desired outcomes must be translated into concrete object interactions.
For example, Put the red things in the bin requires identifying the relevant objects and deciding how to manipulate them.
Second, a temporal granularity gap arises because a task instruction can remain unchanged as execution progresses through approach, alignment, grasp, transport, and release [22].
Descriptive video pretraining does not by itself establish how to resolve these decisions in closed-loop control.
Figure 1 illustrates the sensitivity of video predictions to language specificity, motivating a more explicit interface between task reasoning and motion execution.

To address these requirements, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to video–action generation through an atomic-motion language interface. Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) reasoner uses the task instruction and visual context to describe the next local interaction, including its target and relevant spatial grounding.
A WAM then predicts the corresponding future video and action chunk. The reasoner revises its description as execution changes the scene, while the task-level objective remains fixed.

Learning such an interface requires temporally aligned atomic-motion supervision, which is rarely available in existing robot demonstrations.
We therefore build an automatic pipeline that partitions the DROID dataset [17] into semantically coherent atomic motions. The interface further allows us to improve grasp learning. To this end, we enrich the corresponding descriptions with visible contact details.
The resulting labels supervise both motion selection and execution at the same atomic-motion granularity.

Nevertheless, supervised atomic-motion learning alone does not guarantee that the selected motion is compatible with the learned executor [11, 7]. Existing works introduce intermediate commands, subgoals, or semantic events to decouple high-level reasoning from low-level control [7, 13, 22], yet such intermediate decision policies are typically not optimized directly from the downstream executor. We therefore introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation through EG-GRPO, which closes the loop between the reasoner and the executor: the reasoner selects atomic motions, the executor produces physical outcomes, and these outcomes serve as the learning signal to improve atomic-motion selection.

Building on these advances, Atomic-WAM achieves competitive performance in an out-of-distribution real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab [39], with 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects high-level task reasoning to joint video–action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions.

We develop a scalable atomic-motion annotation pipeline that integrates displacement and gripper cues, multi-view evidence, and visual verification to provide temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision for both motion selection and execution.

We introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation via EG-GRPO, using physical outcomes from a fixed executor to improve atomic-motion selection through closed-loop optimization.

1. We introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects high-level task reasoning to joint video–action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions.

2. We develop a scalable atomic-motion annotation pipeline that integrates displacement and gripper cues, multi-view evidence, and visual verification to provide temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision for both motion selection and execution.

3. We introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation via EG-GRPO, using physical outcomes from a fixed executor to improve atomic-motion selection through closed-loop optimization.

title: Enabling Tidying Tasks in Robotic Vacuum Cleaners via a Geometry-Induced Self-Locking Deployable Linkage
authors: Eunseok Song,inwoong Kim,Sohee Lim,Taehyeong Kim,Yongkook Kim,Hyeontaek Lim,Hyungmin Son,Seungyong Hyung
abstract: Robotic vacuum cleaners must extend their functionality within tight limits on size, cost, and durability. Deployable linkages with few actuators meet these limits, but their backdrivability makes it difficult to hold a load-bearing posture without continuous motor torque. We introduce a two-stage deployable linkage that is self-locking, in the sense used for toggle and singularity-based linkages, through its own geometry: at full deployment an internal three-link subchain approaches a collinear, near-singular configuration where the input–output transmission ratio approaches zero, so that plate loads produce a small residual back-driving torque, absorbed by drive-train friction and a lightweight magnetic detent. A single actuator performs deployment and locking, a passive chassis-mounted trigger releases the lock for retraction, and a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height. We integrate the mechanism into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner and validate it through a 100-cycle repeatability test, a quasi-static load test in which the locked plate held 50 N with the motor de-energized, and 140 pushing-type tidying trials on seven household objects against a commercial arm-equipped vacuum robot under a documented protocol. We derive the analytical holding condition and discuss its limits as an intermediate design point between passive compliance and articulated manipulation.
introduction:
Robotic vacuum cleaners are among the most widely deployed domestic robots [1], and recent studies emphasize that they could be repurposed for simple assistance tasks during their substantial idle time [2, 3]. Any such extension, however, must fit within a commercial product’s fixed footprint, low-profile chassis, battery budget, and bill-of-materials cost. Adding a multi-DoF arm is possible, as recent products demonstrate, but it brings grasp planning, payload limits, and cost that are disproportionate to the simple pushing and containment actions that most floor-level tidying requires.

A low-cost alternative is a deployable linkage with few actuators. Such designs reduce actuation cost and, in the underactuated case, provide passive adaptability [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Their well-known weakness is the converse: a backdrivable linkage cannot hold a posture under load without continuous actuator torque, which wastes battery energy, and it may collapse or deviate when pushing against objects [10, 11]. The design challenge is therefore to obtain a rigid, load-bearing configuration on demand without adding locking hardware.

Three families of prior work are relevant. Locking devices add brakes, clutches, or ratchets to hold a joint once a configuration is reached [10, 12]; Hsu et al. [13], for instance, combine a differential with a friction brake so that an underactuated gripper locks automatically once a grasp is formed. Non-backdrivable transmissions such as worm gears or high-friction differentials achieve the same effect intrinsically [14]. These are true self-locking solutions, but they add mass, cost, and, for worm gears, efficiency loss in both directions.

Toggle, over-center, and bistable mechanisms exploit linkage geometry instead. A toggle clamp obtains a large mechanical advantage as two links approach collinearity and is held by driving the joint slightly past dead-center against a hard stop [15]; bistable compliant mechanisms store elastic energy to hold either of two states [16, 17]. The proposed mechanism belongs to this family but stops before dead-center (Section II-C): the plates must fold flush into a curved chassis, which leaves no room for a far-side hard stop or a preload spring.

Singularity-based stiffness is a classical principle of closed-loop kinematics: at an input singularity the output loses a degree of freedom and the mechanical advantage becomes unbounded [18, 19, 20]. Closest to our work, Jeon et al. [21] proposed a six-bar toggle linkage for a finger clamping unit that holds its clamping force at an over-singular configuration, using added linkage compliance. Our design differs in its stopping point (before, rather than past, the singular configuration, with no stored elastic energy), its object (a deployable sweeping plate), its topology (a six-bar whose ternary link is the output plate), its release strategy (passive, body-triggered, and kinematically decoupled from the load direction), and its integration into a commercial chassis without modification of the primary structural frame or the stowed external envelope. We claim no new mechanism-theoretic principle; the contribution is the design instantiation and its system-level validation.

Two simpler alternatives deserve comment. A fixed scoop cannot be stowed: it would enlarge the footprint, block the bumper and cliff sensors, prevent docking, and obstruct navigation. A single-stage two-finger gripper can be stowed, but its sweep width is limited to the plate length, whereas the two-stage linkage roughly doubles the deployed width from the same stowed length; it must hold objects against lateral loads with continuous motor torque or a brake, whereas the proposed linkage holds with the motor de-energized; and a straight plate cannot conform to the curved front housing when stowed. The proposed linkage is the option that satisfies stowability, sweep width, and zero-torque holding simultaneously within the existing chassis volume.

A compact two-stage deployable linkage, driven by a single deployment actuator, that transitions between backdrivable motion and a load-supporting near-singular configuration, integrated into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner without modifying its primary structural frame, its stowed external envelope, or its navigation pipeline (a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height).

A compact two-stage deployable linkage, driven by a single deployment actuator, that transitions between backdrivable motion and a load-supporting near-singular configuration, integrated into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner without modifying its primary structural frame, its stowed external envelope, or its navigation pipeline (a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height).

A kinematic and static analysis of the locking condition, consisting of the loop-closure model, the scalar input–output Jacobian, and an analytical holding condition that identifies what resists the residual back-driving torque and how the load direction and manufacturing tolerances enter.

Experimental validation of deployment repeatability (100 cycles), zero-torque load holding (50 N, in-plane), and pushing-type tidying on seven household objects, with a documented comparison protocol against a commercial arm-equipped vacuum robot.

title: Tactile-Guided Robot Learning: From Representation Learning to Foundation Models
authors: Kiyanoush Nazari,Luchen Li,Haoshu Fang,Nima Fazeli,Zhibin Li,Fumiya Iida,Thomas George Thuruthel
abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at paper web page.
introduction:
Dexterous manipulation remains a major challenge in developing robots capable of human-level adaptability in unstructured environments (Lepora, 2024). Despite substantial advances in perception, planning, control, locomotion, and embodied AI, robots still struggle with everyday contact-rich tasks such as precision insertion, deformable-object manipulation, and assembly under uncertainty (Billard and Kragic, 2019). Unlike more structured robotic tasks, manipulation requires continuous regulation of physical interactions among the robot, objects, and environment (Cui and Trinkle, 2021). Successful manipulation therefore depends not only on detecting contact, but on estimating and regulating evolving contact locations, forces, friction, compliance, and interaction dynamics, often across multiple simultaneous contacts. These quantities are difficult to infer reliably from vision alone, particularly under occlusion and during fine manipulation, making tactile perception and tactile-guided control essential for robust and dexterous interaction (Li et al., 2025a).

Recent tactile sensors can capture high-resolution contact geometry, force distributions, deformation, and slip (Team, 2026; Zhao et al., 2025b), while advances in imitation learning (Tsuji et al., 2025), reinforcement learning (Kim et al., 2026), diffusion policies (Chi et al., 2025), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Ma et al., 2026b), and embodied AI (Feng et al., 2026b) have substantially expanded robots’ ability to learn complex manipulation skills from data (O’Neill et al., 2024). Yet these developments remain only partially connected, where modern policies are still predominantly vision-centric and often treat touch as auxiliary information (Comanici et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024). This limits their ability to reason about physical interactions in tasks where contact dynamics, rather than visual appearance alone, determine successful execution.

The role of touch in robot learning is consequently shifting from estimating low-level quantities such as contact, slip, force, and object properties (Howe, 1993) toward providing physically grounded information throughout the learning and control pipeline. Tactile observations now support representation learning (Higuera et al., 2024), multimodal policy learning, physical reasoning (Huang et al., 2025b; Morissette et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024), adaptive decision making, and embodied world modeling (Cheng et al., 2026). This shift reframes the central question from how robots can sense touch to how robots can learn from and act through touch.

Despite rapidly growing work across tactile sensing, robot learning, computer vision, and embodied AI, this literature remains fragmented. Existing surveys largely emphasize sensor hardware, sensing principles, classical tactile perception, or earlier tactile-guided manipulation and control (Li et al., 2020; Kroemer et al., 2021). Many also predate recent developments in foundation models and VLA systems and therefore do not capture the emerging role of touch within modern learning-based manipulation (Lepora, 2024; Jin et al., 2023; Meribout et al., 2024; Mandil et al., 2023; Jahanshahi and others, 2025; Cho et al., 2024; Yu and Liu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Xie and Correll, 2025; Hu et al., 2023; Yao and Wang, 2024; Xu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024b; Man et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Kroemer et al., 2021). A unified learning-centric account of how tactile information contributes across representation, policy learning, embodied reasoning, and generalization is therefore still lacking.

To address this gap, we organize the review according to the functional role of tactile information within learning-based manipulation (Fig. 1). We examine six research questions. RQ1 considers how tactile observations are represented, encoded, and fused with other modalities, covering self-supervised (Dave et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025b), multimodal (Cheng et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026a), and cross-modal representation learning (Fu et al., 2024a). RQ2 examines how touch conditions action generation through imitation learning (Funk et al., 2026), reinforcement learning (Miller et al., 2026), diffusion policies (Xue et al., 2025), and multimodal policy architectures. RQ3 investigates tactile-informed foundation and world models, including tactile-enhanced VLAs (Hao et al., 2026), multimodal world models (Zhang et al., 2026d), and foundation controllers (You et al., 2026), where touch supports physically grounded reasoning and planning. RQ4 considers predictive and adaptive tactile control, where tactile feedback supports interaction-state estimation, feedback regulation, contact prediction, online optimization, and adaptation under uncertain physical interactions (Yin et al., 2025a; Xu and She, 2024; Zhao et al., 2026b; Nazari et al., 2025; Nazari et al., 2023). RQ5 evaluates generalization beyond training conditions across objects, tasks, sensors, robot embodiments, environments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Finally, RQ6 synthesizes these developments to identify the remaining challenges and research directions toward scalable tactile foundation models, general-purpose manipulation, and lifelong tactile learning.

title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
authors: Hongyu Ding,Kanyu Xu,Mingjia Chen,Zixuan Chen,Jieqi Shi,Jing Huo,Yifan Zhang,Yang Gao
abstract:
Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots.
Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description.
Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing.
To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3.
A team of KK agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of MM object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description.
HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation–assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL.
We further contribute two baselines.
HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis.
Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16–27% SR, while our baselines reach 38–41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes.
Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team.
Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
introduction:
Consider a home with several robots and a resident who asks them to find a nightstand, the couch in a photo, and “the plant by the sliding glass door”.
Nothing in this request is exotic.
Rapid progress in AI agents and robot hardware places such teams within the near future, and the request has the shape everyday instructions take: several goals at once, each given in whatever form is at hand.
What is missing is a way to measure how well a team handles it, since the goals have to be divided, recognized under three different specifications, and tracked jointly.

Standing in that future and looking back at the present, the landscape of navigation benchmarks is fragmented, as Table I summarizes.
Single-agent object-goal navigation asks for one instance of one category, recently from an open vocabulary [1, 6]. Multi-object variants give one agent several category goals [3, 10]. Multi-modal variants mix category, image, and language goals, but present them sequentially and score each sub-task on its own [7].
Multi-robot semantic navigation evaluates teams, but on a single goal of a single modality, and grants success as soon as any robot arrives [11, 12].
Recent systems combine all three [13, 14], yet they are evaluated on episodes borrowed from single-agent benchmarks with per-sub-task scoring.
No benchmark defines the joint task, generates episodes for it, or measures the team as a whole.

The intersection is not a concatenation of its parts.
Allocation happens under partial observability, since who should pursue which goal depends on heterogeneous evidence that arrives as the map grows. Verification becomes instance-level, since an image or a description refers to one specific object. Completion is joint, since the natural cost is the team makespan, so an idle or redundant robot is not free.

To fill this gap, we present HM3D-M3, a benchmark for Multi-agent, Multi-modal, Multi-object goal navigation in photorealistic scans of real buildings [15, 16], illustrated in Fig. 1.
An episode places KK agents at distributed, jointly reachable start positions and gives the team an unordered set of MM goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories.
Each goal is specified as a category (ON), an instance image (IIN), or an instance description (TN).
A goal counts as found when an agent declares it while standing within 1 m of that instance, and every episode stores the oracle team makespan d∗d^{\ast} for budgeting and normalization.

We further contribute two baselines, one trained and one training-free.
HiGA, short for Hierarchical Goal Assigner, is a trained method in which a transformer reads the shared map, agent poses, and per-goal CLIP heat maps, assigns goals to agents, and hands each assignment to a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy [6]. It is trained with behavior cloning and DAgger [17] from an oracle assigner.
LaViRA-M3 is a training-free method that extends the vision-language model (VLM) navigation agent of LaViRA [18, 19] to a team coordinated only through a shared map, a shared goal board, and shared natural-language progress analysis.
We also adapt four existing multi-robot and zero-shot methods [20, 21, 11, 13] to the benchmark.

The results expose a task that is far from solved, with adapted methods at 16–27% SR, HiGA at 37.9%, and LaViRA-M3 at 41.0%, and two baselines with complementary strengths.
HiGA is the strongest on category goals but weak on image goals and inefficient, whereas LaViRA-M3 is the strongest on image and text goals and the most efficient.
Their failures differ, since LaViRA-M3 mostly declares a goal from the wrong place, whereas HiGA mostly fails to detect or match it.

Our contributions are:

HM3D-M3, the first benchmark for multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation, with a standardized episode generator, a validation set of 1,000 episodes and 3,926 goals on 36 held-out scenes, a training set of 100K observation–assignment samples on disjoint scenes, and team-level metrics.

Two baselines, the trained HiGA and the training-free LaViRA-M3, plus adaptations of four existing methods, evaluated with ablations, scaling studies over KK and MM, and a per-goal failure attribution.

A real-world deployment of LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous team of three robots running local VLMs, which complete mixed-modality goal sets in an office through the same coordination channels as in simulation.

title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
authors: Bingao Chen,Lihan Zha,C. Karen Liu,Guy Tevet
abstract:
We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector’s surroundings.
External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost.
FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on π0.5\pi_{0.5} in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.870.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.177.1%, versus 52.152.1% for the wrist-equipped π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
introduction:
Recent progress in robot manipulation has been driven by large models trained on diverse robot datasets [1, 2, 3]. Most of these models take a wrist camera as input [4, 5, 6], which provides close-up observations that learned policies often depend on [7, 8, 9]. This close-up view comes at the cost of scene coverage: the camera moves with the end-effector, so distant targets and surrounding context can lie outside its view, more so when manipulation spans a larger workspace or involves a mobile robot. The wrist camera also adds hardware and creates an observation mismatch with human demonstrations recorded without a wrist view [10, 11]. Can a policy get the close-up detail it needs from external observations alone, so that the robot no longer needs a wrist camera?

External cameras record high-resolution images, but resizing a whole scene to the policy’s low input resolution reduces the detail available for the gripper and object, and uniformly increasing the input resolution spends computation on background regions. External views also lack a consistent geometric frame: a wrist camera maintains a fixed pose relative to the end-effector, whereas an external view depends on the camera’s placement relative to the robot. Prior work reports lower success for policies learned without wrist observations [12, 7]. We observe a similar gap on our four real-world task suites: π0.5\pi_{0.5} post-trained on two external RGB views alone achieves 25.025.0% success, compared with 52.152.1% with the wrist view.

Existing approaches obtain close-up observations through additional sensing or constructed viewpoints. Generative methods synthesize wrist images from external observations [13, 14]. Others render virtual views from 3D scene representations [15, 16], or move a camera on a dedicated arm or neck [17, 18]. Human-gaze-guided foveation is closer to our goal of selecting detail within an existing image [19, 20], but relies on gaze recorded during data collection. We instead learn where to crop from existing robot demonstrations, supervised by their interaction annotations.

Human vision allocates detail selectively. Peripheral vision provides scene context while central vision resolves the detail needed to grasp an object [21], and gaze reaches the next contact point before the hand does [22]. We take the same approach in FoveaVLA, which replaces the wrist camera with a learned foveation action that selects where to look next. Cropping the predicted interaction region from the original-resolution image and resizing it to the same 224×224224\times 224 encoder input devotes many more pixels to the gripper and object than the resized full view does. Feeding this crop alongside the full view gives the policy both the close-up detail it needs for manipulation and the layout of the whole scene.

We build FoveaVLA on π0.5\pi_{0.5} [23]. From the current observation, it generates a robot action chunk and predicts one bounding box per external view for the interaction region at the next policy query. The predicted boxes crop the newly captured images, and the crops are added to the next policy input alongside the full views. We derive supervision from RoboInter annotations [24] on DROID demonstrations [5], constructing a bounding box around the components involved in each annotated skill, such as the gripper, object, and target region. Annotations at the next query provide targets for future-box prediction. We instantiate the method as FoveaVLA-Single and FoveaVLA-Dual, using one and two external stereo cameras, respectively, with full and foveal RGB images and aligned depth estimated from each stereo pair. Both operate without a wrist camera; Dual adds a second external viewpoint to the same foveation mechanism.

We post-train both configurations on DROID and evaluate them on the four real-world task suites. FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.870.8% success using one external RGB-D view, exceeding the wrist-equipped π0.5\pi_{0.5} at 52.152.1%, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.177.1%. The largest gains are on pick-and-place with distractors, where Single raises success from 25.025.0% to 58.358.3%, and on moving far objects, from 41.741.7% to 75.075.0%. On MolmoSpaces [25], FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 22.422.4% average zero-shot success versus 17.817.8% for π0.5\pi_{0.5}-DROID [26], outperforming it on seven of nine tasks.

title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
authors: Ziyan Liu,Jiting Liu,Weihong Zhong,Wenda Yu,Yeqiu Chen,Jason Li,Xiaojiang Peng,Shuyuan Hu,Kai Wang,Bo Zhao
abstract:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision–language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct11
1
“Morph,” rooted in Greek morphē (“form”), means “to transform.”, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision–language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy’s computational dependency: vision–language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
introduction:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments, operations, and interactions (Driess et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025). This expansion brings together heterogeneous perceptual and control demands within a shared model. Such diversity arises not only across tasks but also within a single interaction: placing an object in a tray involves approaching it, establishing contact, transporting it, and positioning it precisely. These operations require different visual cues and control behaviors, often under an unchanged instruction. As environmental and operational coverage expands, a central challenge is how a shared model can effectively accommodate these heterogeneous demands.

Vision–language–action (VLA) models provide a promising foundation by combining pretrained multimodal representations with action prediction (Brohan et al., 2023a; Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). However, conventional VLA policies execute diverse interactions using a shared, static parameter configuration. Context changes their activations and predicted actions, but their effective weights remain fixed, including after full fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation (Hu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2025a). Different operations must therefore be learned through shared parameters, even when their training signals favor competing updates—a source of interference in joint optimization (Yu et al., 2020a). This raises the question of how effectively shared parameters reconcile the demands of different operations.

We investigate this question through operation-level diagnostics using demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026). At a common policy checkpoint, we examine gradient alignment, the effect of a single update on other tasks, and the contributions of individual parameter groups. The diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both the vision–language and action modules. Every measured source-improving update also increases loss on batches from other tasks, while opposing parameter-group contributions can cancel within a module. These findings expose local adaptation trade-offs in shared parameter space. They motivate a shared parameter-generation mechanism whose outputs vary with the interaction context.

To address this challenge, we introduce MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that enables robot policies to morph with changing interaction contexts (Figure 1). MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank parameter updates for the vision–language and action modules, allowing a shared policy to adjust its effective weights to the current interaction. Because vision–language adaptation changes the representations used for control, MorphAct couples the two generators by conditioning action-side parameter generation on the adapted representations. Both generators learn jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. Low-rank factors provide an efficient implementation of these contextual updates.

We evaluate MorphAct on X-VLA, π0\pi_{0}, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Zheng et al., 2026; Black et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) using LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020b), comparing each backbone’s baseline with MorphAct. Across the three backbones, MorphAct improves Meta-World average success by 7.57–16.30%; on LIBERO, X-VLA, π0\pi_{0}, and π0.5\pi_{0.5} gain 4.15%, 2.50%, and 1.75%, respectively. Real-world evaluation with π0.5\pi_{0.5} further yields gains of 8.00–14.00% across four manipulation tasks. Controlled X-VLA ablations on LIBERO show that fixed generation conditions, single-module adaptation, and action-side generation conditioned on pre-adaptation features each reduce mean success. These results support contextual parameterization and representation coupling for accommodating diverse manipulation demands.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We identify parameter conflicts as a challenge to scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions through operation-level diagnostic experiments. (2) We introduce MorphAct, whose representation-coupled generators produce context-dependent vision–language and action parameter updates and learn jointly through the native action objective. (3) We demonstrate success gains on three VLA backbones, two simulation benchmarks, and four real-world tasks, with ablations supporting contextual generation and representation coupling.

title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
authors: Baekseung Kim,Junhoo Lee,Sohyeon Hong,Suhyun Jeon,Minkyu Kim,Seungyeon Kim,Donghoon Han,Nojun Kwak
abstract:
World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs
substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs.
Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action
generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail
required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines
instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens
during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame
and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based
phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation
during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance
degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world
manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups.
At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of
1.191.19–1.27×1.27\times while improving task success rates.
At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.291.29–1.33×1.33\times average
speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success
rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
introduction:
Extending foundation models to physical environments, particularly robotic manipulation, has recently attracted significant attention, due to their potential to enable robots to generalize across diverse tasks and environments. Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent a prominent approach (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024), while world action models (WAMs) based on video diffusion models have emerged to better capture scene geometry, physical dynamics, and future state evolution (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026b). However, deploying these models on real robots requires not only high task performance but also low-latency inference (Black et al., 2025). Since robotic manipulation requires repeated action generation throughout a task, inference latency accumulates across policy queries, delaying action execution and substantially increasing the overall task completion time. This problem is especially critical for WAMs due to the substantial computational overhead of video diffusion models, making efficient inference essential for their practical use in real-world manipulation.

WAMs jointly generate robot actions and multiple future frames, introducing dense spatiotemporal token grids that account for a substantial portion of the computation in the video diffusion backbone. While VLAs address a similar bottleneck by pruning observation tokens (Yang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025), directly pruning future-frame tokens is difficult because they constitute the model outputs in conventional video diffusion models and support action generation through future-state prediction in WAMs. Video diffusion acceleration therefore modifies attention masks (Xi et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025), but the cost of determining effective masks can offset the gains in few-step WAMs. Existing WAM methods instead reduce denoising steps (Ye et al., 2026b) or redesign the model to bypass future generation (Yuan et al., 2026); the former retains the per-step token burden, whereas the latter requires retraining. Consequently, existing WAM acceleration methods do not directly reduce future-frame tokens without additional training.

We propose CF-Prune (Complementary Future token Pruning), a training-free method for pruning future-frame tokens in WAMs. Our key insight is that, while video diffusion models are designed to generate high-fidelity videos, WAMs use future-frame prediction primarily as an intermediate reference for action generation. Therefore, as
illustrated in Figure 1, future representations must preserve task-relevant semantics and dynamics but need not retain every fine-grained visual detail. Allocating a dense grid of tokens to future frames is thus unnecessarily redundant for action prediction, motivating selective pruning that retains only the tokens needed for action generation without retraining. Realizing this potential requires identifying which future-frame tokens matter for action prediction early in denoising, when their representations remain highly noisy and their relevance is not yet explicit.

Specifically, CF-Prune constructs an attention-based pruning criterion by analyzing the concentration of visual information with respect to action and instruction tokens, enabling effective token selection even when the action and future-frame latents remain highly noisy. Using only the initial forward pass, CF-Prune identifies redundant tokens early in the denoising process, thereby maximizing pruning efficiency while demonstrating that the internal representations available at the beginning of generation are sufficient to select future-frame tokens needed for action generation. Finally, CF-Prune introduces a phase identification mechanism that exploits entropy differences across camera views and temporal positions within the action sequence to identify precision phases and selectively relax pruning, mitigating performance degradation.
Across RoboLab (Yang et al., 2026), RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), and real-world tasks, CF-Prune achieves consistent efficiency gains at a 35% pruning ratio: a 1.23×1.23\times speedup with a 1.3 percentage point success rate gain on RoboLab, a 1.19×1.19\times speedup with a 4.0 percentage point gain on RoboCasa, and a 1.27×1.27\times speedup with a 5.4 percentage point gain in real-world experiments. At a 50% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves at least a 1.29×1.29\times average inference speedup across both simulation benchmarks, while keeping success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the dense baseline.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We reconsider the auxiliary role of future frames in WAMs and formulate token pruning from the perspective of action prediction, exposing redundancy that is not considered in conventional video generation.

We propose CF-Prune, a framework requiring no additional training that identifies redundant future frame tokens from noisy initial latents using their information concentration with respect to action and instruction tokens, while selectively relaxing pruning based on cross-view and temporal attention-entropy contrasts.

We extensively evaluate CF-Prune on the RoboLab and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in inference efficiency while preserving manipulation performance.

We propose CF-Prune, a framework requiring no additional training that identifies redundant future frame tokens from noisy initial latents using their information concentration with respect to action and instruction tokens, while selectively relaxing pruning based on cross-view and temporal attention-entropy contrasts.

title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
authors: Xiangyi Wei,Hanzhe Yao,Jingwen Shang,Zhenhong Wu,Yang Li,Changbo Wang
abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, limits capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initiation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and heterogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.

title: Active Perception of Upper-Limb Functional Mobility through Human-Robot Handovers
authors: Francesco Semeraro,Marta Lagomarsino,Alberto Ranavolo,Arash Ajoudani
abstract: The reintegration of people in the workplace after an upper-limb injury is often a long process. Collaborative robots and humanoids operating in shared workspaces must adapt their behaviour to the physical capabilities of their human partners. Achieving this requires robots to autonomously estimate task-relevant human mobility during interaction, without relying on external clinical assessments. In this work, we formulate the estimation of upper-limb functional mobility as an active perception problem. We model task-available upper-limb functional ranges of motion through impairment coefficients that parameterise reductions of healthy joint limits, and integrate this representation into a human model used by the robot during interaction. Based on this formulation, we propose an online active perception pipeline in which the robot actively probes the user through repeated handover requests while progressively updating a Bayesian belief over the impairment coefficients. This enables the robot to continuously refine its internal model of the user’s joint-level capabilities through interaction rather than passive observation. The proposed framework was evaluated through simulation studies and a proof-of-concept physical validation with a robotic platform and enacted human impairments, demonstrating that the pipeline can accurately recover the impairment coefficients during real human-robot handovers.

title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation

introduction:
Human demonstrations provide behavioral supervision for manipulation policy learning.
Teleoperation Wu et al. (2024); Zhao et al. (2023) collects demonstrations directly on the target robot but requires robot hardware, limiting data scale and diversity.
Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) Chi et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2024) has therefore been widely explored for scalable demonstration acquisition in diverse real-world environments.
However, collecting contact-rich manipulation demonstrations with these handheld interfaces remains challenging because a lack of intuitive force feedback can limit human operators’ ability to perceive object interaction forces and adjust actions in real time Liu et al. (2025c), resulting in more failed attempts and lower collection efficiency Wu et al. (2025).

A key factor is the interface’s mechanical design, which determines how directly interaction forces are transmitted to the human operator.
Common handheld interfaces in robot-free demonstration collection employ trigger-driven rack-and-pinion mechanisms Chi et al. (2024); Choi et al. (2026).
These mechanisms transmit object interaction forces through multiple intermediate components, where mechanical backlash weakens force feedback Wu et al. (2025).
Alternatively, interfaces with active force feedback Zhang et al. (2025); Citron et al. (2026) combine force sensing with motorized actuation to convey interaction forces to operators, requiring additional sensing hardware, actuators, and feedback control.
These limitations motivate a mechanical interface that provides intuitive force feedback for real-time action adjustment during contact-rich demonstration collection without additional force sensors or active feedback actuators.

Inspired by the comfortable handling and intuitive force feedback of scissors, we design a scissor-shaped mechanism to support contact-rich demonstration collection.
Each handle forms a rigid assembly with its sector gear and actuation link, preserving a direct mechanical path for force transmission without additional transmission stages between the handle and the actuation link.
To match the target parallel gripper, the two identical sector gears mesh with each other, constraining the two branches to open and close symmetrically.

Building on this mechanical design, we introduce FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface, together with a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations.
Through calibration and mapping, the system further converts sensor measurements of FOMI’s pose changes and gripper opening into robot end-effector pose targets and gripper width commands, enabling teleoperated demonstration collection with the same interface.

Mechanical design for intuitive force feedback:
We design a scissor-shaped interface in which each handle is rigidly integrated with its actuation link, providing a direct force path for intuitive force feedback during robot-free collection, with meshing sector gears matching the symmetric motion of parallel grippers.

title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
authors: Qisen Ma,Yixiang Chen,Yuan Xu,Peiyan Li,Jiabing Yang,Kai Wang,Jianhua Yang,Jianlou Si,Jun Huang,Jing Liu,Nianfeng Liu,Yan Huang,Liang Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025) have achieved notable success in robotic manipulation by adapting pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to continuous physical control.
However, standard VLAs mainly predict actions from the current observation.
Without modeling how the scene evolves under robot interaction, they struggle in long-horizon tasks and fail to adapt to distribution shifts or dynamic environments (Yang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026b; Lyu et al., 2026).

To overcome this limitation, a promising direction is to integrate world models into VLAs to anticipate world dynamics (Cen et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025b).
By incorporating world dynamics, such models have demonstrated improved long-horizon execution (Chen et al., 2026a), dynamic manipulation (Fang et al., 2026), environmental robustness (Sun et al., 2026), and sample efficiency (Chen et al., 2026b).
Despite these empirical successes, existing studies adopt heterogeneous world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones.
Specifically, they combine representations ranging from pixel details to semantic latents with designs such as implicit alignment and explicit conditioning across different VLA backbones (Zheng et al., 2025b; Lv et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026).
Consequently, the true sources of empirical gains remain obscured, leaving it unclear which design choices fundamentally matter when integrating world modeling into VLAs.

Among these challenges, four core questions stand out:
(1) World Representation: Is there a universally optimal world representation for robot policy learning, or is representation effectiveness fundamentally coupled with the integration paradigm?
(2) Integration Paradigm: What are the performance trade-offs among different integration paradigms, and is coupled or decoupled world modeling more effective?
(3) Backbone Generalization: Do world modeling integration paradigms remain effective across policy backbones, spanning models without robot pretraining and pretrained foundation VLAs?
(4) Comprehensive Performance: How do different world modeling integration paradigms perform under diverse task conditions?

In this work, we present the first systematic, controlled empirical investigation of world modeling in VLA policies, as shown in Figure 1.
To isolate world modeling choices, we conduct our study under a unified pipeline with a shared policy backbone and training protocol within each comparison, systematically addressing the four core questions:
First, to answer World Representation, we examine diverse world representations spanning pixel details (ImageVAE (Tian et al., 2024), WanVAE (Wan et al., 2025)), 2D semantics (DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025), SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023)), 3D spatial geometry (VGGT (Wang et al., 2025)), and spatiotemporal video dynamics (V-JEPA 2.1 (Mur-Labadia et al., 2026)).
Second, to answer Integration Paradigm, we formalize existing architectures into four integration paradigms defined by how world dynamics are conditioned on and decoupled from the policy, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
We instantiate these paradigms as representative designs within our unified framework.
Third, to answer Backbone Generalization, we benchmark world modeling paradigms across representative policy backbones spanning a standard VLM backbone (Qwen3-VL-2B (Bai et al., 2025)) and a dedicated robot foundation VLA (π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Intelligence et al., 2025)).
Finally, to answer Comprehensive Performance, we evaluate these integration paradigms across diverse settings spanning in-domain and out-of-domain distributions, long horizons, dynamic objects, few-shot data, as well as real-world experiments.

Our extensive experiments yield four primary findings corresponding to our core questions:
(1) World Representation:
No single world representation is universally optimal.
Pixel-level features do not consistently translate in-domain gains into OOD robustness, while geometric and spatiotemporal representations are sensitive to the integration paradigm. DINOv3 and SigLIP provide consistent gains across paradigms.
(2) Integration Paradigm:
No paradigm dominates across all settings, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness.
Implicit Future Alignment is lightweight but less effective on dynamic tasks, while Explicit Future Query is more task-dependent.
The External World Predictor achieves the best low-data in-domain performance.
(3) Backbone Generalization:
Integration effectiveness differs across policy backbones.
World modeling generally benefits policies built on standard VLMs, whereas decoupled designs offer substantially better compatibility when adapting pretrained foundation VLAs.
(4) Comprehensive Performance:
World modeling provides clear gains over action-only policies, particularly on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
We believe these systematic findings provide actionable design principles for integrating world modeling into VLA systems.

title: Learning from Demonstrations meets Symbolic Control - A Supervisory Control Architecture for Formal Certification of Learned Motion
authors: Ashok Kumar,Mahathi Anand,Angela Schoellig,Abdalla Swikir
abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot’s dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.
introduction:
lfd (lfd) is an efficient paradigm to teach robots highly complex tasks directly through demonstrations [1]. A popular approach is the  ds (ds) method [2], where the demonstrations are encoded via a dynamical system. Here, a vector field governs the velocity of the desired trajectories and issues commands to the low-level controller to track. The key advantage is generalizability: the ds is a time-invariant state-feedback policy over the whole domain, it can be evaluated from any state, and can quickly react to runtime perturbations. Nevertheless, additional properties such as stability and safety need to be imposed in order to ensure goal reaching, robustness to perturbations, and collision avoidance. Moreover, the learned vector field is not guaranteed to generate feasible trajectories that satisfy velocity and actuator constraints, as these limits are only imposed implicitly through robot demonstrations, if at all.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for safe and robust realization of learned trajectories via symbolic supervisory control. Agnostic to the method used to learn the ds, our framework operates at the control layer as a certified supervisor that verifies the safety, reachability, and realizability of the resulting motion at runtime. When the nominal tracking controller threatens these guarantees, a symbolic controller intervenes to produce a certified input respecting actuator limits. The resulting motion is guaranteed to reach the goal set within finite time, remain safe against (possibly dynamic) obstacles, and recover from deviations once the environment is clear.

Formal stability and safety guarantees on learned dynamical systems are typically certified through certificate construction — Lyapunov functions for asymptotic stability  [3] and barrier functions for safety [4]. A common strategy is to synthesize these certificates concurrently with the ds [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The synthesis strategy, and subsequently, the optimization tool used, vastly depends on the characterization of the ds. For instance, [5, 6, 7] learn a  lpv (lpv) dynamical system, and use conservative quadratic Lyapunov candidates for certifying stability. On the other hand, [8] learn polynomial dynamical systems along with polynomial certificates using sum-of-squares [10] tools, while [9] propose neural network characterizations for the system and certificates.

Independent of parameterization, certificate search suffers from a fundamental trade-off between the expressiveness of the learned dynamics and the tractability of the underlying optimization. An alternative is to modify the learned stable dynamics at runtime [11, 12], eliminating certificate optimization for collision avoidance, or to pass the generated velocity through a safety filter via a quadratic program with hand-crafted control Lyapunov and barrier functions [13]. Our approach departs from these in three respects. First, rather than modifying the learned dynamics, we operate one layer below it, designing control inputs that track the ds closely and intervening only when obstacles block the desired path. Additionally, physical realizability is guaranteed through velocity and actuator constraint satisfaction. Second, while Lyapunov-based approaches guarantee only asymptotic convergence, we guarantee reachability of a neighborhood of the goal within finite time. Finally, our synthesis does not require any certificate functions, only finite state abstractions of the model.

Our work also borrows from symbolic control, where finite approximations of control systems inform controller synthesis through simple fixed point computations [14, 15]. This has been applied primarily in the context of motion planning for mobile robots and autonomous vehicles [16, 17].
While [18] addresses motion planning for manipulators via symbolic control, we utilize symbolic control strategies for safely modifying controllers obtained via lfd.

The contributions of our paper are as follows:

Starting with a ds learned from demonstrations with a preferred method, we propose a novel supervisory architecture that functions in the control layer and (i) monitors the safety of the reference paths generated by the ds, and (ii) modifies it so the robot can still reach a small neighborhood of the goal, while ensuring collision avoidance against dynamic obstacles. The designed methodology avoids computation of certificate functions while retaining formal guarantees of reachability and safety under standard assumptions on the real world (c.f. Section III-C).

Our architecture relies on finite state abstractions on the manipulator’s operational space dynamics through sample-perturbed-system representations. Based on the discretized system dynamics and regions of interest (i.e, goals and obstacles), a symbolic controller is constructed as a fail-safe certified backup plan. Synthesis is performed either offline, suited for static obstacles, or online at low frequencies for dynamic obstacles.

At runtime, a nominal tracking controller is designed to faithfully follow the paths generated by the ds, and ensures convergence to the desired paths in the presence of deviations. A certified control input, computed to provide less-conservative modifications based on a ranking scheme, overrides the nominal control action when it is rendered to be unsafe or not goal-reaching. A full overview of our approach is presented in Figure 1.

We validate our approach through several simulation experiments (MuJoCo) for learning handwriting motion with static and obstacles, and particularly compare the performance of approach against the closely related-work [13]. The results show that our approach is competitive with SoA and excels with high task success rates and formal guarantees. Additionally, our robot experiments on dynamic 3​D3D environments emphasize the flexibility of our approach while demonstrating that formal guarantees hold even in the real world.

title: Design and Characterization of a Unified Continuum Robot Actuation Platform
authors: Yunti Xu,Aedan Mangan,Miheer Potdar,Alex Lu,Tania K. Morimoto
abstract: Continuum robots enable dexterous access to confined spaces in applications such as minimally invasive surgery and industrial inspection. However, their actuation systems are often custom-designed for specific robot architectures and tasks, limiting reuse across publications, institutions, and applications. This paper presents a unified actuation platform that decouples actuation hardware and software from continuum robot design. The platform provides modular actuation across continuum robot classes, scales to a large number of degrees of freedom (DOFs), and integrates with conventional serial manipulators for hybrid architectures. We validate the platform on an open-sourced surgical robotic system and experimentally characterize the actuation modules, achieving sub-millimeter translational accuracy and less than 5∘5^{\circ} rotational error over ranges of 3030 mm and 180∘180^{\circ}, respectively. We further demonstrate the platform in two surgical use cases: teleoperation of a continuum camera in a constrained environment and bimanual manipulation using 2.532.53 mm concentric-tube-robot-based forceps alongside a conventional wristed instrument. All hardware designs and ROS-based software are open-sourced to facilitate reuse and further research in continuum and surgical robotics.
introduction:
Continuum robots, with their continuously bending structures and small size, are well suited for navigating constrained and cluttered environments [1], making them promising platforms for minimally invasive surgery and industrial inspection [1, 2]. However, researchers typically develop custom, proprietary actuation hardware and software for specific robot designs and tasks, limiting reuse across publications, institutions, and applications. For example, a study of concentric tube robots found that 61.1%61.1\% of prototypes appeared in only a single publication, with similar trends observed across other continuum robot classes [3]. The need for a generalized actuation platform is further highlighted by the diversity of existing continuum robot classes and configurations [1], as well as hybrid systems that integrate continuum robots with conventional rigid manipulators [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. In this work, we present a unified, robot design-agnostic actuation platform for continuum robots that can easily integrate with other robotic systems.

Although the working principles of continuum robots can vary, their actuation commonly relies on a combination of three main modes: linear translation, axial rotation, and tendon-induced motion.
For tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs), tendon displacement can be generated directly using lead-screw mechanisms [12, 13, 14] or through capstan drives [15, 16, 5, 4]. Concentric tube robots (CTRs) [17, 18] are actuated through the relative translation and axial rotation of nested, pre-curved Nitinol (NiTi) tubes, typically with diameters on the order of 11–22 mm. These motions can likewise be realized using different mechanisms, including gear-based [19, 20], belt-based [21], and screw-based [22] mechanisms for linear translation, and gear-based [19, 21], and pulley-based [22, 23] mechanisms for axial rotation.

Different modes of actuation impose different actuation requirements. For TDCRs, small inaccuracies in tendon displacement can produce large unintended motions at the distal tip [24, 6, 15, 16], requiring accurate tendon displacement and sufficient actuation force [24, 6, 15, 7, 10]. For CTRs, high tube pre-curvature can generate substantial axial and torsional friction during relative translation and rotation [25], requiring sufficient force and torque while maintaining positioning accuracy under load [19]. Together, these differences in actuation requirements and mechanism design make a custom actuation system developed for one continuum robot difficult to transfer directly to another.

Grassmann et al. [26] addressed this challenge with a modular actuation system built around a common rotational module. Mode-specific mechanisms convert rotational input into tendon displacement for TDCRs or tube translation and axial rotation for CTRs. This work uses the same drive modules to actuate a 4-DOF CTR, a 2-DOF planar TDCR, and a 3-DOF spatial TDCR, with minimal module hardware changes between robot classes. However, the number and arrangement of drive modules vary with the robot design, resulting in substantially different actuation architectures and physical footprints. Thus, while the drive modules themselves are reusable between actuation modes, the actuation architecture remains configuration-dependent and must be re-conceived for each robot design. This dependence makes scaling the actuation system to higher-DOF configurations more challenging and can limit its mechanical integration with other robotic systems.

To date, researchers have combined continuum robots with serial manipulators in both surgical and general robotics applications. For surgical applications, Ma et al. [4] and Zhang et al. [5] mounted TDCRs on serial manipulators for laparoscopic visualization, while Zhang et al. [6] and Qi et al. [7] developed TDCR-based instruments for neurosurgical and spinal applications. Dwyer et al. [8] and Francis et al. [9] integrated CTRs with serial manipulators for fetoscopy. Beyond surgery, Ma et al. [10] combined a TDCR with a 6-DOF movable base to investigate dexterity, manipulability, and obstacle avoidance, while Shentu et al. [11] incorporated a 6-DOF movable base into motion planning for a TDCR to improve follow-the-leader (FTL) behavior. Across these applications, the continuum robots ranged from two to nine DOFs and employed robot design-specific actuation assemblies. This variation highlights the need for a unified actuation platform that scales across different DOFs and configurations and integrates with conventional serial manipulators.

We present a unified actuation platform—including the mechanical, electrical, and software components—that decouples actuation from continuum robot design, enabling:

actuation of multiple classes of continuum robots with arbitrary DOFs,

deployment across many diverse use cases, such as a flexible camera or surgical instrument,

hybrid continuum–serial robot architectures.

1. actuation of multiple classes of continuum robots with arbitrary DOFs,

2. deployment across many diverse use cases, such as a flexible camera or surgical instrument,

3. hybrid continuum–serial robot architectures.
