title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
authors: Hanlin Liu,Zichen Zhou,Jiacheng Zhang,Liuyuan Na,Jin Jin,Guangyan Chen,Yufeng Yue,Gen Li,Fangqiang Ding
abstract: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71×\times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations.
introduction:
Closed-loop manipulation policies must generate effective actions quickly enough to replan as the environment changes. Diffusion Policy (DP) and flow-matching (FM) policies commonly generate these sequences by transforming an unstructured noise sample into an observation-conditioned action trajectory through repeated network evaluations [1, 2]. This iterative process can improve task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. To reduce inference latency, a computationally lightweight policy can first produce an executable action proposal for a generative model to refine. Instead of generating the entire action sequence from noise, the model can then focus on correcting errors in the proposal.

BRIDGeR and Action-to-Action (A2A) flow matching explore related approaches by replacing noise with policy samples or action-history representations [3, 4]. However, improving the starting point does not by itself determine how much refinement is needed. For an executable proposal, the appropriate choice may range from direct execution to additional correction, depending on the current state. Figure  contrasts direct generation, iterative generation, fixed refinement, and our policy with adaptive refinement. The problem is therefore to determine whether the expected improvement over direct execution justifies additional computation, before invoking the refiner.

Making this decision before refinement presents two challenges. First, predicting how much refinement will improve action quality requires assessing refined actions before they are generated. Proposal uncertainty alone does not establish whether the refiner can improve a proposal or how much correction is worthwhile, while evaluating alternative refinements online consumes the computation we seek to save. Second, offline demonstrations provide expert actions, but no direct labels for refinement needs or the benefit of each allocation. The router must therefore learn from demonstrations to predict action errors at different refinement levels, including no refinement. These predictions allow it to decide whether and how much to refine by weighing the expected reduction in error against the additional computation.

We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed) to address these challenges through offline comparative supervision and pre-refinement risk prediction. Here, risk refers to the predicted deviation of an action chunk from expert actions. At demonstration states, frozen proposal and refiner models generate candidates whose deviations from the same expert action chunk provide continuous surrogate targets for a risk ensemble. Offline calibration balances predicted risk, uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. The router then selects direct execution or only the chosen refinement, without online reward optimization or refinement probes. We instantiate this framework with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [5] as the proposal policy and flow matching as the refiner.

We evaluate the framework on eight ManiSkill tasks [6] and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success at 0.322 ms/action of amortized policy latency, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate. On the real robot, it improves success over ACT by 17.5 percentage points with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls further show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level while reducing policy latency by 15.7%.

The paper makes three contributions:

RAIN, an adaptive action-refinement framework that decides whether and how much to refine an executable action proposal before invoking a generative refiner, preserving a direct-execution path.

A demonstration-only learning procedure that predicts continuous candidate risks from expert-action deviations, with offline calibration of uncertainty, computation cost, and temporal consistency.

Evaluation on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks demonstrating the success–efficiency benefits of executable-proposal refinement, with matched controls isolating the additional computation savings from dynamic routing.

1. RAIN, an adaptive action-refinement framework that decides whether and how much to refine an executable action proposal before invoking a generative refiner, preserving a direct-execution path.

2. A demonstration-only learning procedure that predicts continuous candidate risks from expert-action deviations, with offline calibration of uncertainty, computation cost, and temporal consistency.

3. Evaluation on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks demonstrating the success–efficiency benefits of executable-proposal refinement, with matched controls isolating the additional computation savings from dynamic routing.

Technologies, such as co-simulation, in particular, digital twins (DTs) are used
for comprehensive and reliable prototyping, verification and validation (V&V) of control
systems. There, the combination of feedback loops across multiple
realities (e.g., simulations, physical setups) enables various forms of
experimentation with robots and autonomous systems.
However, the handling of multiple realities requires a more specific
support by the modelling techniques used in control engineering.
To streamline the latter in the system life cycle, we propose a
framework for mixing (i.e., fusing, defusing) control input and
feedback signals (i.e., stimuli, responses) in simultaneously operated
plants for multiple realities.
introduction:
Co-simulation, in particular, DTs are used for comprehensive
prototyping as well as V&V of control systems. In this area,
the combination of feedback loops across multiple realities (e.g.,
simulations, physical setups) enables various forms of experimentation
with robots and autonomous systems.

For example, in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) engineering, stable flight depends heavily on
the accurate modelling and validation of all control loop elements.
Simulation is used before deployment in physical experiments to reduce
equipment damage and safety hazards. Simulation enables parameter
pre-tuning and pre-testing of controllers, while physical experiments
introduce further realism for validation.
Differences in dynamics, disturbance models, sensor noise, and timing
inconsistencies cause discrepancies between simulated and physical
behaviour. Controllers doing well in simulation may behave poorly on
a physical UAV. The simulation-to-reality (S2R) gap underlying such discrepancies
can reduce performance and stability of a controller validated on
actual hardware [10]. These issues
are exacerbated in multi-UAV applications.

Mixed reality (MR) environments [4]
narrow the S2R gap by co-executing physical and virtual
experiments in real time. This way, sensor data can be observed in a
physical plant along with the evolution of virtual quantities in a
simulation. For example, disturbances (e.g., wind), perhaps infeasible
to apply on a physical UAV, can be handled in the simulator and
virtual (dynamic) obstacles prevent from collisions during physical
tests. MR environments combine advantages of both worlds for
precise, effective, and robust controller V&V.

Nevertheless, MR requires the handling of issues, such as
physical/virtual parameter mismatches caused by neglected disturbances
and sensor noise [8]. One cannot conclude
MR stability from the individual stability of the involved
realities (i.e., processes, plants, twins). Physical/virtual
couplings require logical
synchronisation and consistency in parameters between the realities
[3, Secs. 6.1 and 6.2]. Plants may
operate with independent clocks, such that their virtual and physical
states evolve asynchronously. Timing mismatches can be worsened by
model inaccuracies and de-synchronisation.
Moreover, clock synchronisation—establishing a global clock across
all environments—does not ensure comparable parameter (e.g., state)
measurements. The latter might not match temporally because of
different sampling rates or disassociated parameters on either side.
Such issues obstruct the comparison and fusion of signals and
require additional alignment.
In our UAV example, the two twins in a UAV-DT need to
be aligned for controller V&V.

Parameters (e.g., state, input, output, disturbance) from all
considered MR environments (e.g., physical, virtual) must be
combined into an MR concept for controller design and
V&V. A naïve parameter union or vector concatenation lacks
flexibility, may reinforce inconsistencies, propagate errors in the
control loop, and lead to undesirable feedback. A framework for
handling MR parameter combinations is needed.

title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Yiming Meng,Yanming Shao,Weijie Shen,Kunyang Lin,Jiayu Sun,Ping Luo,Yao Mu
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm–hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-π\pi, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-π\pi represents the right- and left-side arm–hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence–control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-π\pi achieves state-of-the-art performance under both rand-obj and rand-full, improving the average success rate over π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 31.9% to 51.3% and from 18.3% to 32.3%, respectively. Coordi-π\pi also consistently outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5} across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong progress
in general-purpose robotic manipulation [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. While early generalist policies largely focused on single-arm manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers, recent work has extended VLA-based control to higher-DoF embodiments, including dexterous hands, humanoid robots, and dual-arm systems [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Bimanual dexterous manipulation further requires each side to control a high-DoF arm–hand system while coordinating actions across
the two sides [13], substantially increasing both the
dimensionality and structural complexity of the joint action space.

Despite recent progress, action representation remains underexplored
for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Conventional approaches typically
concatenate the right- and left-side arm–hand actions at each control
timestep,

To address these representation issues, we introduce Coordi-π\pi, a structured action representation framework for bimanual dexterous manipulation, as illustrated in Fig. . Coordi-π\pi first represents each bimanual action chunk as an
interleaved sequence of right- and left-side arm–hand tokens. A learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides within the shared action representation. We further introduce sequence–control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE), which assigns each action token both a sequence-position coordinate and a control-timestep coordinate. In this representation, RhR_{h} and LhL_{h} occupy different positions
in the token sequence while sharing the same control-timestep
coordinate, explicitly representing their temporal synchronization.

We evaluate Coordi-π\pi on five bimanual dexterous manipulation
tasks in DexJoCo [12] under both rand-obj and
the more challenging rand-full setting, and further evaluate
it on four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
Coordi-π\pi achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo,
improving the average success rate over π0.5\pi_{0.5} from 31.9%31.9\%
to 51.3%51.3\% under rand-obj and from 18.3%18.3\% to 32.3%32.3\%
under rand-full. Coordi-π\pi also outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5}
across all four real-world tasks. Ablation studies further show
complementary contributions from the interleaved action representation,
hand-identity embedding, and sequence–control-timestep factorized RoPE.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are threefold:

We propose Coordi-π\pi, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation that represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as individual tokens and organizes them in an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence.

We introduce a learnable hand-identity embedding and sequence–control-timestep factorized RoPE to represent hand identity and temporal synchronization in the interleaved action representation.

We show that Coordi-π\pi achieves state-of-the-art performance
across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo under both
rand-obj and rand-full, and outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5}
across all four real-world tasks.

title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Qi Chen,Yuwei Wu,Quan Chen,Kunpeng Gao,Jin Chen,Che Sun,Zhi Gao,Yunde Jia
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation.
However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited. Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios.
To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro,
a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen
manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video.
CapPro consists of two components. First, a phase-aware human video
representation module constructs a compact video representation through
learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query
representations under phase-caption supervision. Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the
compact video and query-derived representations into the
action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy.
In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution
guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate,
without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task
fine-tuning. Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for developing general-purpose robot manipulation systems by integrating visual perception, language understanding, planning, and action generation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models, recent VLA approaches have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse manipulation tasks, including object rearrangement, pick-and-place, stacking, and tool-use tasks [5, 6, 7, 8]. These advances establish VLA models as a strong foundation for building versatile robot manipulation policies.

Despite these advances, current VLA models still have limited ability to
rapidly adapt to manipulation tasks beyond their training distributions [9, 10, 11].
Although large-scale pretraining equips these models with reusable
manipulation skills, successful adaptation to a new task often still
requires task-specific knowledge of interaction patterns and execution
procedures that may not be fully specified by the current observation and
language instruction. Existing adaptation methods therefore often rely on
additional robot demonstrations and task-specific fine-tuning to provide
the required task knowledge [12, 13, 14]. These procedures introduce substantial data
and computational requirements, making it difficult to efficiently extend
VLA policies to new manipulation tasks encountered at deployment.

Human demonstration videos provide a natural source of task-specific
knowledge for adapting VLA policies to new manipulation tasks [15, 16, 17, 18].
By showing
how a person interacts with objects and progresses through a task, they
capture visual information about interaction patterns, execution
procedures, and task goals that may not be fully conveyed by language
instructions alone [19, 20, 21, 22].
In addition, such demonstrations can be collected
without executing the task on a specific robotic platform, making them
easier to obtain for new manipulation tasks [23, 24].

Using human demonstration videos for VLA adaptation introduces two key
challenges. First, human demonstrations contain substantial visual
redundancy, while different stages of execution convey different
task-relevant information, making it difficult to identify the
information that is most useful for guiding robot execution.
Second,
substantial differences in embodiment, observation perspective, and
action space create a substantial gap between human demonstrations and
robot execution, making direct behavior transfer difficult [25, 26, 27].
Together,
these challenges make it nontrivial to exploit human demonstrations for
VLA adaptation.

In this paper, we propose CapPro, a one-shot human-video-guided adaptation
framework that enables a VLA policy to acquire task-specific execution
guidance from a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two
components. First, a phase-aware human video representation module learns
a compact video representation and task-relevant query representations
under phase-level supervision, allowing the model to focus on
stage-dependent execution information in the demonstration. Second, a
video-conditioned adaptation module incorporates these representations
into the conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy, enabling
task-specific information from the human demonstration to guide robot
action generation without requiring direct human-to-robot behavior
transfer. In this way, CapPro uses the human demonstration as task-specific
guidance while retaining the original action-generation structure of the
base VLA policy.

We evaluate CapPro on the RoboTwin benchmark [28] under a one-shot adaptation
setting across 26 unseen manipulation tasks organized into three groups
with increasing levels of task shift, and further validate its
cross-task adaptation capability on real-world manipulation tasks.
CapPro improves the average success rate across all unseen target-task
groups compared with the pretrained VLA baseline, while maintaining
comparable performance on the source tasks. The real-world experiments
further demonstrate that human-video guidance can support adaptation to
new manipulation tasks beyond simulation.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate one-shot human-video-guided adaptation for pretrained
VLA models, where a single human demonstration provides task-specific
execution guidance for an unseen manipulation task without requiring
target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning.

We propose CapPro, which combines phase-aware human video
representation with video-conditioned adaptation to capture
stage-dependent task information from a single demonstration and
incorporate it into robot action generation without direct
human-to-robot behavior transfer.

We evaluate CapPro on 26 unseen manipulation tasks in RoboTwin
with different levels of task shift, together with real-world
manipulation tasks. The results show improved adaptation across
unseen target-task groups while maintaining comparable performance
on source tasks.

1. We formulate one-shot human-video-guided adaptation for pretrained
VLA models, where a single human demonstration provides task-specific
execution guidance for an unseen manipulation task without requiring
target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning.

2. We propose CapPro, which combines phase-aware human video
representation with video-conditioned adaptation to capture
stage-dependent task information from a single demonstration and
incorporate it into robot action generation without direct
human-to-robot behavior transfer.

3. We evaluate CapPro on 26 unseen manipulation tasks in RoboTwin
with different levels of task shift, together with real-world
manipulation tasks. The results show improved adaptation across
unseen target-task groups while maintaining comparable performance
on source tasks.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Self-Play for Robust Multi-Agent Driving Policies
authors: Sajad Marvi,Julian Schmidt,Alessandro Canevaro,Julian Jordan,Abhinav Valada
abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors’ epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8×\times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.
introduction:
Object-level behavior planning is a core challenge in autonomous driving where a policy must control agents through complex multi-agent scenarios involving dynamic interactions with other vehicles, pedestrians, and road structure. Imitation learning [1, 2, 3] trains policies from logged human trajectories but underrepresents rare, safety-critical events. Reinforcement learning [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] scales well and produces competent drivers, but policies reflect only the scenarios seen during training and may not generalize to novel domains. Training separate adversarial policies [9, 10] can expose the ego agent to harder situations, but such policies are expensive to maintain and tend to produce unrealistic behaviors.
A promising alternative is conditioned self-play, where all agents share one network and a conditioning signal selects the behavioral mode for each agent. Prior work conditions on return targets [11], skill indices [12], or entropy bonuses [13], but these face a fundamental tension. Achieving meaningful behavioral diversity typically degrades driving performance, even when conditioned to drive normally. We term this the diversity tax. Can a conditioned policy, set to its normal driving mode, not only match but exceed an unconditional self-play baseline?

Our key insight is that epistemic uncertainty, which measures the policy’s confidence, provides a natural proxy for behavioral diversity. We train half the agents to increase their neighbors’ uncertainty while the other half learn to drive safely under this probing pressure. Uncertainty is an inexpensive, automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Rather than hand-engineering diverse training scenarios, probing agents find the hard cases automatically by targeting exactly where the current policy is most confused. This self-play scheme generates an automatic diversity-driven curriculum of challenging interactions. Among the conditioned methods we evaluate, our method is the only one to outperform a strong unconditional self-play baseline.

In each training episode (Fig. 1), 50% of agents are designated probing agents (rewarded for increasing the epistemic uncertainty of their K=3K{=}3 nearest neighbors) while 50% are neutral (pure task reward). As neutral agents adapt, probing agents must discover increasingly novel challenging situations, generating a diversity-driven curriculum without hand-crafted scenario design. At evaluation, all agents use the neutral role, benefiting from exposure to this broader training distribution. This relates to adversarial training [14] and domain randomization [15] where both improve robustness by exposing the learner to challenging conditions during training.

Our contributions are:

An uncertainty-driven self-play scheme using epistemic uncertainty change (Δ\Deltaunc) as the probing reward, showing that a conditioned policy can surpass an unconditional self-play baseline, an outcome not achieved by any other conditioned method we evaluate.

Empirical demonstration that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertainty scenarios exhibiting 14.8×\times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertainty scenarios (ECE==0.014).

Comprehensive evaluations across 10,000 Waymo scenarios and zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 and Argoverse 2, with comparisons against DIAYN, entropy-conditioned, and GIGAFLOW-style baselines.

Ablation studies identifying neighborhood size (K=3K{=}3), warmup scheduling, conditioning mechanism (FiLM vs. Concatenation vs. none), and probing fraction (50%) as essential design choices, with warmup improving score by 0.57% and role conditioning being load-bearing for any gains over the unconditional baseline.

The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) with no fine-tuning, while reducing the failure rate by 17% on Waymo validation scenarios compared to the baseline. It also achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage, indicating a broader range of learned behaviors that explains the improved transfer.

title: ACRO: Actor-Critic Rollout Orchestration
authors: Junhoo Lee,Seungyeon Kim,Baekseung Kim,Minkyu Kim,Suhyun Jeon,Jimyeong Kim,Nojun Kwak
abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor–Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and π0.5\pi_{0.5} across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro.
introduction:
Teaching a robot to act leaves open the question of when to trust its policy to continue and when to intervene. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b). These models can succeed on a task in one execution and fail on the same task in another, suggesting that the outcome of a single execution may fall short of the policy’s capabilities. Orchestration that translates this potential into successful task completion could improve the performance of an existing VLA without retraining the policy.

Effective orchestration requires two decisions: when to intervene, and how far that intervention should go. RoboMonkey and CoVer evaluate and select action proposals from the current observation (Kwok et al., 2025; Kwok et al., 2026), while AutoHorizon adjusts how much of a predicted action chunk to execute (Wang et al., 2026). These decisions improve the policy’s next execution, but evaluating an unfavorable proposal does not itself specify a physical intervention that would enable a better continuation. External orchestrators such as Pigey organize subgoals and skill calls, verify their outcomes, and apply retry and fallback rules (Galanti et al., 2026). In Pigey’s VLA interface, however, the orchestrator reassesses execution after a bounded rollout returns. Such verification and routing rules do not directly determine when to interrupt an ongoing VLA execution or how much to change its state before returning control. Intervening only as much as is useful requires evaluating the policy’s prospects both if the current action proceeds and if execution resumes after an intervention.

We introduce ACRO, an Actor–Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions according to the deployed VLA’s probability of task completion. ACRO learns action- and state-value estimates from execution outcomes. The Critic evaluates the VLA’s proposed action to determine when to interrupt execution. To turn this assessment into a tractable intervention, we introduce Trajectory Retraction, which reconstructs the observed execution path into a constrained region for intervention search. Within this region, ACRO uses state values to select a promising target reachable under the intervention budget. The Actor moves the robot to the selected configuration and returns control to the VLA, which observes the resulting state and generates a new continuation. Repeating this process within the remaining budget allows a minimal intervention layer to support alternative successful executions while leaving task execution to the existing policy.

We evaluate ACRO in simulation and on real-robot manipulation tasks. ACRO improves task success under the same execution budget, even when the physical steps used for trajectory retraction are included. These gains extend to the real robot, where success increases from 43.3%43.3\% to 65.0%65.0\%. As the execution budget grows, ACRO achieves further gains in task completion, demonstrating test-time scaling through rollout orchestration.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate rollout orchestration through the difference in task-success probability between continuing a proposed action and resuming the policy after a physical intervention.

We introduce ACRO, which uses a shared Q/V Critic to decide when to intervene and Trajectory Retraction to select and reach a promising continuation point.

We show that ACRO improves success with fixed VLAs on SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real robots under matched physical execution budgets that include retraction.

1. We formulate rollout orchestration through the difference in task-success probability between continuing a proposed action and resuming the policy after a physical intervention.

2. We introduce ACRO, which uses a shared Q/V Critic to decide when to intervene and Trajectory Retraction to select and reach a promising continuation point.

3. We show that ACRO improves success with fixed VLAs on SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real robots under matched physical execution budgets that include retraction.

title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
authors: Jehun Lee,Hajun Lee,Jimin Ryu,Youhan Lee,Beomseok Kang,Jonghyun Choi,Jae-Joon Kim
abstract:
Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions.
Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixed-length prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused.
For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls.
Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions.
However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections.
To address this limitation,
we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call.
Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples.
PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution.
Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3×\times in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed-horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
The code is available at : https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PICES_VLA-B1BF
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions conditioned on visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions (Brohan et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025).
Recent VLA architectures pair a vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action expert that transforms initial noise into an action chunk, a sequence of future actions (Bjorck et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025).
In conventional action chunking, the robot executes fixed-length actions of each predicted chunk before replanning as illustrated in Figure 1(a).
The number of actions executed before update observations defines the execution horizon (Black et al., 2026).
The cumulative policy invocations across policy rollout makes task-completion time dependent on both per-call latency and the number of policy calls (Zhou et al., 2026; Jing et al., 2025).

At comparable success rates, shorter task-completion times enable a robot to complete more tasks within a fixed time budget (Shukor et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025).
This makes cumulative inference latency as an important consideration for onboard VLA deployment, where edge platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor operate under compute and memory-bandwidth constraints (Yang et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026).
For example, GR00T N1.7 requires 80.4ms per policy call on Jetson Orin and 150.9 ms on Jetson Thor (Li et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025), whereas observation acquisition and actuation can operate up to 60Hz and 1kHz, respectively (Jiang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020).
In observation-inference-execution pipeline, reducing the number of policy calls lowers cumulative inference latency and shorten task-completion time (Jing et al., 2025).
For action chunking policies, executing only fraction of each predicted action chunk incurs inefficiency. However, applying long horizons uniformly across task phases delays the incorporation of updated observations when precise control is required.
This motivates adapting execution horizons to reduce repeated inference while preserving task success.

Prior works have explored diverse action-chunk execution strategies to balance temporal consistency and reactivity, including temporal ensembling, adaptive chunk updates, and guided candidate selection (Zhao et al., 2023; So et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025a).
AAC estimates action entropy of action candidates to decide a shared exceuction horizon (Liang et al., 2026).
AutoHorizon derives the execution horizon from self-attention within a predicted chunk (Wang et al., 2026).
A3A^{3} selects a representative trajectory from multiple candidates and then performs additional flow-matching verification to determine execution horizon (Zhao et al., 2026).
Our objective is to reduce wall-clock inference time while achieving comparable success rate by jointly selecting an action chunk and its execution horizon.
This raises our key question: Given a bounded set of candidate action chunks generated in a single policy call, how can we select the action chunk and execution horizon to reduce the wall-clock inference time?

We propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free inference time method that jointly selects an action chunk and its execution horizon. For each initial-noise sample, PICES constructs a locally perturbed counterpart by adding a small Gaussian perturbation.
A single batched policy call generates the corresponding nominal and auxiliary action chunks using shared conditioning features encoded by the vision-language-model (VLM).
Based on the arithmetic intensity analysis of action expert and hardware ridge-point in our motivational analysis, we restrict total batch size to a range with negligible incremental latency.
For each candidate, the stepwise differences between nominal and auxiliary action chunks yield a local sensitivity value.
We exploit these values to retain candidates with low initial sensitivity and estimate execution horizon for each candidate.
From the candidate pool, PICES selects and executes the nominal chunk with the longest execution horizon.
Figure 1(b) illustrates the reduction in policy calls: two calls execute eight actions, compared with four calls with fixed horizon execution.
Savings from fewer policy calls outweigh the additional cost of candidate generation, reducing cumulative inference time as shown in Figure 1(c).

Our key contributions are as follows:

Through an open-loop study, we show that oracle selection from multiple action chunks can yield lower reference-action error over a longer execution horizon than a single-candidate, short-horizon baseline. We also characterize the cost of generating candidates in a batch.

We propose PICES, a training-free method to reduce cumulative wall-clock inference time. PICES uses sensitivity to initial-noise perturbations to guide the joint selection of an action chunk and its execution horizon.

We evaluate PICES across multiple VLA models in simulation and on real-world robot tasks. Compared with fixed-horizon baselines, PICES reduces policy calls by 25.4–60.3% and achieves 1.2–2.3×\times speedups in wall-clock inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor, while maintaining higher success rates.

1. Through an open-loop study, we show that oracle selection from multiple action chunks can yield lower reference-action error over a longer execution horizon than a single-candidate, short-horizon baseline. We also characterize the cost of generating candidates in a batch.

2. We propose PICES, a training-free method to reduce cumulative wall-clock inference time. PICES uses sensitivity to initial-noise perturbations to guide the joint selection of an action chunk and its execution horizon.

3. We evaluate PICES across multiple VLA models in simulation and on real-world robot tasks. Compared with fixed-horizon baselines, PICES reduces policy calls by 25.4–60.3% and achieves 1.2–2.3×\times speedups in wall-clock inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor, while maintaining higher success rates.

title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
authors: Yuhang Hu,Junlin Lyu,Yuan Fang,Xiaoying Shen,Lechen Zhang,Jiong Lin,Judah Goldfeder,Steven Tian,Hod Lipson
abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot’s 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
introduction:
Gaze is a fundamental channel of nonverbal communication, regulating attention, conversational turn-taking, intimacy, and emotional signaling [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Appropriate eye contact has further been shown to increase perceived trustworthiness [7]. In Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), embodiment allows robots to emulate these social cues through physical motion [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13], which makes faithfully reproducing human gaze both a substantial challenge and a promising path toward more natural interaction [14].

Scripted eye and head controllers provide a useful starting point, but fixed rules have limited flexibility across targets and motion styles [15, 16, 17]. Gaze also influences first impressions in social interaction [18, 19], making the timing of robot movements worth studying alongside endpoint tracking. We therefore ask whether a prior learned from human motion can improve joint-space reproduction under target-conditioned, closed-loop robot control (Fig. 1). The framework separates a deliberative decision about the attended referent from the frame-rate generation of motor commands. A VLM selects a referent asynchronously, a reactive perception module maintains its fixation between VLM calls, and the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) predicts coordinated neck, binocular-eye, and eyelid commands from recent motion and a planned eye trajectory.

The action model is pretrained on retargeted human recordings and then fine-tuned autoregressively, so training includes histories containing its own predictions rather than only recorded frames. Its latent bottleneck summarizes the motion history while the target trajectory enters the decoder after that bottleneck. The 11-DoF output combines seven neck/eye joints from the learned motion path with four eyelid joints and a separate blink-template playback path. This differs from generating body motion for an avatar: commands must remain in the robot’s joint coordinates, track a binocular target, and roll out at the control rate. The hierarchy permits a slow semantic decision and faster reactive control without requiring the VLM to issue each joint command. It also lets us examine motion generation separately from errors in choosing or tracking a referent.

Our contributions are (i) a VLM-guided, reactive targeting interface for a humanoid face, (ii) a target-conditioned Transformer-VAE with a latent bottleneck and autoregressive fine-tuning for coordinated robot gaze, and (iii) a markerless data and evaluation pipeline that tests closed-loop fidelity, stochastic diversity, participant adaptation, and runtime. The quantitative benchmark supplies every controller with the same ground-truth eye target and scores seven neck/eye channels; physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting pipeline. Code and simulation materials are linked at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/eye_robot_pub-CF64/.

title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
authors: Cheng Fan,Bingyang Zhou,Gang Yang,Zixuan Zhuang,Aoqian Zhang,Pengzhi Yang,Xin Liu,Chunzheng Wang,Yan Rui Tan,Fan Shi
abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
introduction:
Quadruped robots have shown strong potential for operation in human-centered environments [1, 2], where obstacle avoidance often extends beyond planar navigation. In cluttered scenes, a velocity-commanded robot may encounter obstacles with diverse heights and geometries, such as tables, shelves, chairs, and suspended boards. To navigate such environments effectively, the robot must not only track commanded motion, but also adapt its body posture and locomotion strategy in three dimensions, e.g., bypassing obstacles laterally or lowering its body to crawl underneath them. Enabling such command-conditioned 3D obstacle avoidance is therefore important for the practical deployment of quadruped robots [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

Recent studies have explored quadrupedal locomotion in complex environments through both optimization-based and learning-based approaches [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 3, 4]. Traditional optimization-based methods, such as Duality-based DCBF NMPC [7], incorporate safety constraints into online trajectory optimization for safe quadrupedal locomotion in narrow spaces. However, their reliance on online constrained optimization and simplified model representations makes it difficult to simultaneously avoid challenging obstacles while maintaining responsive velocity tracking. Model-free reinforcement learning offers an alternative, but typically treats the simulator as a black box and estimates gradients only from sampled returns [12], requiring large amounts of interaction data in contact-rich obstacle-avoidance tasks.

Differentiable simulation has recently emerged as a promising alternative for more efficient policy learning [12, 13, 14]. Prior work has also shown that differentiable physics can improve motion performance. Notably, Zhang et al. [15] demonstrate high-speed drone navigation through complex environments with both static and dynamic obstacles, achieving substantial gains in speed and success rate. In addition, Schwarke et al. [16] achieve robust proprioceptive quadrupedal locomotion by proposing a novel differentiable contact model, enabling seamless sim-to-real transfer with remarkable sample efficiency. These results suggest that differentiable physics can improve both optimization efficiency and control performance. We therefore seek to bring these advantages to quadrupedal 3D obstacle avoidance.

Nevertheless, applying differentiable RL to quadrupedal obstacle avoidance remains challenging. Intermittent contacts, hard collision constraints, and early termination induce severe non-smoothness and gradient discontinuities. Consequently, first-order optimization methods become highly susceptible to suboptimal local minima. Existing differentiable RL methods for quadruped robots mainly address blind locomotion or simulated 2D tasks [17, 18], leaving the integration of differentiable learning into deployable visuomotor policies for 3D obstacle avoidance unexplored. In this setting, the central challenge is not simply to add an obstacle-avoidance cost, but to design a training surrogate that keeps obstacle interactions informative for first-order policy optimization while discouraging nonphysical penetration.

In this letter, we present E2DRL, an end-to-end differentiable reinforcement learning framework for quadrupedal 3D obstacle avoidance under velocity commands. The framework trains a privileged teacher with SAPO in a differentiable simulator, distills it into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, and blends the student with a proprioception-based locomotion policy through a terrain-aware gating module. A key innovation of this work is a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation, used as a training-time surrogate rather than a physical contact model, which allows simulated penetration and applies differentiable multi-keypoint penalties with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping. The gating module preserves nominal locomotion in free space while triggering active avoidance near obstacles. Experiments show that E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO during training, while outperforming both Duality-based DCBF NMPC and PPO in velocity tracking and traversal of challenging 3D obstacles.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation for contact-rich quadrupedal obstacle avoidance, which addresses the local-optima and gradient-truncation issues of hard obstacle formulations by penalizing continuous penetration of multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping, enabling stable first-order optimization across overhanging and ground obstacle configurations.

We propose a deployment-oriented differentiable end-to-end obstacle avoidance framework that transfers differentiable RL skills for crawling and bypassing to a recurrent depth-based student policy.
Furthermore, to improve velocity tracking in obstacle-free regions, we introduce a gating module that seamlessly integrates the student policy with a nominal locomotion policy.

We present the first sim-to-real validation of an end-to-end differentiable RL policy for overhanging and ground obstacle avoidance on a physical quadruped robot in both static and dynamic real-world environments.

title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
authors: Seyed Ali Mirghasemi,Alireza Taheri
abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
introduction:
Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to locate a target object in an unfamiliar environment without being given its position in advance [1]. Unlike point-goal navigation, where the destination is specified geometrically, ObjectNav requires the agent to infer where the target may be located, explore the environment, identify potential instances, navigate toward them, and determine whether an observed candidate satisfies the intended goal. Successful execution therefore depends on the coordinated operation of perception, exploration, navigation, and target verification over an extended sequence of decisions [1, 2].

This coordination remains challenging because the information available to the agent is partial and changes throughout the mission. A target may initially be outside the field of view, object detections may be uncertain or incorrect, and visually similar objects may produce misleading candidates. Navigation can also become inefficient when the agent repeatedly visits previously explored regions, fails to reach a candidate, or continues using a search strategy that no longer produces useful progress. These difficulties make ObjectNav not only a perception or path-planning problem, but also a problem of deciding how different capabilities should be used as the mission evolves [2, 3].

Modular ObjectNav approaches address part of this challenge by separating functions such as semantic mapping, exploration, object detection, goal selection, and navigation into specialized components. Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration, for example, combines semantic mapping with goal-directed exploration, while PONI explicitly separates the questions of where to search and how to navigate toward a selected location [2, 3]. Such designs improve interpretability and allow individual modules to be developed or replaced independently. However, modularity alone does not provide mission-level adaptation. When the selection and interaction of these components are fixed before execution, the resulting pipeline may continue to apply the same strategy despite changes in mission conditions. A configuration that is effective during straightforward search may become less suitable after repeated exploration or ambiguous detections, whereas continuously invoking computationally expensive semantic reasoning may be unnecessary when conventional perception and navigation are sufficient.

Recent work has also demonstrated the value of pretrained semantic knowledge for target search. Methods such as L3MVN use large language models to provide object–scene priors for frontier selection, while ESC combines vision–language grounding with commonsense reasoning to support zero-shot exploration [4, 5]. These studies show that semantic knowledge can support search decisions when geometric exploration alone provides limited guidance. At the same time, such reasoning does not necessarily need to remain active throughout an entire mission. This motivates a complementary question: not only which semantic capabilities should be available, but also when they should be invoked and how they should interact with conventional perception and navigation components.

This question was first examined in Stage I of the present study through a fixed modular ObjectNav framework. Different combinations of exploration, detection, and target-validation methods were evaluated to characterize their trade-offs in navigation performance, validation reliability, task time, and model-related cost. The experiments showed that the relative advantages of the evaluated configurations changed with environmental complexity and mission conditions. Configurations incorporating semantic or multimodal reasoning often provided stronger validation reliability or navigation performance in more demanding conditions, whereas lighter configurations could operate with lower computational overhead. Importantly, no evaluated fixed configuration provided the most favorable balance across all considered criteria. These observations motivated investigating event-driven coordination as an alternative to committing to an unchanged combination of capabilities for the entire mission.

Motivated by these findings, this work introduces F2A-ObjectNav, an adaptive agentic architecture that extends modular ObjectNav with mission-level, event-driven coordination. The name F2A (Fixed-to-Adaptive) reflects the progression from the fixed modular configurations examined in Stage I to the adaptive architecture developed in Stage II. Rather than replacing conventional perception and navigation with a general-purpose reasoning model, the proposed architecture organizes specialized functions under a rule-based Supervisor that monitors mission progress and coordinates their use according to the current execution state. Mission Memory preserves relevant episode-level information, including rejected candidates and repeated or ineffective search behavior, while recovery and strategy revision provide mechanisms for responding to navigation or exploration failures. Semantic guidance is invoked selectively when the ongoing search does not provide sufficient progress, rather than operating continuously throughout the mission.

This design separates routine execution from adaptive intervention. Under normal conditions, navigation, exploration, and object detection proceed without requiring continuous high-level semantic reasoning. When events such as candidate rejection, navigation stagnation, repeated exploration, or insufficient search progress occur, the Supervisor can revise the current behavior, use previously stored mission information, activate recovery, or request semantic guidance. Detection is also separated from final target acceptance: detected objects are treated as candidates and are validated only after the agent reaches an appropriate observation point. The resulting architecture provides a structured mechanism for adapting the interaction among ObjectNav components while retaining their modularity, interpretability, and independent functional roles.

F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated in three complementary simulation environments: AI2-THOR [6], RoboTHOR [7], and ProcTHOR [8]. Standard ObjectNav performance is measured using Success Rate (SR) and Success-weighted Path Length (SPL), with SPL following the embodied-navigation evaluation formulation introduced by Anderson et al. [9]. Additional system-level measures include task time, target-validation accuracy, and model-related cost. The evaluation further records architecture-specific behavioral indicators describing semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, Mission Memory involvement, and supervisory decision stability. Together, these measures characterize both mission-level performance and the internal behavior of the adaptive coordination mechanism.

The main contributions of this work are:

An empirical analysis of fixed modular ObjectNav configurations that characterizes the trade-offs among navigation performance, target-validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, and provides the experimental motivation for moving from fixed execution toward adaptive coordination.

F2A-ObjectNav, an event-driven adaptive architecture for ObjectNav in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and episode-level Mission Memory.

A set of mission-level adaptation mechanisms for responding to execution events through candidate management, memory-informed decisions, recovery, strategy revision, and conditional semantic guidance, without relying on a language model as the primary navigation controller.

A multi-environment evaluation across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR that combines standard ObjectNav metrics, system-level performance measures, architecture-specific behavioral indicators, and an execution-trace mechanism analysis based on evaluation-wide statistics and recorded execution traces.

title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
authors: Fan Huang,Dezhong Tong,Changyu Chen,Haewoon Kwak,Jisun An
abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program’s own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration’s single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
introduction:
Language models can generate programs that invoke robot primitives, so that a manipulation request can be expressed through a familiar code interface [1, 2, 3]. Prior work grounds actions in robot capabilities and current state [4, 2] and uses feedback to recover from failures [5, 3], while rearrangement evaluation compares the achieved scene with a specified goal [6]. These considerations go beyond syntactic correctness and motivate inspecting how a task becomes an executable program.

Two issues motivate this study. First, our one-shot baseline produces a complete program without a separately generated instruction artifact. Prior work combines code with execution-grounded reasoning [7]; we investigate a trainable instruction stage for tracing downstream failures. Second, one stochastic code sample can confound instruction quality with sampling variation, motivating our reward-averaging analysis. Separately, imperfect reward signals can favor unintended behavior or diverge from intended performance [8, 9]. Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation and code synthesis over a fixed robot API for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo [10]. The intermediate action is the entire generated instruction text, which in practice contains both prose and a reference-code block (median code-line fraction 79.3% across the 32 instructions of the final step of the main binary-reward training run), so it is a language-to-code interface rather than a short symbolic plan.

We ask three questions. RQ1: how do one-shot code generation and ICMC compare under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter reshaping, and how do same-backbone Chain-of-Code and iterative-correction implementations compare on reshaping? RQ2: what happens when an open-weight instruction policy is trained by GRPO [11] through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto letter-shaped layouts, with rewards parsed from program execution? RQ3: what do the archived comparisons of reward sampling (M=5 versus M=1), learning rate and update epochs establish, and which effects remain confounded?

This paper makes four contributions. First, a language-to-code decomposition over a fixed UR5e API that trains an inspectable instruction policy through a frozen code generator; retained records link instructions to syntax errors, undefined names and discrepancies between reward labels and logged geometry. Second, an audit of reward consistency: the main run’s logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% between the first and last five steps, while inspection identifies at least 19 positive-reward logs reporting geometric failure in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run and 5 with one program per instruction (M=1). The audit traces success labels to the generated program’s output stream. Third, a characterization of downstream reward variance: an estimator argument for averaging M program rewards per instruction, supported by the observation that 302 of the 640 instructions in the main run received mixed rewards across their five programs. Fourth, an independent evaluation protocol for checking task completion against fixed specifications, with simulator state and scoring controlled by a separate software supervisor. Its CPU implementation passed ten negative controls; a hand-authored reference controller completed all 40 predeclared scenes under this protocol.

The study characterizes simulated execution through one archived training trajectory per configuration. Evaluation of model-generated programs under the independent protocol, replication across training seeds, and matched tests of learning-rate and epoch effects remain future work.

title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
authors: Hyunsik Oh,Seunghun Jeon,Donghoon Youm,Jungwoo Hur,Hyeongjun Kim,Jeong Hyun Lee,Moonkyu Jung,Jemin Hwangbo
abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot’s URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.
introduction:
In the field of robotics, significant progress has been made through various control methodologies, including Model Predictive Control (MPC) [22] and learning-based approaches such as imitation learning (IL) [16, 23] and reinforcement learning (RL) [7, 18]. Among these, model-free RL has become a powerful tool for legged robot control because it directly optimizes policies from environment interactions without requiring explicit dynamics models. This makes RL particularly effective for complex and underactuated systems, enabling robust locomotion over challenging terrains such as rough slopes, stairs, and deformable terrain [15, 10].

Most existing studies on legged locomotion focus on enabling a single platform to perform a specific task [9, 14]. However, policies trained for one robot often fail to transfer to another due to differences in morphology, including degrees of freedom, link masses, inertias, and kinematic configurations. Adapting a policy to a new robot typically requires redesigning the environment, observations, action space, and reward functions, which demands substantial engineering effort. This motivates the development of general controllers that can operate across diverse legged robots.

In this work, we address the following question: Can we train a single locomotion policy that operates across legged robots with diverse morphologies, including different numbers of legs and actuators, and deploy it on real hardware without per-robot retraining? We argue that such a controller must not only observe the robot’s current state but also reason about its morphology, and that achieving this in practice requires addressing training-level imbalances that arise when robots with very different reward magnitudes and learning difficulties are trained together.

To this end, we propose PolyMorph, a cross-embodiment locomotion framework with a URDF-conditioned policy interface. As shown in Fig. 1, the same policy is deployed across diverse legged morphologies on various rough terrains in both simulation and the real world. Each robot is represented as a sequence of joint-link modules parsed from its URDF, and padding with valid-action masking allows the same policy to handle variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and joint configurations without redesigning the action interface. The policy combines a recurrent state encoder that summarizes proprioceptive history, a Transformer that conditions on URDF-derived graph structure, and per-joint decoder heads that generate actions only for actuated joints.

A unified locomotion policy across heterogeneous morphologies can shorten the robot design-test cycle by allowing new designs or modified configurations to be evaluated without retraining a separate controller for each platform, which is particularly useful for rapid robot design workflows [11, 1]. It also enables policy reuse across heterogeneous robot platforms and exposes the policy to broader morphology and dynamics variations.

Beyond designing a policy that can process robots with different kinematic structures, we observe that jointly optimizing across morphologies introduces training-level obstacles: reward magnitudes can scale with the number of joints and legs, biasing optimization toward certain morphologies; easy-to-learn robots can dominate uniform sampling and reduce the learning signal for harder morphologies such as bipeds; and manually tuned PD gains reintroduce per-platform engineering effort. Complementary to prior multi-embodiment methods that emphasize morphology-conditioned policy architectures, PolyMorph addresses these training-level obstacles through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, URDF-derived PD-gain initialization, together with curriculum learning and domain randomization for robust training. The same policy parameters are shared across all robots, and only morphology-dependent inputs are derived from each robot’s URDF.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

We identify and address training-level obstacles in cross-embodiment optimization, including reward-scale mismatch, sampling imbalance between easy and hard robots, and per-platform gain tuning, through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization.

We adapt joint-link tokenization, embodiment-masked attention, recurrent proprioceptive encoding, and per-joint action decoding into a URDF-conditioned policy interface that handles variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and kinematic structures with shared parameters.

We validate PolyMorph on heterogeneous legged robots in simulation and demonstrate cross-morphology hardware deployment on two real quadruped platforms operated in quadrupedal, tripedal, and bipedal configurations, with additional ablations and comparisons against multi-embodiment baselines.

1. We identify and address training-level obstacles in cross-embodiment optimization, including reward-scale mismatch, sampling imbalance between easy and hard robots, and per-platform gain tuning, through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization.

2. We adapt joint-link tokenization, embodiment-masked attention, recurrent proprioceptive encoding, and per-joint action decoding into a URDF-conditioned policy interface that handles variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and kinematic structures with shared parameters.

3. We validate PolyMorph on heterogeneous legged robots in simulation and demonstrate cross-morphology hardware deployment on two real quadruped platforms operated in quadrupedal, tripedal, and bipedal configurations, with additional ablations and comparisons against multi-embodiment baselines.
