title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Xuan Han,Zinuo Jin,Tianlin Li,Yunfan Lou,Xin Liu,Yuchen Xue,Yuanpeng He,Boxian Yao,Shuhan Zhan,Ruihai Wu,Zhibo Pang
abstract:
Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with
physical observations that can guide action selection and execution.
However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings
across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration
designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating
six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol.
ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference,
resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with
1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria.
We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on
a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success
of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves
success rates across all three task categories.
Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on
physical-property inference, while both temporal designs
underperform the baseline on assembly.
Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports
the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion
achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline,
but only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
These findings support ForceBench’s practical value for identifying
the benefits and limitations of force integration across
manipulation demands.
The project page is available at
https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual and language pretraining
to robotic action, enabling a shared backbone to learn diverse manipulation
skills [1, 2, 3, 4].
Physical interaction additionally requires responding to properties and
conditions revealed through action, such as object mass and resistance.
Learning-based policies increasingly exploit such feedback, extending
diffusion-based visuomotor policies [5] with compliance-
or force-aware learning [6, 7, 8] and
incorporating force into VLA models. Wrist force provides a six-dimensional
observation of these interactions, combining three force and three torque
components. These measurements can refine a visually specified motion or
inform decisions about conditions that appearance alone does not reveal,
supporting both action selection and execution.

Existing systems incorporate force into action generation through adaptive
fusion of force tokens with vision–language
features [9] or temporal force encoding
with high-frequency feedback [10, 11].
Force also supports reactive execution through contact prediction that
regulates feedback usage [12], while joint action–wrench
modeling supports reinforcement-learning post-training [13].
Other work removes the force sensor
at deployment by distilling force knowledge into vision [14].
Although standardized data and benchmarks have matured for vision-based
manipulation [15, 16],
differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across
force-aware systems hinder direct comparisons. Moreover, aggregate
success rates can obscure differences across physical-property inference,
resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. We therefore
ask how force integration designs can be reliably compared under a unified
protocol, and how their benefits vary across manipulation demands.

To address this gap, we introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark
dedicated to comparing six-axis wrist-force integration in robotic
manipulation (Fig. ). ForceBench combines parameterized
physical conditions, 1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations,
a shared observation–action interface, and evaluation on task instances
initialized with shared seeds. Seven tasks vary physical properties and
resistance conditions to examine behavior beyond object appearance;
a complementary contact-rich assembly task tests geometrically
constrained execution. Task-specific success criteria and category-level
metrics support comparison across these manipulation demands. We further
assess the practical relevance of the benchmark through real-world
experiments.

Using this framework, we compare a no-force baseline and six force
integration designs on a shared π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, using the same task
demonstrations and training protocol. The six designs comprise three
current-sample conditioning interfaces—Token Fusion, Prompt Fusion,
and Cross-Attention—a Token Fusion variant with auxiliary future-force
prediction, and two temporal reference systems, Temporal Prompt and
Dual-Path Fusion. ForceVLA provides an external comparison.
Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success
of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the no-force baseline, and provides
the most consistent improvements across task categories.
In simulation, predictive supervision and temporal representations
provide task-dependent gains that concentrate on physical-property
inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on
contact-rich assembly.

Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the
main qualitative trends. Prompt Fusion raises mean success from 40.00%
to 63.00%, tying Dual-Path Fusion overall while exceeding the no-force
baseline on every task. Both temporal designs achieve higher
physical-property inference success than current-sample Prompt Fusion,
but lower assembly success than the no-force baseline. These results
show that similar overall success rates can conceal different tradeoffs
across manipulation demands, supporting ForceBench’s practical value for
comparing force integration designs.

Our contributions are threefold:

A unified benchmark for force integration.
ForceBench provides eight tasks with parameterized physical conditions,
1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, and shared evaluation
with task- and category-level outcomes for six-axis wrist-force
integration.

A systematic comparative study.
We evaluate observation conditioning, auxiliary predictive
supervision, and temporal force representations on a shared VLA
backbone, characterizing their benefits and limitations across
physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction,
and contact-rich assembly.

Real-world evaluation of benchmark findings.
We evaluate eight systems across five real-world tasks in 800 trials.
The results support the main qualitative trends observed in
simulation and reveal task-dependent tradeoffs that overall success
rates alone can obscure.

1. A unified benchmark for force integration.
ForceBench provides eight tasks with parameterized physical conditions,
1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, and shared evaluation
with task- and category-level outcomes for six-axis wrist-force
integration.

2. A systematic comparative study.
We evaluate observation conditioning, auxiliary predictive
supervision, and temporal force representations on a shared VLA
backbone, characterizing their benefits and limitations across
physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction,
and contact-rich assembly.

3. Real-world evaluation of benchmark findings.
We evaluate eight systems across five real-world tasks in 800 trials.
The results support the main qualitative trends observed in
simulation and reveal task-dependent tradeoffs that overall success
rates alone can obscure.

title: RoboSpan: Learning Modular Coordination Policies for High-DoF Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation with Teleoperation
authors: Keqiang Ren,Xuecheng Ye,Hanyu Liu,Zhihua Wang,Tao Jian,Yunsheng Ma,Jiayi Wen,Xinran Li,Zhigong Song
abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
introduction:
Imitation learning, which acquires manipulation skills from human demonstrations, offers a core route for robots to rapidly learn complex interactive capabilities  [1, 2]. Driven by the demands of unstructured real-world scenes, robots are increasingly moving beyond fixed workbenches toward whole-body mobile manipulation systems that integrate mobile navigation, bimanual manipulation, and multimodal perception  [3, 4, 5]. This evolution also raises two core challenges: motion coordination among heterogeneous body modules and error accumulation in long-horizon complex tasks.
A whole-body mobile manipulation robot typically comprises a mobile base, manipulators, and dexterous hands, which differ markedly in action-space dimensionality, motion scale, control period, and optimization objective  [6, 7, 8]: the base handles large-range locomotion and global pose adjustment with a long control period, whereas the arms and hands perform close-range, high-precision fine manipulation  [5, 6]. Modeling all modules jointly within a single policy sharply expands action dimensionality, increasing learning difficulty while masking the motion characteristics of each module and degrading per-module control precision  [9]. Realizing efficient inter-module information exchange and coordination while preserving each module’s specialized control capability is thus a central problem for whole-body embodied intelligence, since forcing heterogeneous modules into one shared output space inevitably trades global mobility for local dexterity and ultimately limits real-world deployment.
Expanding the workspace also complicates task workflows and lengthens execution time. Methods designed for short-horizon, single-scene tasks are prone to cumulative error over multi-stage, long-cycle real-world tasks, causing a steep decline in the middle and late stages  [10]. Vision-language models (VLMs) can decompose high-level natural-language instructions into executable sub-task sequences through semantic understanding  [11, 12], offering new possibilities for hierarchical long-horizon execution. However, combining hierarchical task decomposition with low-level body-module coordination into a complete pipeline from semantic instructions to whole-body actions still lacks a systematic solution, which is the gap this work aims to close.
At the manipulation level, existing platforms mostly employ simple grippers or suction cups inadequate for complex dexterous interactions  [13, 14]. Bionic dexterous hands add DoFs and manipulation flexibility, yet without contact-state feedback they still suffer from unstable grasping and poor precision under vision-limited conditions. Distributed tactile sensing captures contact-force distribution and slip trends that vision cannot, offering an important route to improving fine manipulation  [15, 16, 17] Most tactile studies, however, target hand manipulation itself; how tactile information propagates across modules to assist the coordinated decisions of the arms and the mobile base remains largely unexplored.
To address these issues, this paper proposes HMF, a hierarchical modular learning framework for high-DoF whole-body mobile manipulation, together with the companion teleoperation and demonstration platform RoboSpan. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

1) A high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration-collection platform:: RoboSpan integrates mobility, manipulation, and multimodal perception with 29 control DoFs in total, and a foot-IMU-based locomotion/elevation interface enables synchronous multi-module teleoperation and time-aligned data collection.

2) Full-palm distributed tactile sensing and 2-D representation: a full-palm sensing scheme with a 2-D image representation preserves the distribution of contact pressure and yields a tactile–visual isomorphic representation, providing a unified feature basis for cross-module tactile empowerment.

3) The HMF framework and COMET policy: HMF suppresses long-sequence error accumulation through VLM-driven stage decomposition, while COMET uses inter-modular cross-attention to improve whole-body coordination and task success while preserving per-module control precision.

title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
authors: Colton Crosby,Hao Wang,Mac Schwager,Somil Bansal
abstract:
State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice.
We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy’s progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model π0.5\pi_{0.5} and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control.
Additional results and videos are available on the project website.
introduction:
Visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of complex tasks from rich sensory observations [1, 2, 3], yet they remain brittle at deployment and can fail in ways they cannot recover from on their own.

The dominant response is to scale policy learning itself, with more data, more compute, and larger architectures [4, 5].

While effective, these approaches are expensive and require access to the policy’s parameters and training pipeline — access a practitioner increasingly does not have, since strong policies are increasingly served as inference APIs or shipped with closed weights. When the weights are out of reach, deployment-time correction is a promising avenue.

We therefore ask how a policy that has already been trained and deployed can be improved without modifying the policy itself. We assume only black-box access: the parameters, architecture, and action-generation procedure are unknown, and the policy can only be queried for actions. Fine-tuning and methods that steer the policy’s internal sampling are therefore inapplicable, and improvement must come from an external wrapper that monitors execution and intervenes through actions alone. Two requirements make this demanding: policy rollouts are costly, so the wrapper must be learned from few labeled on-policy executions, and all monitoring and planning must keep pace with the control loop while the policy executes.

Our approach is based on monitoring-and-intervention, or filtering [6, 7], which in control theory most often enforces safety: a filter watches the nominal policy and overrides it only when a constraint would be violated [8, 9]. We instead filter for task completion. Rather than characterizing and avoiding every failure mode, an intervention seeks to return the system to a state from which the nominal policy can complete the task. The intuition is that a capable policy need not be replaced or retrained when it falters; a short corrective action is often enough to put it back in its basin of success.

The framework has two components. A monitor tracks the nominal policy’s execution and detects when it is no longer progressing toward task completion; we instantiate it with a policy-conditioned liveness value function [10], learned from on-policy rollouts with sparse episode-level outcome labels, that estimates how close the policy is to completing the task. When the value indicates a loss of progress, a planner briefly overrides the policy and searches a compact latent world model — trained on the same rollouts plus auxiliary play data — for a short corrective action sequence, then hands control back.

Critically, the same value that triggers intervention also scores the futures the world model imagines, directing the planner toward states from which the nominal policy can recover.

Methods that generate video futures report seconds-scale intervention times [11, 12], forcing either a pause or a control rate too low for responsive manipulation. We therefore design around deployment latency: the world model is compact, candidate futures are evaluated in parallel, and planning emits an action chunk rather than a single action. In our hardware experiment a planning cycle takes 108108 ms, which, amortized over the chunk, keeps the monitor–planner loop above 1010 Hz.

We summarize our contributions as follows. First, we formulate deployment-time improvement of visuomotor manipulation policies under a strict black-box access model and cast it as liveness filtering: an external wrapper intervenes briefly to return a fixed nominal policy to its basin of success. Second, we present a real-time instantiation in which a single policy-conditioned liveness value both monitors execution and guides corrective planning in a compact latent world model, with a data-informed action proposal that makes the search efficient. Third, we validate it across policy classes: on the ten-task LIBERO-Goal suite our method improves π0.5\pi_{0.5} [13] from 72.6%72.6\% to 81.5%81.5\%, outperforming offline-RL and safety-filtering baselines, and on a Franka Panda manipulator it improves a diffusion policy [14] from 40%40\% to 60%60\% while operating within the policy’s control loop.

title: GS-PRM: Gaussian Visual Roadmap for Image-Goal Navigation
authors: Ashraf Siddique,Kyung Min Han,Young J. Kim
abstract:
Image-goal navigation requires a global planner that connects visually specified endpoints while providing observations that a local policy can follow. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides map-registered RGB, opacity, and depth renderings, but does not explicitly encode navigable topology. We introduce GS-PRM, a Gaussian visual roadmap whose milestones, local connections, and visual references are constructed directly through 3DGS rendering without deriving an occupancy grid or signed distance field. We define render-based collision-free (RC-free) configurations and paths. Panoramic depth supplies conservative clearance for milestone validation and adaptive coverage, while edge-aligned orthographic rendering tests the robot’s swept volume.
We establish conditional soundness and sufficient conditions for deterministic query completeness and probabilistic construction completeness of GS-PRM.
To validate the performance of GS-PRM, we conduct experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating long-horizon navigation using goal-conditioned policies guided by GS-PRM. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS-based navigation system, our GS-PRM-based navigation system achieves up to a twice higher average success rate and reduces travel time by up to 57.2% when both systems complete the navigation task.
introduction:
Image-goal navigation is a visual navigation problem that requires an agent to navigate to the location represented by a given goal image [1]. The image conveys appearance, but neither the goal pose nor a traversable route, and the destination is usually outside the current camera view. A goal-conditioned visual policy can reliably act only toward a nearby, recognizable observation within its training and control horizon. Long-horizon navigation, therefore, requires a persistent global topology that connects the localized query images and decomposes the route into reachable visual subgoals. It must also provide map-registered observations for repeated pose correction, since odometric drift can otherwise cause the physical robot to deviate from the planned route.
This task requires two forms of persistent scene information: a global planner needs the connectivity of traversable space, whereas the online robot needs map-registered visual observations for localization and feedback.

Probabilistic roadmaps (PRMs) construct a reusable graph by sampling collision-free milestones and connecting them through geometrically validated local paths [2, 3]. However, conventional PRMs assume sufficiently accurate workspace geometry for collision checking, which can require many expensive collision tests. For physical robots, reconstruction and localization errors can further invalidate these geometric tests. Moreover, conventional PRMs lack the visual observations needed for image-based localization and feedback.

Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is attractive in this setting because it represents metric, map-registered appearance and supports fast rendering of RGB, opacity, and depth from arbitrary viewpoints [4]. These renderings can provide visual references for localization and geometric evidence for planning through a common scene representation.
However, since raw Gaussian primitives are optimized for view synthesis and do not directly correspond to physical obstacles, a render-native planner must explicitly define what its renderer certifies.

Existing Gaussian-map planners take several approaches to this problem. SplatNav performs collision checking against Gaussian confidence ellipsoids and constructs safe volumes [5]. GaussNav and related systems derive voxel, bird’s-eye-view, or other planning maps from a Gaussian scene [6, 7]. Other work directly renders visual subgoals for a learned navigation policy [8]. These methods demonstrate that 3DGS is useful for navigation. Still, they do not provide a persistent coverage-induced roadmap in which the same rendering interface defines milestone validity, local connectivity, image queries, and visual route references.

We address these limitations with GS-PRM, a coverage-driven Gaussian visual roadmap. PRM provides a persistent multi-query topology, while 3DGS provides map-registered observations that are absent from a conventional roadmap.
Using a single rendering interface, GS-PRM evaluates milestones and local connections, attaches image-defined endpoints, and generates visual references along the selected route.
We introduce the concept of render-based collision-free (RC-free), a conservative notion of free configuration space under some rendering assumptions,
providing a relationship between rendered evidence and planning. Clearance-adaptive coverage then reduces redundant
milestones in open areas while retaining finer resolution near constrained
regions.

The contributions of this work are:

We construct a Gaussian visual roadmap from the same map-registered 3DGS renderings used for planning, localization, and image-goal guidance, without deriving a separate occupancy or distance-field planning map.

We define RC-free milestones and local connections using conservative, thresholded depth, and state the assumptions under which their accepted configurations and paths lie within physical free space.

We construct a connected roadmap from certified clearance-adaptive regions and establish sufficient conditions for probabilistic construction completeness and deterministic query completeness of a completed roadmap.

For long-horizon visual navigation, we integrate image-based endpoint localization, validated roadmap attachment, and rendered visual subgoals for a goal-conditioned local policy.

We conducted a diverse set of experiments in both simulated and real-world
environments, demonstrating the effectiveness of GS-PRM for long-horizon
navigation. In particular, DevGRU combined with GS-PRM achieves a 50%
success rate, whereas standalone DevGRU achieves a 0% success rate.
Compared with another 3DGS-based planner, SplatNav, our GS-PRM combined with straight-line planner (SLP) also
achieves up to twice higher success rate and a 57.2% reduction
in travel time.

2. We define RC-free milestones and local connections using conservative, thresholded depth, and state the assumptions under which their accepted configurations and paths lie within physical free space.

3. We construct a connected roadmap from certified clearance-adaptive regions and establish sufficient conditions for probabilistic construction completeness and deterministic query completeness of a completed roadmap.

title: Dual-arm Cooperation for Tabletop Wiping with Temporal Object Removal
authors: Pengqi Zhang,Longchang Yu,Daohan Li,Liang Yan,Hangxin Liu
abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as  milp (milp). By integrating  lbbd (lbbd), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencing and timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ  komo (komo) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to  tamp (tamp) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9×9\times and execution makespan by approximately 40%40\%.
introduction:
Wiping a tabletop surface to remove dust, stains, or liquid spills is a common domestic chore, and automating this task with service robots is highly desirable [1, 2]. Effective wiping requires the robot’s end effector to thoroughly cover the entire planar surface. This could be accomplished by solving a coverage problem [3, 4, 5] in robotics, which has been extensively studied in the  cpp (cpp) literature [6, 7, 8, 9]. CPP-based methods have achieved great success in applications such as robotic vacuum cleaning [10, 7, 8], surface inspection and polishing [11, 12, 13, 14], where obstacles are typically modeled as static occupancy to be avoided.

However, in real-world domestic settings, desks, kitchen counters, and workbenches are often scattered with everyday objects that partially occlude the tabletop surface. When standard CPP is directly applied in such situation, the robot’s end effector is instructed to detour around objects, leaving large portions of the surface uncleaned (see Fig. 1(a)). Moreover, such detouring motions increase the risk of collisions and lead to inefficient trajectories. As a result, achieving complete, safe, and efficient surface coverage in cluttered tabletop environments remains a challenging open problem.

To address this problem, we leverage a dual-arm robot that incorporates temporary object removal to clear obstructions. In particular, one arm performs coverage wiping while the other temporarily removes obstructing objects by picking them up and placing them back after the corresponding surface region has been wiped. This cooperated behavior enables the robot to reach regions that would otherwise be inaccessible. In principle, such behavior can be formulated within a  tamp (tamp) framework [15, 16, 17], where symbolic actions such as pick, place and others are defined at the task level and instantiated into continuous motions after proper sequencing.

However, directly applying conventional TAMP to this problem is often suboptimal for tabletop wiping. Standard TAMP frameworks typically focus on generating feasible sequences of symbolic actions, relying heavily on the assumption of atomic actions and instantaneous state transitions. Under this discrete modeling paradigm, the system state is updated instantaneously between action steps, making it especially difficult to represent the continuous temporal overlap required for coordinated execution. Consequently, without an explicit mechanism to coordinate motion duration, the two arms are forced to operate sequentially rather than concurrently [18, 19, 17], leaving one arm idle while the other performs its task, as shown in Fig. 1(b). This not only increases the overall task completion time but also prevents the robot from fully exploiting the advantages of bimanual cooperation. Although TAMP provides a natural formalism for dual-arm tabletop wiping, an additional mechanism is required to coordinately plan bimanual actions to achieve efficient and complete surface coverage.

In this work, we propose a dual-arm cooperative planning framework that explicitly reasons about concurrent wiping and temporary object removal to achieve efficient and complete tabletop cleaning. Our approach first constructs a set of primitive actions for wiping and object handling, and formulates a  milp (milp) problem to optimize their sequencing and temporal coordination, promoting concurrency between the two arms (see Fig. 1(c)). Crucially, to ensure physical feasibility in cluttered environments, we incorporate a  lbbd (lbbd) strategy that iteratively refines the MILP schedule using geometric feedback from the motion planner. The resulting high-level plan is then refined using  komo (komo) to generate smooth, collision-free motions that are physically feasible for execution on a real robot. The simulation and physical experiment demonstrate that our framework achieves significantly larger surface coverage while reducing task completion time compared to conventional TAMP approaches.

Surface cleaning
has long been studied as a coverage problem in robotics. Classical cpp has succeeded in static surface cleaning tasks like floor and window wiping [6, 7]. However, tabletop wiping introduces manipulable clutter. Existing approaches predominantly treat obstacles as immutable constraints, focusing on passive collision avoidance that inevitably leaves occluded regions uncleaned [8, 20, 21, 3, 10]. To guarantee maximal coverage, our formulation integrates CPP with active, reversible object rearrangement to explicitly recover obstructed workspace.

Bimanual Manipulation
research has extensively explored safe motion synchronization [22, 1] and compliance [23, 24, 25], but it primarily focuses on collision-free execution. Relying solely on low-level coordination limits overall efficiency due to the lack of proactive action scheduling [26, 27]. To overcome the limitations of purely reactive coordination, our approach elevates dual-arm synchronization to the task planning level. By explicitly optimizing the timing of wiping and rearrangement, we maximize bimanual concurrency rather than merely avoiding collisions.

Task and Motion Planning
seeks to formally integrate discrete high-level reasoning and continuous low-level control [16]. In standard TAMP implementations, the task planning layer typically relies on symbolic planners (e.g., PDDL-based [18], VKC-based [17]) to resolve causal dependencies [28, 29].
However, a fundamental limitation of these approaches is the assumption of atomic actions and instantaneous state transitions. Since they optimize for logical plan length rather than continuous execution time, standard planners lack the intrinsic metric to seek concurrency, typically converging to sequential solutions. To address temporal reasoning, planners such as POPF [30] and LPG [31] introduce durative actions and heuristic search over temporal action graphs, enabling partial concurrency. However, they primarily operate in a symbolic domain and do not explicitly incorporate continuous geometric feasibility during planning.
More recent work on multi-arm and makespan-aware planning considers coordination across multiple manipulators [32] and explicitly optimizes execution time under coupled task constraints [33], highlighting the importance of temporal coordination in multi-robot systems.
In contrast, our work focuses on a task-specific dual-arm tabletop wiping problem with temporary object removal. We emphasize coordination between coverage wiping and object rearrangement under fixed primitive abstractions, where geometric feasibility is handled by an external motion optimization module.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (i) We propose a hierarchical dual-arm planning framework that integrates coverage wiping with active, reversible object removal, enabling complete access to occluded regions that are unreachable by conventional collision-avoidance strategies. (ii) We introduce Geo-MILP, a task planner that explicitly optimizes the temporal coordination of dual-arm actions, and combine it with a lbbd scheme to iteratively refine the schedule with geometric feedback, ensuring that the generated concurrent plans are not only time-efficient but also physically executable. (iii) We validate the proposed framework which achieves near-complete cleaning coverage in cluttered environments through extensive simulations and physcical experiments.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II provides a high-level system overview of the proposed coordinated framework and its hierarchical modules. Section III details the formulation of Geo-MILP task planner, and the LBBD-based geometric feedback mechanism. Section IV describes the KOMO-based motion planner used for trajectory generation and feasibility verification. Section V presents the simulation and physical experimental results. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper with discussions.

title: Dungeon and Visibility World Generator
authors: Edwin Mériaux,Antonio Loría,Gregory Dudek
comment: This points to our git repo used in our many projects for standardization and reproduction of scientific work

introduction:
Robotic exploration, coverage and deployment algorithms require reproducible
environments whose geometry and visibility can be varied independently of
the algorithm. This work provides a configurable generator for two- and
three-dimensional worlds, with continuous free-space geometry, discrete
occupancy grids and geometric line-of-sight queries. It supplies benchmark
worlds and observations, rather than exploration policies.

The generator supports six geometry classes (orthogonal,
polygonal/polyhedral and curvilinear in 2D and 3D) and six construction
families (scattered rooms, clusters, winding passages, caverns, branches
and loops). Room and passage dimensions, obstacle configurations and
placement can be controlled through fixed values, uniform ranges or
probability distributions. Configurations, seeds, geometries and visibility
results are saved for reproducible comparisons.

The implementation is available at
https://github.com/EdwinMeriaux/Dungeon_and_Visibility_World_Generator.

Let d∈{2,3}d\in\{2,3\}. A continuous world occupies a bounded domain
D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, with free space 𝒲⊆D\mathcal{W}\subseteq D. Positions have
real-valued coordinates: (x,y)(x,y) in two dimensions and (x,y,z)(x,y,z) in
three dimensions. Let RR be the combined room region, PP the
combined passage region, and OO the combined obstacle region. Then
𝒲=(D∩(R∪P))∖O.\mathcal{W}=\bigl(D\cap(R\cup P)\bigr)\setminus O.

This combines rooms and passages, keeps them inside the domain, and
removes obstacles.
The continuous representation describes wall locations without imposing a
grid. In 2D, the saved geometry is a polygon; enclosed obstacles appear as
holes, and curved boundaries are approximated by short straight segments.
In 3D, rooms and passages are combined into a solid free region, with
obstacles removed. A surface mesh is also saved for visualization, while
the solid itself is used for geometric checks.

title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning
authors: Linyi Huang,Guowei Huai,Weibin Liu,Shulong Jiang,Ping Tan,Weixuan Zhang,Hui Zhang,Jie Song
abstract:
While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors.
Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning.
However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact.
Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution.
To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks.
Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation.
This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation.
Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances.
The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.
introduction:
Functional dexterous manipulation is central for robot applications from factories to homes.
We study this setting through representative tasks in precise tool use, contact-rich rotation, and constrained-space manipulation.
For example, Thin-Handle Tool Retrieval (Fig. 1C) requires extracting a foam-embedded handle through a narrow opening where direct grasping is blocked.
The robot must place fingertip contact on the exposed handle, coordinate arm motion with multi-finger levering to create access, and form a precision grasp without losing contact.
Small contact errors can cause slipping, trapping, or collisions with the opening.
These stages require precise contact, high-DoF arm-hand coordination, and recovery from contact errors, making functional dexterous manipulation challenging to learn and execute.

Specifically, precise contact requires the robot to place fingertips on task-relevant regions and regulate force as local contact changes.
High-DoF arm-hand coordination requires arm motion, multi-finger contact, and contact timing to be synchronized within one execution sequence.
Because fine-grained contact tasks are sensitive to small deviations, policies must recover from slipped contact, missed insertion, partial progress, or premature force application rather than only reproduce nominal successful trajectories.

Existing learning routes have made substantial progress, but these challenges remain only partially addressed for functional dexterity.
Precise contact can be explored at scale in simulation, enabling robust dexterous manipulation performance
[30, 5, 52, 35, 51, 32]. However, sim-to-real transfer is difficult for functional manipulation due to its intricate contact dynamics.
High-DoF arm-hand behaviors can be represented by imitation learning (IL) and pretrained visuomotor policies from demonstrations and robot datasets [8, 56, 3, 31, 18, 2, 48].
However, collecting real-world demonstrations for functional dexterity remains costly and noisy because each trajectory must jointly specify arm motion, multi-finger contact, and contact timing, which are difficult for an operator to perform at the same time, especially considering the embodiment gap between human and robotic hands [13, 36]. Furthermore, these demonstrations usually focus on successful cases, providing limited evidence for recovery after failures.
Recovery from execution errors can be improved by real-world RL from online physical outcomes [21, 24, 26], but direct exploration and human correction in the full arm-hand action space are inefficient for learning reactive recovery.

To address these limitations, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation.
For fine-grained finger control and precise contact execution, HiFun adapts kinesthetic hand-motion priors with residual RL and real contact feedback, producing functional hand skills grounded in physical interaction.
To improve exploration efficiency in high-DoF arm-hand coordination, HiFun freezes the hand skills as action primitives and trains a coordination policy over arm motion and skill activation, with DMP-augmented rollouts providing initial coverage.
During online fine-tuning, human corrections are provided through the hand-skill interface to make interventions more consistent and effective, while a multi-head critic improves temporal coordination and intervention advantage weighting (IAW) prioritizes useful corrections for reactive recovery.
Together, this factorization reduces the burden of full arm-hand demonstrations, exploration, and correction, enabling reliable functional dexterous manipulation with efficient online training.
We evaluate HiFun on six functional dexterous tasks across two dexterous hands, as shown in Fig. 1.
HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training, outperforms IL and flat human-in-the-loop RL baselines, and remains robust to disturbances, while ablations verify the contributions of the hand-skill and coordination components.

In summary, our contributions are: (1) a hierarchical real-world RL framework that decouples high-DoF arm-hand control into functional hand-skill learning and skill-conditioned coordination, enabling efficient real-world learning of functional dexterous tasks; (2) residual-RL hand-skill learning that adapts kinesthetic priors with real contact feedback for fine-grained contact execution;
(3) skill-conditioned coordination that uses hand skills as action primitives, DMP-augmented rollouts for efficient initial coverage, a multi-head critic for temporal coordination of arm motion and hand activation, and IAW for sample-efficient online recovery learning.

title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
authors: Yunze Liu,Jing Wang,Shenrui Wu,Wenkun He,Guanqi Zhan,Xianzheng Ma,Junyu Chen,Wenhang Ge,Haozhan Tang,Yuchao Gu,Zhuoyang Zhang,Zekai Wang,Dantong Niu,Zhen Dong,Yuke Zhu,Trevor Darrell,Linxi "Jim" Fan,Song Han,Han Cai
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching not only its task,
but also its current stage of execution and the continuation that should
follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first
vision–language–action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three
modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations.
Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints for physical-experience
retrieval, and the resulting representation retrieves historical
continuations as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus
of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, which
evaluates 4,000 queries against a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Our model achieves
47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, surpassing action-free Gemini
Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Across controlled retrieval
studies, removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision,
indicating that execution information is a central part of the retrieval key.
We then study how this shared retrieval space transfers beyond retrieval
metrics through two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses
retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning,
increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8%
on the LIBERO difficult subset. Both interfaces also improve task progress in
real-robot evaluations. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow
task-local memory and refine how retrieved context is used around a frozen
GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success,
compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently
evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the
latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout.
Together, these results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can
support both robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
introduction:
Robot policies increasingly use experience supplied in context.
GEN-1.5 [1] and S1 [2] demonstrate
Robot In-Context Learning from sensorimotor or video examples. In our experiments,
GPT-6 Astra [3] generates robot actions from observations and execution
history. These capabilities make experience selection part of the control problem.
Demonstration-conditioned world action models (WAMs) need useful existing
examples; policies acting repeatedly must organize accumulated experience.
Both raise a representation question:
how should physical experience be represented for task- and stage-sensitive retrieval?

Task similarity alone is insufficient. Reaching toward a bowl and withdrawing
after placement can share objects and an instruction yet require different
continuations. Language specifies the goal, vision the
interaction state, and native action the ongoing motion. The retrieval endpoints
have different temporal roles: the query describes the present, whereas a
candidate records what followed an earlier interaction. Predictive retrieval
therefore requires sensitivity to task intent and execution stage: the goal is
an appropriate recorded continuation, not simply a similar scene.

General-purpose embeddings align vision and
language [4, 5, 6], while
action-aware metric learning connects perception or language with
behavior [7, 8].
We introduce Robota-Embed, a unified vision–language–action
(VLA) embedding model for physical-experience retrieval. To our knowledge, it is
the first to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries
and recorded continuations. Each endpoint yields one vector, so native action
informs retrieval itself. Source-specific projectors handle
heterogeneous action formats.
Retrieval training combines predictive alignment, multimodal grounding and
discrimination, and representation regularization.

We construct a multi-source training corpus and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench,
with 4,000 queries and 8,000 gallery candidates spanning human, simulated,
and real-robot experience. Nearby same-episode clips distinguish finding the
right experience from locating its recorded continuation. Across four sources,
Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level
R@1. Native action adds information beyond text and images: with backbone,
data, and training budget matched on DROID, adding action raises clip-level
R@1 from 59.8% to 78.7%. Complementary retraining and query-masking studies
examine which information the representation learns and uses.

Figure 1 connects retrieval to demonstration conditioning and
memory-based interaction. Embed2ICL supports robot in-context learning
through two policy interfaces. For
DreamZero [9], retrieved videos initialize the visual
cache without policy updates. For Fast-WAM [10], we
fine-tune the policy to condition on precomputed Context Tokens from retrieved
demonstrations. Both interfaces improve simulation task success and real-robot
task progress. Random-reference controls show that useful context depends on
reference selection.

Embed2Evolve extends retrieval to context management for agentic
robots. Repeated attempts grow task-local memory, while execution feedback
refines retrieval, refresh, and retained-history settings around a frozen
GPT-6 Astra policy. Policy and embedding weights remain fixed. Across five
ManiSkill tasks, the selected context harness raises success from 24% with
Direct to 68%, using 43.7% fewer policy tokens per test rollout. To examine
the retrieval model’s role, we independently repeat evolution with
Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B from the same initial memory under the same search
protocol. Its harness reaches 33% success; Embed2Evolve uses approximately
79.5% fewer tokens than this baseline. Token averages include failed tests
and exclude development.

We make four contributions.

Robota-Embed. A unified embedding model that jointly
encodes vision, language, and native action at both endpoints for predictive
physical-experience retrieval.

Data and evaluation. A multi-source training corpus,
Robota-Embed-Bench, and controlled studies of temporal precision, representation
learning, and native action’s contribution beyond vision and language.

Embed2ICL. Training-free and training-based interfaces that
turn retrieved demonstrations into useful policy context, evaluated in
simulation and on real robots.

Embed2Evolve. Embedding-guided memory and context evolution
around a frozen policy, improving success and token efficiency under matched
comparisons of retrieval embedding models.

1. Robota-Embed. A unified embedding model that jointly
encodes vision, language, and native action at both endpoints for predictive
physical-experience retrieval.

2. Data and evaluation. A multi-source training corpus,
Robota-Embed-Bench, and controlled studies of temporal precision, representation
learning, and native action’s contribution beyond vision and language.

3. Embed2ICL. Training-free and training-based interfaces that
turn retrieved demonstrations into useful policy context, evaluated in
simulation and on real robots.

4. Embed2Evolve. Embedding-guided memory and context evolution
around a frozen policy, improving success and token efficiency under matched
comparisons of retrieval embedding models.

title: IMU-Bench: Benchmarking Wrist IMU Representations Across Kinematic, Semantic and Clinical Tasks
authors: Yiquan Li,Aidan Bradshaw,Chenfeng Gao,Karan Ahuja
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a common sensing modality for studying human movement. Embedded in everyday smartwatches, accelerometers and gyroscopes capture motion relevant to activity recognition [78], clinical motor assessment [65] and human–computer interaction [33, 71], with additional cues for articulated pose estimation and inertial odometry. Like the shadows in Plato’s allegory of the cave [50, Book VII, 514a–517a], different downstream tasks reveal distinct aspects of the same underlying human motion, each offering only a partial view [28]. These perspectives raise the question of whether these views share a representation.

Self-supervised learning has demonstrated substantial reuse of unlabeled wearable recordings. Yuan et al. [78] show transfer from large-scale free-living accelerometry to activity recognition across datasets and populations. Inertia-1 examines objectives, architectures, scale and sensing configurations across activity recognition, freezing-of-gait detection and disease prediction [75]. These studies establish transfer across classification tasks and sensing conditions, while leaving less understood how the same representations support articulated joint rotations, metric velocity and motion–language correspondence.

These targets also allow us to examine whether different forms of motion supervision are complementary. Task-transfer studies in vision provide a precedent for measuring such relationships [79]. For wrist IMUs, we ask both how broadly pretrained features transfer and whether supervision for one motion target improves or compromises their usefulness for others.

We present IMU-Bench, a benchmark of ten tasks from eight datasets addressing these questions (Figure 1). We compare six self-supervised methods pretrained on unlabeled activity and daily-living recordings together with simulated wrist motion. Evaluation spans classification, pose and velocity estimation, and IMU–language retrieval, using six-channel inputs from a single wrist. Beyond frozen probing and fine-tuning, we examine supervised source-task transfer and selected joint-training pairs. The results reveal a distinction between broadly useful pretraining and compatible task supervision. Full-body pose and odometry improve over training from scratch after fine-tuning, and each kinematic task’s best frozen source is another kinematic task, whereas under frozen probing no supervised source approaches the pretrained encoder on language retrieval. Five of the six kinematic transfers survive, at about half their size, when the tasks are evaluated on disjoint participants, and the observed trade-offs show why individual-task performance alone is insufficient to characterize a shared wrist representation.

We make three contributions:

A benchmark and comprehensive evaluations. IMU-Bench brings together ten tasks across six families to evaluate wrist-IMU representations through categorical, kinematic and motion–language prediction targets. We compare six self-supervised methods under matched encoder capacity and common task protocols, alongside training from scratch and retrained task-specific systems.

A benchmark and comprehensive evaluations. IMU-Bench brings together ten tasks across six families to evaluate wrist-IMU representations through categorical, kinematic and motion–language prediction targets. We compare six self-supervised methods under matched encoder capacity and common task protocols, alongside training from scratch and retrained task-specific systems.

A reusable pretrained wrist-IMU model. We provide InrtlWrist, a masked autoencoder pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion. Among the six controlled methods, it achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks. Fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of the ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and IMU–language retrieval.

An analysis of cross-task transfer and complementarity. We measure how source-task supervision and joint training affect other prediction targets. The experiments distinguish beneficial transfer between kinematic tasks from the gap that remains to the pretrained encoder on motion–language retrieval under frozen probing, and identify joint-training gains that come at the expense of the paired task. Additional analyses examine pretraining volume and motion coverage.

The benchmark code and the leaderboard are available on the project website, https://spicexlab.github.io/imubench/; pretrained models will be released there.

2. A reusable pretrained wrist-IMU model. We provide InrtlWrist, a masked autoencoder pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion. Among the six controlled methods, it achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks. Fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of the ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and IMU–language retrieval.

Additional analyses examine pretraining volume and motion coverage.

title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
authors: Liqian Ma,Vaibhav Saxena,Utkarsh Aashu Mishra,Shuo Cheng,Yongxin Chen,Danfei Xu
abstract:
Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate Active Generative Simulation: optimizing a simulator’s data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150%150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable.
Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io/
introduction:
While recent large-scale real-robot datasets have advanced generalist policies [1, 2, 3], relying exclusively on real data remains expensive, labor-intensive, and safety-constrained. Generative simulation offers a scalable alternative data source by procedurally synthesizing scene layouts, assets, and tasks [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. We refer to the variables controlling these environments, such as camera poses, object arrangements, visual appearance, and task goals, as data generation parameters.

Given data generation parameters, a generative simulator can instantiate environments and generate large numbers of demonstrations with minimal human intervention [9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. However, the utility of simulation data remains limited by the sim-to-real gap. Domain randomization and system identification can mitigate this mismatch, but often require substantial human effort and cannot eliminate residual gaps [14]. A promising alternative is sim-and-real co-training, where real demonstrations anchor learning to the deployment domain while simulation provides scale and diversity [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Co-training can outperform training on real data alone [17, 16, 20], but not all generated data is useful: misaligned camera poses, object layouts, visual factors, or task goals can provide little benefit, and exact alignment may be impossible when the simulator lacks the target setting. This raises a central question:
Among the vast space of possible simulation environments, which data should be generated to maximize the performance of a sim-and-real co-trained policy?

Current simulation data-generation strategies largely rely on manual heuristics [21, 22] or uniform randomization [23, 24]. Overly broad training distributions can degrade policy learning when many samples are irrelevant to the target task [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. Prior work suggests that task-aware alignment helps [16], but manually tuning high-dimensional generation parameters is laborious, requires expert knowledge, and can be misleading when exact alignment is impossible.

In this work, we formulate Active Generative Simulation: determining a distribution over simulation parameters such that co-training on the resulting synthetic data maximizes target-task performance. To efficiently tackle this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that uses a sparse probing dataset to train an auxiliary rater network, which assigns utility scores to simulation samples based on their contribution to real-world validation performance, automatically guiding the active generation of a targeted synthetic dataset.
In summary, our core contributions are:

We formulate Active Generative Simulation, shifting simulation data generation from fixed distribution to controllable and targeted synthesis.

We introduce MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified parameter space, without manual parameter alignment.

We show that MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and offline retrieval, achieving a 150%150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation while matching the performance of manual expert alignment.

We demonstrate scalability and generalization of MetaGenSim: proxy-curated datasets transfer to fine-tuning π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and MetaGenSim can exploit partially aligned data when exact task alignment is unavailable.

1. We formulate Active Generative Simulation, shifting simulation data generation from fixed distribution to controllable and targeted synthesis.

2. We introduce MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified parameter space, without manual parameter alignment.

3. We show that MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and offline retrieval, achieving a 150%150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation while matching the performance of manual expert alignment.

4. We demonstrate scalability and generalization of MetaGenSim: proxy-curated datasets transfer to fine-tuning π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and MetaGenSim can exploit partially aligned data when exact task alignment is unavailable.

title: Spacecraft Pose Tracking via Kinematic Prediction and Selective Event Correction
authors: Yonglong Zhang,Guanning Yao,Shuo Zhang,Yifan Yang,Yang Liu†,Zongwu Xie
abstract: In initialized spacecraft tracking, a short-horizon motion prediction remains available as event support changes. Observation-Aligned Event Innovation (OA-EI) uses events to correct selected components of this prediction. A constant-body-twist model propagates the complete pose; the event encoder proposes rotational and normalized image-plane translation corrections, retaining propagated axial depth. Candidate magnitudes come from a bounded Scale Gate and a deterministic activity factor, with empty windows returning the prediction unchanged. Evaluation uses four FRESH physical-event trajectories, twenty rollout starts, and three training seeds. Each rollout starts from two reference poses and then uses self-fed estimates. At 7.7 seconds, rotation and translation errors fall from 41.63∘41.63^{\circ}/57.28 mm for prediction alone to 15.73∘15.73^{\circ}/22.41 mm for OA-EI, reductions of 62.2% and 60.9%. Failure rates fall from 20.0% to 1.67%. Matched ablations favor the rotation–bearing interface for overall pose accuracy; combining scaling with activity support gives the lowest errors at every tested event-retention level. On Jetson Orin Nano, the measured in-memory update takes 44.56 milliseconds at the median and 58.77 milliseconds at P95.
introduction:
Event cameras record brightness changes asynchronously, offering fine temporal sampling and a wide dynamic range [1]. For spacecraft tracking, the projected structure changes with motion and illumination, and event support varies in both amount and spatial coverage. Relative navigation, inspection, and robotic servicing require continuous estimates of target orientation and translation through these changes. Sparse observations can coincide with motion that is still predictable over a short interval.

Most spacecraft perception pipelines recover pose from current image evidence. SPEED and SPEED+ benchmark image-based estimation [2, 3]; SPADES and FRESH extend evaluation to synthetic and physical event recordings [4, 5]. Event-based approaches recover geometric keypoints for pose estimation, then use smoothing or optimization to improve temporal consistency [6, 7, 8]. Initialized tracking also has recent pose history. A short-horizon motion model can predict the complete next state before the current event window is used for correction.

With that prediction available, the event branch must decide which components to correct and how much correction to inject. Full-pose re-estimation includes components already represented by the motion model; a selective update leaves the remaining components to the prediction. The magnitude matters beyond the current timestamp. An inaccurate correction enters the pose history used for later predictions, coupling state selection with update scaling throughout the rollout.

Observation-Aligned Event Innovation (OA-EI) applies this selective update to a complete six-degree-of-freedom prior from constant-body-twist propagation. The event branch predicts rotational and normalized image-plane translation candidates relative to the prior, while axial depth stays with propagation. Translation is thus split into bearing correction and depth prediction. Two scale coefficients, learned from error-minimizing scales along frozen candidates, set the correction magnitudes. Event count and spatial activity supply a deterministic support factor. The corrected pose becomes part of the next prediction history; with an empty window, the current prior is returned exactly. Neither CAD geometry nor keypoints are required by the event branch.

Prediction alone, full candidate injection, and OA-EI are evaluated under a common recursive protocol. Matched state-update and injection ablations examine state selection and correction scaling separately from this main comparison.

The contributions are:

The event-to-pose interface corrects rotation and bearing while retaining axial depth from the complete kinematic prediction.

Candidate-scale supervision is combined with event-activity support to bound injection. Empty event windows give an exact prediction fallback.

Multi-start self-fed evaluation on physical event recordings shows reduced recursive pose errors and improved accuracy under severe event sparsification. Matched ablations examine state selection and injection scaling.

1. The event-to-pose interface corrects rotation and bearing while retaining axial depth from the complete kinematic prediction.

2. Candidate-scale supervision is combined with event-activity support to bound injection. Empty event windows give an exact prediction fallback.

3. Multi-start self-fed evaluation on physical event recordings shows reduced recursive pose errors and improved accuracy under severe event sparsification. Matched ablations examine state selection and injection scaling.

title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
authors: Hanlong Li,Sihan Tan,Takeshi Ashizawa,Benjamin Yen,Kazuhiro Nakadai
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA’s success by −38.0-38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over KK paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.816.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores −32.4-32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores −28.0-28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays −27.6-27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy’s success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0+2.0 points, against −32.0-32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy’s reliance on the instruction unchanged.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map a camera image and a natural-language instruction to robot actions (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b). Many are language models fine-tuned to emit actions. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024), for example, is a 7B Llama-2 model that outputs actions as vocabulary tokens. On LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), the standard simulation benchmark for these policies, each released checkpoint is fine-tuned on exactly ten instructions, one fixed string per task, and evaluated on the same ten strings, character for character (Kim et al., 2025), which in NLP terms is an extreme case of single-template instruction tuning. Users will not phrase a request exactly as the training data did, and language models are sensitive to how a prompt is worded (Sclar et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024; Mizrahi et al., 2024), so a benchmark score says little about what happens when the instruction is reworded. We ask how much rewording costs such a policy, and whether that loss can be recovered at test time, without retraining, the way prompt ensembling and self-consistency recover accuracy for language models.

The natural test-time remedy comes from language models. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) samples several answers and keeps the majority, and prompt ensembling (Jiang et al., 2020) aggregates answers over rewordings of a query. The VLA analogue is paraphrase consensus: rephrase the instruction KK ways, query the policy once per phrasing, and execute the medoid, the action closest to all the others, a continuous majority vote that always returns one of the policy’s own actions. It needs no training or verifier, and test-time selection over sampled actions already helps VLAs (Kwok et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2026). Prompt ensembling, however, works for language models pre-trained on many phrasings, where rewordings are comparably good prompts. A VLA fine-tuned on one string per task has seen only one good prompt, and every paraphrase may be a worse one. We implement paraphrase consensus (LCC, Language-Consensus Control) with paired, per-step logging and run it on OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO-Spatial with and without a distractor object, and Goal) and base OpenVLA (Spatial and Long). For these two policies and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on all four suites, we also measure how much of each policy’s success needs the instruction at all. We find that unweighted consensus does not help. The per-step logs trace the failure to the members themselves, which points to a fix at training time.

Test-time consensus does not recover what a paraphrase costs. One paraphrase, held for the episode, changes base OpenVLA’s success by −38.0-38.0 points. Consensus with the training instruction among the members costs base OpenVLA 16.816.8 points and OFT 4.04.0 on Goal; without it, neither the medoid of the paraphrases nor the paraphrase the policy is most confident in comes close to the training instruction (−32.4-32.4, −28.0-28.0). The reason is that paraphrases are not exchangeable. Self-consistency aggregates KK draws from one conditional, whereas KK paraphrases are KK conditionals, only one of which the policy was fit to. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase does reduce variance, beating greedy decoding by +10.4+10.4, yet stays −27.6-27.6 below the training instruction (§4.3).

A paraphrase costs a policy only where its success needs the instruction. A wrong-instruction probe, a partial-input baseline (Poliak et al., 2018; Gururangan et al., 2018; Kaushik and Lipton, 2018; Thomason et al., 2019), gives another task’s instruction in the same scene. Base OpenVLA needs the instruction for nearly all of its success on every suite. OpenVLA-OFT and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) pay a paraphrase cost only on LIBERO-Goal, where all of their success needs the instruction, and lose a far smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA does (§4.4). This qualifies LIBERO-Plus’s conclusion that fine-tuned VLAs “degenerate into vision-action models” (Fei et al., 2026).

The fix is at training time. LoRA post-training on the same demonstrations with paraphrased instructions moves the one-paraphrase effect from −38.0-38.0 to +2.0+2.0, while a matched control trained on the original instructions stays at −32.0-32.0. The result holds for a second seed, transfers to phrasings withheld from training, carries to OpenVLA-OFT on Goal, and leaves the policy reading its instruction. It costs about an hour of training once, whereas consensus queries four instructions at every step (§5).

Contributions. (i) A paired, per-timestep measurement of paraphrase consensus on two policies in five settings, with the mechanism read from the logs and tested by an exchangeable-sampling control and a confidence-weighted selector. (ii) An instruction-reliance probe on all LIBERO suites, a partial-input baseline for embodied models, and the finding that paraphrase cost appears only where reliance is high, across twelve policy–suite pairs from three policies. (iii) The established remedy, training on paraphrases (Xiao et al., 2023), measured with three controls we did not find reported for prior remedies (Hou and Zhao, 2026; Yin and Zhang, 2026): a matched training control, transfer to withheld phrasings and types, and a grounding check.
