title: Learning in Orbit: Onboard Training and Closed-Loop Attitude Control with a Thermal Segmentation Model on a Spacecraft
authors: Elena Sorina Lupu,Hannah Grauer,Phaedrus Leeds,Nikhil Ranganathan,Connor Lee,Sulekha Kishore,Cailyn Smith,Shon Cortes,Brian Hardy,Benjamen Bycroft,Darren W. Rowen,Soon-Jo Chung
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract:
Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations.
A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard.
In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon.
In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
introduction:
One of the goals of space exploration is to enable robotic systems to autonomously explore environments far from Earth [1].
Missions will increasingly rely on spacecraft capable of perceiving and learning from their environment and taking actions without a human-in-the-loop.
Such autonomy is essential for deep space exploration because communication delays, limited bandwidth, and mission complexity make reliance on ground operation impractical.

Achieving this goal requires spacecraft that can run learning algorithms for perception, estimation, planning, and control.
Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) [2, 3, 4] have already improved the capabilities of robotic systems on Earth, for example in quadcopters [5], ground vehicles such as those developed by Waymo and Tesla, and walking robots [6, 7].
These capabilities have become core components of autonomy stacks in terrestrial robotics, where perception models are tightly integrated with control systems.

From a robotics perspective, space can be treated as another environment in which robotic systems must operate.
Although physical conditions differ from those of Earth [8], perception, state estimation, planning, and control remain the same. The robotics community has made substantial progress in addressing these problems in terrestrial settings, and there is no fundamental reason why similar technologies cannot be deployed in space, provided that they are rigorously tested and their failure modes are characterized and mitigated at reasonable cost.

Spacecraft autonomy has historically relied on more classical algorithms due to the lack of available compute.
For example, the primary flight computer onboard the Perseverance rover (launched in 2020) is based on the RAD750 processor, a radiation-hardened CPU operating at 200 MHz and with 256 MB of RAM [9].
Recently, Mars Helicopter used a Qualcomm Snapdragon 801 processor [10], a commercial smartphone processor, showing that COTS compute can fly on Mars.
Other recent missions have demonstrated the feasibility of running machine learning (ML) models onboard spacecraft, but were focused on inference and training tasks on the CPU [11, 12].

In this work, we demonstrate that a spacecraft can learn and adapt in-flight, and use its learned perception models to act autonomously in orbit with minimal human supervision. Specifically, we present a flight demonstration of a closed-loop system in which a vision segmentation model is trained directly on a spacecraft in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and used to command the spacecraft’s attitude control system to point the spacecraft to a desired location, in this case the Moon. Our primary contributions are as follows:

onboard, vision-based model learning: We successfully performed both training and inference on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX’s GPU on a CubeSat. Based on publicly available information, this marks the first time that machine learning models were trained on a GPU on a free-flying spacecraft11

title: Benchmarking 3D Reconstruction for Under-Ice Robotic Perception in Arctic Environments
authors: Klára Orbán,Ashwin Nedungadi,Ana-Ştefania Kogălniceanu,Bianca-Marcela Sava,Bastian Cieply,Raul-Alexandru Simon,Kuderna-Iulian Benţa,Stefan Lüdtke
comment: Presented at the ICRA 2026 Workshop "From Sea to Space: Advancing Perception in Harsh Domains" (S2S), Vienna, Austria, June 1, 2026. 8 figures, 2 tables. Workshop:this https URL
abstract: As the Arctic transitions toward a seasonally ice-free state, capturing the complex morphology of submerged sea ice is crucial for advancing models of ocean-ice-atmosphere heat exchange and monitoring under-ice habitats.
introduction:
The complex morphology of the underside of sea ice poses significant challenges for robotic perception and mapping in polar environments. Under-ice exploration relies on onboard sensing to operate in regions inaccessible to direct human observation, making accurate geometric representations of surrounding ice structures critical for navigation and situational awareness [1]. Features such as ridges, keels, and melt-induced cavities create highly irregular surfaces that complicate both visual and acoustic sensing. High-resolution surface mapping of the ice underside therefore plays a key role in developing and evaluating computer vision and sensor fusion pipelines, improving localization and obstacle awareness for under-ice robotic systems, and enabling realistic testing of autonomous navigation in these challenging environments.

Traditionally, acoustic sensing has been used to characterize subsurface ice textures [2]. The predominant modality for obtaining large-scale geometry has involved upward-facing multibeam sonars operated from Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) or Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs).

While acoustic sensing provides robust geometric data, it is inherently insensitive to color variations and unable to capture optical information such as light transmittance, albedo or surface texture. Visual photogrammetry, specifically Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [3], offers a framework to address this information gap. However, the subsurface ice remains a significant challenge to computer vision approaches because of extreme light attenuation, backscatter from suspended scatterers, and the sparse feature texture of ice surfaces, which are often repetitive in nature, leading to significant geometric instability.

In this work, we introduce a benchmark for under-ice robotic perception based on data collected during the MOSAiC expedition [4]. We evaluate vision-based 3D reconstruction methods by comparing Structure-from-Motion (SfM) reconstructions generated using Agisoft Metashape [3] and monocular depth estimation using Depth Anything V3 (DA3) [5] against coincident upward-looking multibeam sonar measurements and analyze their domain-dependent behaviour across real and simulated under-ice environments.

The main difficulty in enabling such a comparison is the lack of direct spatial correspondence between acoustic and visual data, as the two modalities differ in sensing principle, sampling density and observable coverage. To address this, we establish a common evaluation domain that enables consistent comparison between the two sensing modalities.

Collecting additional real-world data is logistically impractical, considering that Arctic expeditions are infrequent, costly, and weather-constrained. A simulated environment is a highly controlled setting where lighting, turbidity, ROV paths, and sensor settings can be precisely defined and consistently reproduced. Utilizing the geometry data from real-world MOSAiC sonar surveys ensures that our simulated environment is realistic and also fully controllable.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are:

a benchmark for evaluating vision-based 3D reconstruction methods against spatially aligned under-ice multibeam sonar data,

a cross-modal alignment procedure that defines a shared sensing region for quantitative comparison between optical and acoustic reconstructions,

a simulation pipeline in HoloOcean based on sonar-derived ice geometry for generating controlled multimodal under-ice datasets.

1. a benchmark for evaluating vision-based 3D reconstruction methods against spatially aligned under-ice multibeam sonar data,

2. a cross-modal alignment procedure that defines a shared sensing region for quantitative comparison between optical and acoustic reconstructions,

3. a simulation pipeline in HoloOcean based on sonar-derived ice geometry for generating controlled multimodal under-ice datasets.

title: DexMimic: A Generalist Dexterous Hand-Object Tracking Policy via Value-Guided Reset Allocation
authors: Zhexi Luo,Zhixuan Xu,Rui Yang,Zeyu Xiao,Yiwen Hou,Lin Shao
comment: including of supplementary material. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Achieving human-like dexterous manipulation remains a central challenge in robotics. Learning from human hand–object interaction (HOI) datasets offers a promising pathway to diverse dexterous skills, yet existing physics-based approaches train specialist policies for individual trajectories, thereby limiting skill reuse at scale. We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand–object tracking policy jointly trained across diverse HOI trajectories. Efficient joint training requires allocating each rollout to both an undertrained phase and a starting state that supports continued tracking. DexMimic realizes this insight through Value-Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts the initialization distribution online to prioritize difficult phases and select reset states with higher expected tracking returns. We further introduce a benchmark spanning training, fine-tuning, and generalization. Experiments show improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster fine-tuning, and the potential for zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects; larger training sets further improve efficiency and generalization. Finally, we validate DexMimic on a real-world dexterous manipulation platform.
introduction:
Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control show that a single reference-conditioned policy can learn diverse motor skills from large-scale motion datasets and reuse the learned control prior beyond individual training motions [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Extending this paradigm to dexterous hand–object interaction could enable robots to acquire diverse manipulation skills from human demonstrations [8, 9, 10, 11]. These demonstrations capture fine-grained finger coordination, contact transitions [12, 13, 14], and regrasping behaviors that are difficult to specify through task-specific rewards. A generalist hand–object tracking policy could provide a reusable low-level control interface conditioned on human demonstrations. Realizing this vision requires bridging the substantial embodiment gap between human and robot hands in morphology, actuation, and contact dynamics [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23].

Recent physics-based reinforcement learning methods have made substantial progress in bridging this gap for individual demonstrations, using general tracking objectives for hand motion, contact states, and object motion [16, 17]. However, these methods typically train a specialist policy for each trajectory or a small trajectory subset. This specialist formulation limits the reuse of learned control priors across trajectories and incurs repeated training costs as the demonstration set grows. To overcome these limitations, we investigate what prevents existing trajectory-specific training pipelines from scaling to a generalist policy that jointly learns diverse hand–object interaction (HOI) trajectories and transfers the learned interaction prior to unseen references.

We find that Reference State Initialization (RSI) [1], a standard mechanism for initializing training episodes, becomes a key bottleneck when diverse trajectories share a limited rollout budget. RSI initializes each episode with a state sampled from a human motion retargeted to the robot’s morphology. This initialization scheme introduces inefficiencies in both the choice of starting states and the allocation of training across reference phases. First, kinematically retargeted states may contain physically inconsistent contacts, causing fast-fail resets before useful interaction experience is collected. Second, uniform timestamp sampling oversamples simple phases while undertraining difficult phases. As the trajectory set grows, these inefficiencies reduce the useful interaction experience available to each trajectory, limiting the scalability of joint policy learning.

We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand–object tracking policy built on the insight that effective joint training requires adapting the initialization distribution alongside policy learning. Its Value-Guided Reset Allocation uses critic estimates to prioritize under-learned reference phases and select starting states that support continued tracking from phase-conditioned reset buffers. Each training iteration collects rollouts from the current initialization distribution and uses the same experience to update the policy and critic, refine reset candidates, and adjust phase priorities, thereby shaping the distribution for subsequent rollouts. On 50 challenging bimanual tasks, DexMimic achieves 88.40% success versus 56.64% for ManipTrans, while reducing average training time per trajectory by a factor of 15.5. Scaling co-training from 20 to 500 trajectories raises zero-shot success on unseen objects from 2.00% to 51.65%, demonstrating an increasingly transferable interaction prior. We further validate DexMimic on a real-world robotic platform.

In summary, our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand–object tracking policy with Value-Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts reset state and phase allocation alongside policy learning. (2) We introduce a benchmark for generalist hand–object tracking that evaluates joint-training performance and efficiency, fine-tuning on unseen references, and zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects. (3) We demonstrate improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster adaptation, and stronger zero-shot generalization as training scales. We further validate DexMimic on a real-world robotic platform.

title: Receding-Horizon Next-Best-View Planning for Highly Occluded Target Perception
authors: Ayse Gul Yildiz,Rekha Raja
abstract:
Robotic systems that must acquire information about a specific target often face severe occlusion from surrounding structures or from the target itself, such that a single camera viewpoint provides only partial information. Active perception must therefore select viewpoints that progressively reveal unobserved regions. However, conventional local next-best-view (NBV) methods typically select viewpoints according to their immediate utility, which can overlook views that provide limited information initially but enable more informative observations from subsequent viewpoints. We formulated local target perception as a short-horizon sequential view-planning problem and proposed a Receding-Horizon Next-Best-View (RH-NBV) planner that evaluates candidate sequences of future viewpoints rather than isolated views.
RH-NBV is evaluated on a UR5e manipulator with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera in simulation as well as on physical robot against a gradient-based NBV planner, and random search, using a coffee mug and Stanford bunny under controlled occlusion and a tomato plant with natural self-occlusion. Under heavy occlusion, RH-NBV achieves substantially higher target information recovery, reaching 63.8% ROI coverage versus 34.2% and 85.5% occluded-surface recall versus 7.4% for the single-step NBV baselines on the most occluded mug configuration. A controlled horizon ablation shows that this improvement arises from multi-step reasoning rather than additional computation. RH-NBV provides the greatest benefit for strongly occluded targets, while myopic NBV remains competitive and substantially cheaper when visibility is less constrained.
introduction:
Active perception enables a robot to acquire information that cannot be obtained from a fixed sensor configuration [1]. By moving its sensor to different viewpoints, a robot can improve the visibility of task-relevant regions and acquire complementary observations of the environment [2, 3]. This capability is particularly important when a target is partially occluded by surrounding structures or by itself, as in object inspection, manipulation, harvesting, and active 3D perception.
Next-best-view (NBV) planning provides a framework for actively selecting such viewpoints according to their expected utility. While many NBV approaches address global scene exploration or reconstruction, local target-centric perception requires sensing to be focused on a specific region of interest (ROI).
Under occlusion, however, viewpoint utility can be sequential: a view with limited immediate information may reveal regions that enable more informative subsequent observations. Conventional local NBV methods typically select the viewpoint with the highest immediate utility and therefore do not explicitly account for these downstream effects.

We formulated local target perception under occlusion as a short-horizon sequential view-planning problem and proposed a Receding-Horizon Next-Best-View (RH-NBV) planner. RH-NBV samples candidate sequences of future viewpoints and evaluates each sequence using a semantic, occlusion-aware utility while propagating the belief state through the sequence. The planner executes only the first viewpoint of the selected sequence, incorporates the acquired observation into the belief, and recomputes the planning horizon. This formulation enables the planner to account for the future visibility that a viewpoint can create while retaining the feedback and adaptability of conventional single-step planning. We evaluate RH-NBV on a UR5e manipulator with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera against a gradient-based NBV planner, and random search. Experiments use a coffee mug and the Stanford bunny under a controlled six-stage occlusion ladder, as well as a tomato plant exhibiting natural self-occlusion.
The results show that RH-NBV provides its greatest advantage under strong occlusion, while myopic NBV remains competitive and substantially cheaper when the target is more readily visible.

The paper makes several contributions: (i) a formulation of local target perception under occlusion as a short-horizon sequential NBV problem, where a viewpoint depends on the future visibility it enables; (ii) RH-NBV combines semantic target information, occlusion-aware utility, and in-horizon belief-state propagation; (iii) an evaluation across controlled and natural occlusion conditions showing that the benefit of non-myopic planning increases as target visibility becomes more constrained, (iv) implemented the method on a physical systems and showed the validation and effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Tread: A Visuo-Inertial Framework for Terrain and Locomotion Context-Aware Gait-Phase and Speed Estimation in Wearable Robotics
authors: Debadrata Sarkar,Akash Bachhar,Aman Arora
comment: Supplementary video: A video demonstrating real-time operation of the complete visuo-inertial inference pipeline is available atthis https URL
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Powered lower-limb exoskeletons, exosuits, and active prostheses
require timely information about the user’s locomotion for adapting assistance to gait
phase, walking speed, and terrain. Errors in timing or locomotion mode can reduce
assistance quality and compromise stability [8, 15].
Recent reviews identify intention recognition and synchronization with the user as
key requirements for wearable-robot autonomy [14]. Accordingly,
a practical perception layer should estimate four quantities continuously: upcoming
terrain, locomotion mode, gait phase, and walking speed. Although these quantities
are often estimated separately, their integration into a single body-worn pipeline
remains less explored.

Vision provides anticipatory information about terrain, with egocentric datasets
supporting terrain recognition and its use for terrain-aware assistance [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
IMUs mounted on the lower limbs provide low-power, illumination-independent
measurements for locomotion-mode, gait-phase, and speed estimation
[6, 9]. Gait phase estimation has been addressed using both discrete and continuous formulations
[11, 12, 10], while walking speed is commonly estimated
with a dedicated regressor [13]. While plantar Force Sensitive Resistor (FSR)s are also widely used to derive ground truth [8] of gait-events, they are rarely used in deployment.

Several limitations in state-of-the-art literature motivate the framework proposed through this work. Existing systems commonly treat terrain, locomotion mode, gait phase, and speed as independent tasks, while coupled approaches may rely on hard switching between mode-specific estimators, which produces undesirable estimations near terrain/locomotion mode transitions [7]. Gait-phase estimation accuracy has also been reported to degrade during terrain changes [9]. In addition, a unified system requires synchronized
vision, multi-segment inertial measurements, gait-phase ground truth, and speed
labels, although these are most conveniently collected under different protocols.
Preparatory leg movements pose further challenge because stationary fidgeting can
otherwise be mistaken for walking. Finally, raw accelerometer and gyroscope signals can be sensitive to sensor mounting and re-donning variability [16].
Table I compares the proposed framework with representative
studies.

The main contribution of this work is a connected visuo-inertial pipeline that
produces terrain, locomotion mode, bilateral gait phase, and walking speed estimation using
a unified sensing suite deployed for onboard edge inference. Anticipatory Terrain Perception (ATP)
uses vision to estimate the upcoming terrain, while Terrain-Aware Locomotion Mode
Identification (TALMI) estimates the locomotion being executed. Rather than
passing only a hard locomotion label downstream, the full TALMI softmax posterior
is retained as a Probabilistic Locomotion Context (PLC) vector. Gait phase and
walking speed are then decoded from a shared Gait Kinematic Encoder (GKE) through
lightweight task-specific heads. A dedicated fidgeting class separates stationary
leg movements from walking and a terrain-conditioned hierarchy allows datasets
collected under different protocols to be combined within one estimation chain.

All inertial models use pitch and yaw Euler angles obtained from onboard sensor
fusion rather than raw accelerometer and gyroscope channels. This representation
is gravity-referenced and expresses limb orientation in an anatomically meaningful
frame, reducing dependence on sensor-frame rotation and small mounting variations
[16], that otherwise make the reproducability and scalability difficult when used in a new wearable hardware. The experiments therefore evaluate whether this compact
representation, combined with terrain and locomotion context, is sufficient for
terrain-aware mode identification, continuous bilateral gait-phase estimation, and
walking-speed regression.

title: RingNav: Task-Shaped Circular Memory for Visual Heading
authors: Naitri Rajyaguru,Aryan Tajne,Stephen Jardim,Cornelia Fermuller,Yiannis Aloimonos
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation
systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether
persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present
RingNav, a 10.610.6k–parameter visual heading estimator that
constrains its memory to the circular manifold S1S^{1}. RingNav learns only
the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on
the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge,
RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by 27%27\% and
accumulated heading error over 44 sec by 15%15\% relative to a
similarly sized learned-memory model.
The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and
exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav
transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation.
RingNav runs at 27.327.3Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at 33.433.4Hz.
introduction:
Autonomous visual navigation remains difficult to deploy on small robots because computation and memory are limited. Visual odometry (VO) estimates camera motion from an image sequence, while simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) additionally maintains a representation of the environment for localization [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. These systems recover rich motion and scene information, even when a task may require only a small part of that state.

Recent work has reduced the cost of visual navigation for resource-constrained robots through smaller estimators and task-specific representations [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. These methods reduce the cost of estimating or storing navigation information. A second source of complexity is what the robot must remember over time. Different behaviors require different information, ranging from no persistent state for reactive control to full pose for metric navigation. This idea is consistent with purposive and task-driven estimation, which seek representations sufficient for the behavior rather than recovering the full physical state [12, 13, 14].

We call this principle task-shaped memory: when the state to be remembered and its update rule are known from the task, learning is needed only to estimate how that state changed from the observations. Different tasks can therefore require different memory structures, as shown in Table I.

These examples illustrate the design principle; this work experimentally studies only heading on S1S^{1}.

For heading, the state has one degree of freedom but is periodic: after a full rotation, the robot faces the same direction again. Its possible values therefore form the circle S1S^{1}. A recurrent network can instead encode heading in a latent hidden state ht∈ℝnh_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, whose representation and update are learned from data. Task-shaped memory instead fixes the heading state to S1S^{1} and its update to circular rotation, leaving only the visual turn between consecutive images to be learned.

This leads to RingNav, a 10.610.6k-parameter monocular heading estimator. A lightweight image-pair network estimates the visual turn Δ​ψt\Delta\psi_{t} between consecutive frames, and this turn directly rotates the stored heading on S1S^{1}. The estimator is further constrained so that identical images produce exactly zero turn and reversing the image order reverses the predicted turn. To isolate the effect of these choices, we compare RingNav with similarly sized alternatives that learn the persistent state, its update, or both.

We present RingNav, a 10.6k-parameter monocular heading estimator that learns the turn between images while storing heading on S1S^{1} and updating it directly with the predicted turn, rather than learning the persistent state and its update.

We constrain the visual turn estimator so that identical frames produce exactly zero predicted turn and reversing the image order exactly reverses the prediction.

We provide controlled evaluation under unseen, degraded, repeated, and missing visual information, together with comparisons to rotation-only and full visual-motion estimators, zero-shot transfer to real Crazyflie flight data, and edge-runtime evaluation.

1. We present RingNav, a 10.6k-parameter monocular heading estimator that learns the turn between images while storing heading on S1S^{1} and updating it directly with the predicted turn, rather than learning the persistent state and its update.

2. We constrain the visual turn estimator so that identical frames produce exactly zero predicted turn and reversing the image order exactly reverses the prediction.

3. We provide controlled evaluation under unseen, degraded, repeated, and missing visual information, together with comparisons to rotation-only and full visual-motion estimators, zero-shot transfer to real Crazyflie flight data, and edge-runtime evaluation.

title: Contact-UAN: Unsupervised Actuator Networks as a Residual World Model for Humanoid Control
authors: Nolan Fey,Khai Nguyen,Yash Prabhu,Gabriel B. Margolis,Pulkit Agrawal
abstract:
Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts.
This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques.
We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator’s physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces.
We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.
introduction:
Humanoid robots can perform diverse tasks by virtue of their general-purpose morphology, and recent advances in learning-based control within physics simulators have enabled increasingly complex behaviors [sleiman2026zest, liao2025beyondmimic, wu2026perceptivehumanoidparkourchaining, margolis2025softmimic].
For sim-to-real humanoid control, qualitative motion transfer is only a coarse measure of success; the robot must also generate force profiles with the magnitude and timing needed to move efficiently, regulate loads, and absorb impacts.
Policy optimization can exploit imperfect actuator dynamics, producing policies that may transfer qualitative motions but not force interactions, leading to excessive torques, poor commanded-force tracking, or failures during high-impulse phases (Section 4.2).
Because these forces are mediated by joint torques, we study how improving the actuator model used during policy training reduces force-level sim-to-real gaps.

The actuator model fidelity required for sim-to-real transfer is task-dependent: simple models may suffice for quasi-static behaviors, while behaviors such as efficient running, force tracking, jumping, and landing depend on accurate actuator response, force generation, and impact absorption. Analytic simulators [NVIDIA_Isaac_Sim, mujoco] provide useful physical structure, yet they often approximate actuator effects such as torque saturation and load-dependent nonlinear friction, precisely the effects that shape ground-force generation, external-force regulation, and impact absorption [Hwangbo_2019, fey2025bridging].
Domain randomization improves robustness by training over parameter ranges, but it can produce conservative policies that under-utilize hardware [tobin2017domain, muratore2022robot, xie2021dynamics, campanaro2024learning]. Online adaptation and SysID can recover performance by estimating dynamics parameters, but require choosing which simulator parameters to randomize and identify [kumar2021rmarapidmotoradaptation, liu2025locoformer, bjelonic2025towards, liao2025beyondmimic, sleiman2026zest, margolis2022rapidlocomotionreinforcementlearning, margolis2023learningphysicalpropertiesactive].
Fully learned world models (WMs) take another approach: fit dynamics directly from data and can, in principle, capture effects omitted by analytical simulators [hou2026world, li2025robotic, hansen2025hierarchical, wu2023daydreamer], but must model the full robot-environment dynamics needed for policy optimization. We therefore follow prior work in residual modeling and actuator learning [gruenstein2021residual, zeng2020tossingbot, golemo2018sim, gao2024sim, jiang2021simgan, yu2025neural, Hwangbo_2019]: retain the physical priors of an existing simulator and learn only the sim-to-real gap in the actuator command channel.

Learning such an actuator-channel residual to improve downstream transfer requires a training signal. Supervised actuator networks use measured motor torques as this signal [Hwangbo_2019], but reliable output torque sensing is unavailable on many humanoid platforms.
Without such labels, residual methods can use trajectory replay-based training instead: reset the simulator to a recorded hardware state, apply the recorded commands, and train residual commands so the simulated rollout matches the recorded hardware trajectory [fey2025bridging, he2025asap]. Critically, this objective isolates modeling error only if replay begins from a hardware-equivalent simulator state. Otherwise, the residual model may learn to correct simulation reset artifacts rather than underlying actuator discrepancies.

Matching a given hardware state in simulation is a kinematics problem for suspended, free-space motions [fey2025bridging, bjelonic2025towards]. However, such motion lacks the contact information needed to capture load-dependent actuator behavior during stance, force generation, impact, and landing.
he2025asap collect data with contacts and use a motion capture system to provide ground-truth body poses. However, consider a humanoid robot standing still: on hardware, ground-reaction forces balance its weight, but initializing a soft-contact simulator with the feet exactly at the ground surface may not produce equivalent forces. Instead, matching the hardware force interaction requires introducing slight ground penetration via adjustments to the simulated foot height and orientation, not a precise height measurement.
This is necessary because millimeter-scale foot-height and degree-scale orientation errors can substantially change simulated contact wrenches (Fig. 3).
These observations point to a critical need to address contact-consistent state initialization for replay-based residual learning.

We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world-modeling approach to training humanoid policies for force- and impulse-sensitive behaviors. The core contribution is contact-consistent state initialization from proprioception, which enables replay-based residual learning from hardware trajectories with contacts. From proprioception alone, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose, including the small ground penetration and tilt needed to initialize replay with contact wrenches consistent with the hardware trajectory, together with the base velocity needed to complete the reset state. With replay initialized in this contact-consistent state, the UAN residual can learn to correct true actuator modeling errors in simulation.

We evaluate Contact-UAN on a Unitree G1 using the state-of-the-art BeyondMimic G1 parameters as the nominal simulator [zakka2026mjlab, liao2025beyondmimic], and compare policies trained with and without UAN (Section 4). We choose downstream tasks that expose distinct actuator-sensitive force and impulse regimes: running requires torque-efficient ground-force generation, force and impedance control require accurate external-force regulation, and jumping requires takeoff impulse and landing absorption. A single UAN trained from 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data improves transfer across these behaviors.

Training in this corrected simulator yields a running policy that preserves velocity tracking while reducing hardware torque usage by 20% relative to the no-UAN baseline, showing that the UAN gives policy learning a more accurate torque signal. The same residual reduces force-tracking error by 43% and improves jumping: both reference-tracking policies transfer, while task-reward fine-tuning for higher jumps transfers with UAN but fails without it (Section 4.2). Sim-to-sim experiments reveal the importance of contact-consistent initialization and show that Contact-UAN remains effective under larger actuator gaps (Sections 4.1 and 4.3).

title: $λ_0$: Scaling Open-World Egocentric Human Data for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Lambda-humanoid Team
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly.
Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution.
We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion.
Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination.
We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations.
Building on this pipeline, we develop λ0\lambda_{0} 11
1
λ\lambda resembles “人” (human in Chinese), symbolizing learning from everyday human experience., a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training.
Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress.
λ0\lambda_{0} achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks.
We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world.
introduction:
Learning humanoid loco-manipulation across tasks and environments requires demonstrations that capture coordinated locomotion, posture, and manipulation (Jiang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026b; Hu et al., 2026; Figure AI, 2026a; Figure AI, 2026b).
Whole-body teleoperation provides visual observations paired with robot actions, but requires operators to guide a physical humanoid through each demonstration (Fu et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026b; GEAR Team et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b).
This dependence on robot availability and operation makes broader task and environment coverage costly to obtain (Shi et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026).
Scaling humanoid learning motivates a source of whole-body interaction experience that can grow beyond robot-operated collection.

Egocentric video records people’s everyday interactions across tasks and environments without requiring robot operation (Grauman et al., 2022; Kareer et al., 2025; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026; Figure, 2026).
Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning (Li et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a).
Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation (Zheng et al., 2026c; Punamiya et al., 2026).
For humanoid loco-manipulation, however, wrist and hand trajectories alone omit the locomotion and postural changes that support whole-body interaction (Shi et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a).
Recording synchronized body and hand motion captures this coordination, but motion retargeting and whole-body tracking can still leave end-effector errors due to geometric mismatch and imperfect execution (Araujo et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b).
These errors can compromise grasping and contact.
This raises our central question: Can egocentric whole-body human experience provide supervision that is both transferable to humanoids and practical to acquire at scale?

We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline that captures human demonstrations without a robot and aligns their observations and actions to the downstream humanoid (Sec. 3.4).
We match the camera and capture height to the robot setup, then remove human forearms and trackers from the images and composite rendered G1 arms.
Action alignment refines motion references and controller inputs offline to improve end-effector accuracy, producing robot-compatible state–action supervision.
We evaluate policies trained with this supervision on Unitree G1 across seven representative tasks spanning coordinated whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation (Sec. 5.1).
Using task-specific human demonstrations without target-task robot demonstrations, the evaluations achieve mean progress of 51.7% and 76.2%, respectively.

Using this capture setup, we build HumanVerse, a 500-hour corpus of human loco-manipulation spanning open-world scenes and tasks.
We record egocentric video and body motion with lightweight wearable sensors, synchronize the streams, and reconstruct hand motion from video.

We develop λ0\lambda_{0}, a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that learns from scalable human experience and progressively adapts it to humanoid control (Fig. 1).
Egocentric hand-motion pretraining draws on diverse human interaction videos.
Mid-training on HumanVerse then provides a scalable, robot-free source of supervision for learning coordinated body and hand actions, bridging video pretraining and limited, costly robot demonstrations.
Robot post-training adapts the learned behaviors to the target humanoid.

Increasing whole-body human data reduces validation loss and raises real-world task progress monotonically from 59.9% without whole-body mid-training to 80.4% with the full corpus.
Ablations identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages.
The full λ0\lambda_{0} policy achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across four real-world loco-manipulation tasks, improving over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9% and 22.5%, respectively.
Human-data training also improves progress on robot-unseen object instances observed in human demonstrations.
Our contributions are:

We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline for whole-body skill transfer and evaluate its collection efficiency and zero-shot transfer on G1 without target-task robot demonstrations.

We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion across open-world scenes and tasks.

We develop λ0\lambda_{0} to progressively adapt egocentric human interaction experience to humanoid control, and demonstrate that scaling human data with whole-body supervision improves downstream loco-manipulation.

1. We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline for whole-body skill transfer and evaluate its collection efficiency and zero-shot transfer on G1 without target-task robot demonstrations.

2. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion across open-world scenes and tasks.

3. We develop λ0\lambda_{0} to progressively adapt egocentric human interaction experience to humanoid control, and demonstrate that scaling human data with whole-body supervision improves downstream loco-manipulation.

title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
authors: Peidong Wang,Ying Chang,Zhiming Ma,Xiaocui Yang,Shi Feng,Daqi Liu,Yuzhe Yang,Xu Cao,Chuang Wang,Jian Su,Daling Wang
abstract:
Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do.
We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents.
A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks.
On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
introduction:
Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) [21, 11, 1] can perform a wide range of manipulation tasks in diverse environments.
Recent models have also made progress on long-horizon tasks [27, 22].
Yet on unseen multi-step tasks they still often fail midway.
A robot may approach the wrong target, misjudge whether a step has succeeded, or fail to execute a required motion.
Some of these failures lie in how the VLA, acting as the executor, is called and others in what it can do, and the failure itself does not tell which.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system turns its own experience into persistent changes that make it better [4, 37, 3], offers a way to repair such failures without collecting human demonstrations for every new task.
An embodied system, made of a coding agent, its skills and harness, and a low-level executor such as a VLA, can improve itself at two levels.
The harness, comprising the agent’s skills, its tools and the procedure that composes them, decides how the executor is called, while the executor’s weights decide what it can do.

Harness-level methods refine the agent’s skills and tools while keeping the executor frozen [16, 6, 18, 31, 33, 38, 30, 26, 17, 25].
Their changes are cheap, readable and easy to revert, but they stall when a task requires a motion the executor cannot perform [33, 29].
Policy-level methods instead update the executor’s weights [12, 9, 34, 5, 15, 10], some of them directing training toward tasks with low recent success [5] or toward high-risk scenarios [9], and systems that act on both levels train on the data that a refined harness produces [32, 7].
None of these methods asks whether a persistent failure lies in how the executor is called or in a motion it lacks, although the two call for different remedies.
Training on a failure that lies in how the executor is called is not only costly but also risky, as a fine-tuned policy can perform a sub-step worse than the executor it started from.

This raises a question that current embodied RSI leaves open: when should a self-improving system change the weights of its executor?
We argue that the answer is a matter of attribution.
The weights should change only for a sub-step that stays unreliable after the agent has tried other ways of calling the executor, such as other instructions, robot poses or approaches.
Refining the harness first therefore does more than fix the failures that lie in how the executor is called.
It also sets the states from which the executor is called, so that a policy trained afterwards learns the motion that is actually missing, from the states in which it will be used.

We answer this question with AdaRSI, an on-demand recursive self-improvement framework for embodied agents.
The agent first refines its harness from execution feedback, so that the harness absorbs the failures that better calling can fix without any training.
It then attributes the failures that persist, retrying a failing sub-step from a saved simulator state under different instructions and approaches, which separates a poor way of calling the executor from a motion it cannot make.
For the sub-steps that no such retry makes reliable, the agent collects demonstrations in simulation and fine-tunes a sub-step policy from the states its harness reaches.
Each new policy is evaluated on held-out start states, and the procedure calls it only where these measurements show that it helps, so a weight change enters the system only after it has been both attributed and validated.
Improvements accumulate over rounds, each starting from the system that the previous round produced.
Experience and a training budget derived from earlier tasks guide later ones, so the system improves not only itself but also the way it improves.
No human demonstrations are used, and privileged simulator state serves only to generate and label data, never at test time.

We evaluate on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365 [19, 20] under the official protocol, with GR00T N1.5 [21] as the executor.
AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites, most of all on unseen composite tasks, where it raises success from 4.6% to 13.8%, about three times the base rate.
The harness provides most of this gain, and fine-tuning, which executes only 15% of the manipulation steps, carries the tasks that the harness alone could not solve, such as one that requires opening a microwave door the VLA never opens on its own.
In paired tests from identical states, fine-tuning teaches motions that the executor lacks, but it can degrade sub-steps that the executor already completes.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step and calling the new policies by default, AdaRSI reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations.
Fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less, and its deployed system calls few of the policies it trained.
Training instead the sub-steps on which the executor succeeds least, under the same budget, gains nothing over the harness alone, even though most of the sub-steps it trains are the same, as attribution also tells the agent from which states a missing motion should be learned.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate on-demand recursive self-improvement for embodied agents, in which the decision to change the executor’s weights rests on attributing each persistent failure to the harness or to the executor, and instantiate it as AdaRSI.

We find that the harness decides whether training pays off, as it absorbs failures that would otherwise be trained on and sets the states from which policies are trained and called, while fine-tuning teaches motions the executor lacks but can degrade sub-steps it already completes.

We show on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, without any human demonstration, that training on demand improves a pretrained VLA on every suite at a fraction of the training cost of fine-tuning every sub-step.

2. We find that the harness decides whether training pays off, as it absorbs failures that would otherwise be trained on and sets the states from which policies are trained and called, while fine-tuning teaches motions the executor lacks but can degrade sub-steps it already completes.

3. We show on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, without any human demonstration, that training on demand improves a pretrained VLA on every suite at a fraction of the training cost of fine-tuning every sub-step.

title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
authors: Sayan Bandyapadhyay,William Lochet,Saket Saurabh,Jie Xue
subjects: Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
We study multi-robot Motion Planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots.
The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain 𝒲\mathcal{W} with nn vertices and kk robots R1,…,RkR_{1},\dots,R_{k} translating in 𝒲\mathcal{W} each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity.
Given a source configuration 𝐬\mathbf{s} and a target configuration 𝐭\mathbf{t} of the robots in 𝒲\mathcal{W}, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from 𝐬\mathbf{s} to 𝐭\mathbf{t} that is shortest with respect to some cost function.
Here a plan is called collision-free if all the robots stay inside 𝒲\mathcal{W} and no two robots collide with each other during the plan.
introduction:
Coordinating the motion of multiple robots that share a common workspace is one of the
oldest and most fundamental problems in algorithmic robotics. Autonomous warehouse
fleets, fleets of cleaning or inspection robots, swarms of drones, and automated
manufacturing cells all require a planner that can move many physical agents from
their initial locations to specified destinations without the agents colliding with
one another or with the static obstacles of the environment. Beyond mere feasibility,
practitioners care about the quality of the resulting motion: a plan that
wastes battery, time, or wear-and-tear on the robots is far less useful than one that
moves the robots efficiently.
Despite decades of study, the understanding of
how to compute, or even efficiently approximate, cost-optimal multi-robot motion
plans has remained remarkably incomplete, in sharp contrast with the
single-robot case, for which shortest collision-free paths can be computed exactly in
polynomial time. This gap between the single-robot and multi-robot settings is the
starting point of our work.

A setting of the multi-robot motion planning problem commonly considered in the literature is as follows.
We essentially follow the terms in the previous work [3, 4, 5].
Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be a polygonal domain in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with nn vertices, referred to as the workspace.
We are given a collection of kk robots R1,…,RkR_{1},\ldots,R_{k}, each of which is typically an axis-parallel unit square (or more generally, a polygon of constant complexity).
In most of the previous work, the robots are required to be identical, but we do not make this assumption in this paper.
A placement of a robot RiR_{i} in 𝒲\mathcal{W} is given by a vector 𝐩∈ℝ2\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that 𝐩+Ri⊆𝒲\mathbf{p}+R_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{W}.
Here 𝐩+Ri\mathbf{p}+R_{i} denote the translate of RiR_{i} with the offset vector 𝐩\mathbf{p}.
The set of all placements of RiR_{i} in 𝒲\mathcal{W} is its free space, denoted by ℱi⊆𝒲\mathcal{F}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{W}.

A configuration is a kk-tuple (𝐩1,…,𝐩k)∈∏i=1kℱi(\mathbf{p}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{k})\in\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{F}_{i},
where 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} specifies a placement of robot RiR_{i} in 𝒲\mathcal{W}.
We say a configuration is feasible if the placed robots are interior-disjoint (or collision-free).
Formally, if we write [k]={1,…,k}[k]=\{1,\dots,k\} and denote by int⁡(R)\operatorname{int}(R) the interior of a region RR, then

A motion plan refers to a scheme that translates the kk robots inside 𝒲\mathcal{W} from one feasible configuration to another one, while keeping the robots collision-free.
Some variants of the problem may care about the time cost of a motion plan.
As such, there is usually an extra unit-speed constraint in the definition of motion plans: each robot can move with a maximum speed 11 during the plan.
Formally, we define motion plans as follows.
Let L2​(⋅,⋅)L_{2}(\cdot,\cdot) denote the L2L_{2}-metric (i.e., Euclidean metric) and πi:(ℝ2)k→ℝ2\pi_{i}:(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} be the projection function defined as πi​(𝐩1,…,𝐩k)=𝐩i\pi_{i}(\mathbf{p}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{p}_{k})=\mathbf{p}_{i}, for i∈[k]i\in[k].

For each i∈[k]i\in[k], πi∘γ\pi_{i}\circ\gamma is a plane curve describing how the robot RiR_{i} moves in the plan.

When the number of robots, kk, is part of the input, even deciding whether there exists an (𝐬,𝐭)(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})-plan (without any optimization objective at all) is already a hard algorithmic problem.
Schwartz and Sharir [19] gave one of the first algorithms for coordinating disk-shaped robots among polygonal obstacles, running in time polynomial in the complexity of the obstacles but exponential in kk.
Soon after, Hopcroft, Schwartz, and Sharir [13] showed that this exponential dependence on kk is in a precise sense unavoidable: they proved that deciding the existence of (𝐬,𝐭)(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})-plans for an arbitrary number of unit-square robots translating in a rectangular workspace is PSPACE-hard, a result later strengthened and extended in several directions [1, 7, 12, 14].
Around the same time, Spirakis and Yap [20] showed that the problem for unit-disk robots is strongly NP-hard.
These hardness results already rule out, under standard complexity assumptions, an algorithm with time
polynomial in both nn and kk for testing the existence of (𝐬,𝐭)(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})-plans, let alone for the optimization variants.

Given that the general problem for unbounded kk is provably intractable, most
algorithmic results restrict attention to a small, constant number of robots, i.e., treat
kk as a parameter rather than part of the input.
For Motion Planning with a single robot (k=1k=1), an exact optimal solution can be computed in polynomial time using classical
techniques for shortest paths amid obstacles [9, 17, 18], which already indicates that the difficulty of the motion-planning problems stems from the interaction between robots rather than from planning for a single robot alone.

For k=2k=2, Motion Planning is already quite challenging, and positive results have been known only very recently.
When the workspace 𝒲\mathcal{W} is rectilinear and the cost is evaluated under the L1L_{1}-metric, Agarwal, de Berg,
Holmgren, Steiger, and Struijs [2] considered the problem with two unit-square robots.
In this setting, they gave an exact O⁡(n4​log⁡n)O(n^{4}\log n)-time algorithm for the min-sum variant and proved that the min-makespan variant is NP-hard.
In a general polygonal workspace 𝒲\mathcal{W} under the Euclidean metric, however, it is open whether the problem is NP-hard or polynomial-time solvable for any of the cost functions.
The best known result with two unit-square robots is a (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)-approximation algorithm, in fact an FPTAS, for the min-sum objective, due to Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, and Steiger [4].
Their algorithm crucially exploits the fact that, for two robots, there is always a near-optimal plan in which the robots
move one at a time; for k>2k>2 robots this property provably fails, since one can construct instances in which every near-optimal plan must move several robots simultaneously, which makes the generalization beyond two robots difficult.

For k≥3k\geq 3, the only known result so far is due to Agarwal, Holmgren, and Steiger [5], who gave a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for Min-Sum Motion Planning with kk unit-square robots, with running time (k/ε)O⁡(k2)​nO⁡(k)(k/\varepsilon)^{O(k^{2})}n^{O(k)}, in the sense that the solution returned by the algorithm is an (𝐬,𝐭)(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})-plan γ\gamma satisfying that 𝖼𝗈𝗌𝗍+​(γ)≤(1+ε)⋅𝗈𝗉𝗍1+ε+ε\mathsf{cost}^{+}(\gamma)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon}+\varepsilon, where 𝗈𝗉𝗍1+ε\mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon} denotes the cost of a min-sum (𝐬,𝐭)(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t})-plan with (1+ε)×(1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)\times(1+\varepsilon) square robots.
Note that 𝗈𝗉𝗍1+ε\mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon} is in general not bounded by any function of the actual optimum, and the bound also has an additive error ε\varepsilon, which can be removed if 𝗈𝗉𝗍1+ε≥1\mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon}\geq 1 [5].
An equivalent view of the algorithm in [5] is that it shrinks each robot by a factor of 1+ε1+\varepsilon and computes the approximation solution with the shrunk robots.
The arguments in [5] relied heavily on this shrink operation, making it difficult to transform the bicriteria-approximation algorithm to an actual FPTAS.
Furthermore, it is not clear whether the approximation algorithms in [4] and [5] can be applied to the min-max and min-makespan objectives as well.

Given the aforementioned approximation algorithms in [4, 5], the most natural question to be asked now is about the approximability of the problems for a general (fixed) kk.
Specifically, the question below has been mentioned in the previous work [4, 5] as an open question.

In this paper, we resolve (in a stronger form) the above open question, by giving the first FPTAS for Min-Sum/Min-Max/Min-Makespan Motion Planning with general polygonal robots (of constant complexity) for any fixed k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.
Specifically, we prove the following theorem.

Min-Sum Motion Planning, Min-Max Motion Planning, and Min-Makespan Motion Planning with polygonal robots admit (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)-approximation algorithms of running time f⁡(k,ε)⋅nO⁡(k2)f(k,\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(k^{2})}, for some function f⁡(k,ε)=kO⁡(k2)​(1ε)O⁡(k)f(k,\varepsilon)=k^{O(k^{2})}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})^{O(k)}.
In particular, for any fixed number k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} of robots, the three problems admit FPTAS.

We remark that the polygonal robots in Theorem 1 are not required to be identical.
In fact, there is no assumptions on the polygons representing the robots, except the constant complexity.
However, for technical reasons, our result does not generalize (without new ideas) to robots with non-linear boundaries, while the bicriteria-approximation in [5] works for unit-disk robots.

Interestingly, our algorithm in Theorem 1 is not restricted to Motion Planning in the plane, but directly generalizes to Motion Planning in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for any fixed d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} with polytope workspace and polytope robots.
To the best of our knowledge, the problem in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for d>2d>2 is widely open.

In terms of the techniques, our algorithms are substantially simpler than the previous approximation algorithms [4, 5].
The proof of Theorem 1 is essentially self-contained and only uses classic techniques in computational geometry and algorithmic graph theory.
Surprisingly, our proof does not rely on any structural results developed in the previous work [2, 4, 5].

This unified treatment is, we believe, of independent interest, since it suggests that the three common objective functions for multi-robot motion planning are algorithmically much closer to one another than their rather different behavior in the discrete multi-agent path finding setting might suggest [11, 22, 21].

subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. introduction:
3D reconstruction from under-ice AUV video is persistently unreliable: turbidity and backscatter flatten contrast, while the ice underside is often smooth and weakly textured [1, 8]. Although mitigations exist, it remains unclear whether the residual failures reflect the shortcomings of any one method or a deeper limitation of the capture geometry itself. Slow-moving AUVs sampled at low frame rates produce near-converging camera trajectories with limited translation between viewpoints, unlike the wide-baseline, well-distributed views on which most reconstruction pipelines are designed and validated. In practice, researchers face large collections of such footage where reconstruction success is difficult to anticipate, and substantial compute is routinely spent on batches that converge to geometrically fragmented output, with the failure only apparent after the fact.

Prior work in this space has largely evaluated individual pipelines in isolation
[11, 5, 13], without asking whether failures across structurally
different methods share a common, measurable cause. This distinction matters: if
failure is method-specific, the fix is method-specific tuning; if failure is
geometric, the fix is a single early warning system that generalizes across
pipelines.

This work tests four structurally unrelated reconstruction approaches: classical feature-matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model – on the same under-ice AUV footage (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream, USAP-DC 601975 [15]), and shows that all four fail for reasons traceable to the same capture regime. The main contributions of this work are:

identification of a single quantified geometric predictor: a narrow camera baseline-to-scene-depth ratio that explains the distinct failure modes of four structurally different reconstruction methods on the same footage,

a lightweight baseline-to-depth check, derived directly from foundation-model camera poses, that flags likely failure in minutes rather than hours,

a negative control against the competing hypothesis that reconstructability is predictable from image content, rather than capture geometry: a texture-usability score, tested against altimeter ground truth, did not hold up.

1. identification of a single quantified geometric predictor: a narrow camera baseline-to-scene-depth ratio that explains the distinct failure modes of four structurally different reconstruction methods on the same footage,

2. a lightweight baseline-to-depth check, derived directly from foundation-model camera poses, that flags likely failure in minutes rather than hours,

3. a negative control against the competing hypothesis that reconstructability is predictable from image content, rather than capture geometry: a texture-usability score, tested against altimeter ground truth, did not hold up.

title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
authors: Annie Bhalla,Dennis Rotondi,Riccardo Giubilato,Kai O. Arras,Wolfgang Stuerzl
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Paper accepted at International Astronautical Congress 2026, IAC-26, A3, IP, 163, x107111
abstract:
Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers remains a fundamental challenge in space
exploration, particularly in environments that are featureless, poorly illuminated,
or visually repetitive. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems based
on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer promising dense mapping capabilities; however,
their loop closure modules rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under
perceptual aliasing–a common failure mode in extraterrestrial terrain where
physically distinct locations appear visually identical to optical sensors.
This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging
(HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system.
Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures that complement
RGB appearance features, providing a modality inherently robust to illumination
changes and visual repetitiveness.
Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: the Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW)
model, which encodes spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted
frequency histograms, and the PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD) model, which captures
first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures.
Both are evaluated in combination with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors
under Strict-AND and Weighted decision-level fusion strategies.
The framework is assessed on a custom multi-modal dataset collected at the
Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) of the German Aerospace Center (DLR),
comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences totalling 65.5 m
across four planetary analog traverses, with evaluation conducted on the
MMOTS-WS loop sequence (8 m).
A key empirical finding is that the sensor’s Red-NIR spectral range (600–860 nm)
provides limited discriminability for planetary analog rock terrain: the best fusion configuration (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves
5.04 cm aligned ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of the best RGB-only configuration
(4.95 cm, SIFT-VLAD alone). The improvement over the NetVLAD baseline (8.81 cm) is attributable
entirely to replacing NetVLAD with SIFT-VLAD, not to HSI fusion;
the sensor’s Red-NIR spectral range is identified as the primary
limiting factor for the HSI contribution.
This motivates future adoption of shortwave infrared (SWIR) sensors,
which capture diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the
600–860 nm range, for planetary SLAM missions.
introduction:
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM)—the joint estimation of a
robot’s pose and a map of its surroundings from on-board sensor data—has
reached remarkable maturity over the past two decades [1].
Classical geometrically-grounded pipelines now achieve centimetre-level
accuracy in structured environments, while recent semantic extensions such as
3D scene graph representations [2] further enrich
these maps with object-level and spatial reasoning. Yet this progress has
been concentrated in information-rich, feature-dense settings: urban streets,
indoor offices, and structured facilities where visual cues are abundant and
predictable. Mapping in extreme environments—planetary surfaces
dominated by featureless regolith, visually repetitive craters, and
mineralogically diverse rocks—remains a frontier where classical SLAM
assumptions break down.

Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers must contend with exactly these
conditions. Rovers must navigate unknown, unstructured terrain autonomously,
performing in-situ scientific analysis while building consistent environmental
representations. Unlike the structured, feature-rich urban environments common
on Earth, extraterrestrial terrain is dominated by craters, regolith, rocks,
and dust that create a visually repetitive landscape. This causes
perceptual aliasing: distinct locations appear nearly identical to
optical sensors. In SLAM, this directly impairs loop closure detection:
the critical process of recognising a previously visited location to correct
accumulated odometric drift. Failed loop closures produce corrupted maps and
irrecoverable trajectory divergence, threatening mission success.

Despite visual similarity, planetary terrain is often mineralogically
diverse. Rocks of different composition, regolith with varying particle
distributions, and exposed bedrock exhibit distinct spectral signatures
in the infrared range, differences entirely invisible to conventional
RGB cameras. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) captures tens to hundreds of
narrow spectral bands per pixel, encoding material composition and
chemical properties as a high-dimensional fingerprint. These signatures
reflect what a surface is made of rather than how it appears,
and are inherently more robust to illumination changes.

Recent advances in 3DGS [3] have transformed dense visual
SLAM by enabling efficient, photorealistic scene representations.
LoopSplat [4], the first 3DGS SLAM system with explicit
loop closure, demonstrates compelling performance in structured indoor
environments using NetVLAD [5] descriptors. However,
its reliance on RGB appearance limits applicability to the visually
uniform terrain of planetary environments.

This paper introduces HyperLoop, extending LoopSplat by
integrating hyperspectral sensing into its loop closure module.
The key contributions are:

A 3DGS-SLAM architecture integrating HSI loop closure detection, the
first such combination, to the best of our knowledge.

Two HSI descriptor families: BoSW and PCAK-VLAD, adapted from
visual retrieval literature to spectral signatures.

Evaluation of Strict-AND and Weighted decision-level fusion
strategies combining RGB and HSI descriptors.

The first empirical analysis of hyperspectral loop closure on
a planetary analog dataset, yielding an empirically motivated
spectral range hypothesis for future mission hardware selection.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows:
Section 2 covers relevant background;
Section 3 reviews related work;
Section 4 describes the HyperLoop methodology;
Section 5 presents the experimental setup;
Section 6 analyses descriptor performance;
Section 7 reports trajectory and loop closure results;
Sections 8 and 9 discuss findings and conclude.

title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
authors: Julia Barth,Armin Sommer,Kunvar Thaman,Jannik Schilling
comment: main text, total. Code:this https URL
abstract:
Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents.
Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy–goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues.
We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths.
Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal’s location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0%16.0\% to 95.3%95.3\%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6%31.6\% to 84.3%84.3\% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works.
Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning specifies the intended goal only indirectly, through rewards that mark it.
Whenever a proxy co-occurs with the goal during training, the rewards cannot tell the two apart, and the agent can learn the proxy in its place.
This is why goal misgeneralization is common in reinforcement learning, and it is dangerous because the agent stays competent and its misalignment only becomes visible once the co-occurrence breaks.

So far, goal misgeneralization has mainly been characterized behaviorally, in large language models (Shah et al., 2022; Maniyar et al., 2026), in toy reinforcement-learning environments such as Procgen (Langosco et al., 2022; Ramanauskas & Şimşek, 2023) and in large pretrained control policies (Jucys et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025).
Interpretability work has studied individual agents in these environments (Mini et al., 2023; Trinh et al., 2024), mostly to understand how they navigate or represent their goal, but not goal misgeneralization itself, and mitigation attempts intervene broadly during training (Langosco et al., 2022; Abdel Sadek et al., 2025; Nait El Barj & Sautory, 2024; Armstrong et al., 2023; Trinh et al., 2024) rather than after it.
Studying goal misgeneralization in depth, from the inside and the outside, closes the gap between these lines of work, and we additionally carry it into a new and wider domain, robot control.
The leading question we ask is therefore quite direct: what actually happens to the true goal in misgeneralized agents?

To answer it, we trace the goal through the agent from the outside and the inside, asking whether the goal is represented, whether the policy reads it, whether behavior is organized around it, and whether goal-directed behavior can be recovered at test time.
We analyze three classic goal-misgeneralization environments from Procgen, Maze, Coin and Maze II, which we call Attribute Maze, and five new robot tasks on a simulated arm and quadruped, such as PushToMarker (Figure 1, Figure 13).

What looks like one failure from the outside is three distinct failures of policy alignment, target substitution, a policy shortcut and cue competition, and the goal gets lost at different depths of the agent.
We find that in Maze, replicated in a simulated arm task, the goal is inert to the policy and a place substitutes for it.
In PushToMarker a place substitutes for the goal as well, but the goal still reaches the policy weakly, which reacts to it without following it.
This is the same depth at which an action shortcut bypasses the goal in Coin.
In Attribute Maze, replicated in three more robot tasks, the goal reaches the decision as a cue or an object that competes with the proxy and loses.
We find that which repair works follows the depth, not the failure type.
Steering the existing policy redirects it to the goal’s location only where the goal reaches the decision.
Relearning the readout recovers goal-directed behavior wherever the goal still reaches the policy, and where the goal is inert, neither repair works.
Misgeneralized agents therefore cannot be understood from their behavior alone, as only knowing where the goal is lost tells us which repair can bring it back.

Our main contributions are:

We trace the intended goal through misgeneralized agents in eight environments and find three distinct failures of policy alignment at three depths, including the first internal characterization of cue and object competition and its geometry (Section 3).

We add an internal view and deepen the behavioral one to better understand goal misgeneralization. We propose the Fisher information of the policy with respect to its internal representations to isolate a policy-directed view of the internals, which lets us characterize, for example, different styles of competition. It also sharpens a proxy characterization of Langosco et al. (2022), as the Maze agent follows the top-right extreme of the current maze rather than a fixed corner.

To our knowledge, we are the first to relate which repair succeeds to where the goal is lost, and to recover goal-directed behavior at test time without further reinforcement learning or retraining the representation (Section 4).

We are the first to induce goal misgeneralization systematically in reinforcement learning for robot control and diagnose it in five simulated arm and quadruped tasks, where the failures recur.
