title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
authors: Diyuan Shi,Yiqi Tang,Hongyin Zhang,You Wu,Donglin Wang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions, enabling robots to interpret their surroundings and carry out user requests. Their potential applications span household assistance, warehouse logistics, and industrial manipulation (Collaboration et al., 2023; Intelligence et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025; Ai et al., ; Xu et al., 2026).

Conventional VLA methods learn from collected demonstrations and could generalize to new situations. However, demonstration-based training alone does not provide a mechanism for gradual adaptation after deployment. A robot may encounter an unfamiliar camera viewpoint, lighting condition, or instruction phrasing, each of which hinders task performance. The central limitation is therefore the inability to turn accumulated deployment experience into adaptive behavior.

Online Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) or interactive Imitation Learning (IIL) provide routes to deployment-time adaptation through parameter updates, using reward feedback or corrective actions, respectively (Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025a; Pan et al., 2026). However, these approaches have several drawbacks: 1) Collecting the samples needed for policy updates takes tens of minutes to hours and involves substantial human effort; 2) They typically require task-specific hyperparameter tuning; and 3) They update policy in each deployment environment, making it difficult to scale to multi-task settings. These motivate us to explore an adaptation mechanism that uses deployment feedback without parameter updates.

In this work, we propose VLRLA, a framework for equipping VLA models with in-context Reinforcement Learning (RL) capabilities. The framework augments a VLA model with a RL module that learns to use past interactions for adaptation. During deployment, action generation is conditioned on a memory of previous interactions and reward feedback, while model parameters remain fixed. As experience accumulates, this memory informs refinements to subsequent behavior, helping policy adapt to the deployment environment. The intended result is gradual improvement in task success through continued interaction during deployment and no parameter updates.

Existing VLA works vary across training datasets, policy architectures, and deployment tasks, we aim to develop a general VLRLA framework that accommodates various learning history construction strategies, policy instantiations, and integration strategies. Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate deployment-time adaptation in VLA models as an in-context reinforcement learning problem, using accumulated interactions and reward feedback to inform subsequent decisions while keeping model parameters fixed.

We propose a general framework that unifies learning history construction and adaptation-module integration to equip pretrained VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities across diverse data construction settings, model architectures, and deployment tasks.

We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on real-world robots to demonstrate the effectiveness of VLRLA. Our results show adaptation across multiple pretrained backbones and improved task success with accumulated experience, including on challenging unseen tasks.

1. We formulate deployment-time adaptation in VLA models as an in-context reinforcement learning problem, using accumulated interactions and reward feedback to inform subsequent decisions while keeping model parameters fixed.

2. We propose a general framework that unifies learning history construction and adaptation-module integration to equip pretrained VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities across diverse data construction settings, model architectures, and deployment tasks.

3. We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on real-world robots to demonstrate the effectiveness of VLRLA. Our results show adaptation across multiple pretrained backbones and improved task success with accumulated experience, including on challenging unseen tasks.

title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
authors: Minghao Guo,Qingyue Jiao,Xiujin Liu,Jianhong Pang,Ruimeng Yang,Naihao Xu,Liwei Che,Haochen Xue,Ziqi Wang,Xinying Cai,Jiaxuan Luo,Jiaxin Deng,Xuesong Ye,Jintao Qu,Wenyao Gao,Jingwen Gu,Chenyang Zhao,Shichun Liu,Guibin Zhang,Zefang Liu,Siyin Wang,Wujiang Xu,Danrui Li,Zeru Shi,Woongyeong Yeo,Shuang Liu,Wei-Chieh Huang,Weizhi Zhang,Tianyu Yang,Kangsan Kim,Yebowen Hu,Bowen Wen,Bowen Jiang,Haohao Su,Ming Yin,Sheldon Yu,Mian Zhang,Yuyan Chen,Hanrong Zhang,Kai Mei,Zihao Zhang,Mingyu Jin,Xi Zhu,Hengyi Wang,Tianxin Wei,Linyong Nan,Zhenwen Liang,Zhendong Chu,Ziqi Huang,Yongye Su,Sixun Dong,Shujian Liu,Kaiqu Liang,Jiaojiao Han,Zhaoye Fei,Kun Wang,Shihan Dou,Zhichun Guo,Xingjian Diao,Zeqi Gu,Heng Wang,Tao Feng,Cheng Qian,Hamid Palangi,Silei Xu,Xi Yun,Yi Zhu,Shilong Liu,Qingsong Wen,Sung Ju Hwang,Zuxuan Wu,Yu-Gang Jiang,Yiyu Shi,Dimitris N. Metaxas,Jiaxuan You,Julian McAuley,Mengdi Wang,Jiawei Han,Philip S. Yu,Ziyi Ye
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities.
However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings.
Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience.
We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory
structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management).
Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action.
Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy.
Based on this framework,
we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time.
Furthermore, we
discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
introduction:
Large foundation models (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026; Google DeepMind, 2026), such as LLMs and MLLMs, have become the reasoning and perception backbones of AI agents that interpret goals, plan, use tools, and act through interaction with users and environments.
An agent places the model within a continuing loop of observation, reasoning, and action (Xi et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026; Plaat et al., 2025; Chen, Celia, 2026), increasingly spanning multimodal digital and physical environments.
As this interaction unfolds over time, later decisions often depend on information and experience accumulated beyond the immediately available context. Memory provides the persistent state that bridges these interactions, carrying relevant information from prior observations and experience into subsequent reasoning and action (Hu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025e; Huang et al., 2026b).

Memory is therefore a core component of AI agents (Xu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025b).
At the most basic level, it enables continuity by preserving task state and relevant experience beyond the current interaction, allowing agents to operate coherently over long horizons (Packer et al., 2023) and across repeated interactions.
Beyond continuity, persistent memory allows agents to accumulate information over time, supporting personalization through user-specific experience (Hong et al., 2026) and maintaining consistent behavior as users, tasks, and environments evolve (Zhong et al., 2024).
By retaining task outcomes, feedback (Shinn et al., 2023), failure traces (Tu et al., 2026), and successful strategies (Fan et al., 2026b), memory enables agents to refine future decisions and accumulate reusable knowledge (Li et al., 2024) and skills (Wang et al., 2024a).

The growing demand for agents that can interpret visual information (Nguyen et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2025c), process temporally structured video and speech (Lin et al., 2026d; Someki et al., 2026), reason about and navigate 3D spaces (Gu et al., 2024), and interact with graphical and physical environments (Agashe et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b) has made multimodal capabilities increasingly essential.
To operate in these settings, an agent must integrate heterogeneous, high-dimensional observations, capture their temporal and spatial structure, and produce appropriate actions or multimodal outputs (Wang et al., 2024b).
Unlike textual-only inputs, these multimodal observations cannot always be compactly or losslessly reduced to a single representation for later use. This shift does not merely increase the volume of experience an agent may encounter; it changes the nature of what must be remembered and organized.
Consequently, multimodal memory must determine both what aspects of experience should persist and how those retained memories should remain useful as new observations accumulate and the underlying world evolves.

To investigate these two requirements, we characterize multimodal agent memory through a lifecycle with two coupled stages: formation determines what experience is retained and in what representation, while management governs how the resulting memory persists, changes, is accessed, and guides later reasoning and action. These stages are tightly coupled: decisions made during formation determine what evidence can later be recovered, revised, or verified, while subsequent use and new observations may require memories to be updated, reconciled, consolidated, or forgotten. Multimodality makes both stages substantially more challenging.

The first challenge arises during formation and representation:
A multimodal agent must decide what experience to retain, how to divide continuous or heterogeneous observations into memory units, and in what form those memories should persist.
Unlike text-centered interactions, which can be retained in a compact textual form that is directly consumable and editable (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Chhikara et al., 2025) by LLMs, multimodal experience may contain perceptual, temporal, spatial, and acoustic information that is expensive to preserve exhaustively and difficult to compress without loss.
A memory unit may correspond to an image (Nguyen et al., 2026b), image region (Wang et al., 2026j), video frame or clip (Song et al., 2024), audiovisual event (Lin et al., 2026d), object track (Fan et al., 2024), interface state (Wang and Chen, 2025), action–observation transition (Zhang et al., 2026d), trajectory (Xu et al., 2026), or complete episode (Zhang et al., 2025c).
Each unit may be stored as source media (Yu et al., 2025c), encoded as modality-specific features (He et al., 2024) or geometric state (Gu et al., 2024), abstracted into textual (Feng et al., 2026) or structured records (Long et al., 2026), compressed into a latent state (Qian et al., 2024), or internalized in model parameters (Suri et al., 2026).
Each choice preserves some aspects of experience while discarding or obscuring others, creating trade-offs among fidelity, efficiency, editability, source recoverability, and compatibility with downstream reasoning and action.

The second challenge arises during memory management: the memory state formed from prior experience must remain valid as new observations arrive, tasks progress, and environments change. The central question of multimodal memory management is not only how the memory system responds as its environment changes and experience accumulates, but also how to reconcile heterogeneous and partial observations into a consistent, evolving state. New evidence may extend an existing record (Long et al., 2026), correct an
earlier belief (Ma et al., 2026), invalidate stale state (Lei et al., 2025), connect previously separate events (Yan et al., 2026), or provide feedback about the effectiveness of prior memory decisions (Bärmann et al., 2026).
Multimodal memory management is particularly challenging because evidence is often partial and viewpoint-dependent, while the same entity or event may be represented across source media, modality-specific features, textual summaries, and structured world states (Fan et al., 2024).
Effective management must reconcile new evidence across these linked
representations (Feng et al., 2026), preserve connections to the supporting
observations (Lin et al., 2026d), and prevent stale or conflicting state from
guiding later actions (Yeo et al., 2026b).
Memory systems differ in where persistent adaptation occurs.
Their responses may range from reusing formed memory without persistent
change (Mu et al., 2026), to updating memory content or organization under a
stable policy (Mondal et al., 2026), to using feedback to improve and evolve the policy
governing future memory writing (Zou et al., 2026a), maintenance (Bärmann et al., 2026), and
retrieval (Fan et al., 2026b).

Motivated by these lifecycle challenges, we present a unified analytical framework for multimodal agent memory spanning images and documents, video and audiovisual streams, audio and speech, GUI interaction, and embodied or 3D environments. Our framework organizes the field along two analytically distinct but operationally coupled axes, illustrated in
Figure 1. Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what experience is retained, how it is organized into memory units, and the representation ultimately supplied to downstream reasoning or action. We distinguish source- and modality-specific representations, textual and structured representations, and latent and parametric representations, while separately examining hybrid architectures that combine multiple paths and often link compact abstractions to recoverable source evidence. Axis II, Memory Management, characterizes where persistent change occurs as experience accumulates: T1 Static Memory systems reuse formed memory without persistent modification; T2 Dynamic Memory systems update the memory state through a stable management policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory systems use feedback to update the policy governing future memory writing, maintenance, or retrieval. Together, these axes capture both what multimodal evidence survives into future computation and how the memory system evolves through continued experience.

Beyond providing a unified taxonomy, this study offers three broader contributions. First, we provide comprehensive coverage of multimodal agent memory across modalities, tasks, architectures, and evaluation settings, including a corpus of 297 memory architectures and 82 benchmark records in the current version of our taxonomy. Second, by jointly analyzing memory representation and management, we identify cross-cutting patterns that are difficult to observe from either dimension alone, including the prevalence of dynamic memory updates, the widespread use of hybrid representations, and the relative scarcity of deployment-time memory-policy evolution. Third, we synthesize the limitations of current systems and derive future directions around recoverable and provenance-aware memory, temporal validity and cross-representation consistency, self-improving memory management, bounded lifelong memory, governed forgetting, and lifecycle-aware evaluation.

This study focuses on
memory mechanisms in multimodal agents.
We define memory as experience-derived state that persists beyond the step in which it is formed and later affects reasoning, generation, planning, or action.
At least one non-text modality must contribute to its formation or use; transient activations, one-pass reasoning traces, and incidental prompt context are excluded unless explicitly persisted and reused.
Existing studies of agent memory classify memory by source (Zhang et al., 2025e), representation (Hu et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025e; Du et al., 2025), function (Hu et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025c; Du et al., 2025), temporal scope (Wu et al., 2025c; Du et al., 2025), and operation (Zhang et al., 2025e; Du et al., 2025), while others trace its evolution from storage to reusable experience (Hu et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2026b; Luo et al., 2026a).
Multimodal extensions cover LLM or MLLM memory types (Jia et al., 2025), VLM taxonomies (Xia et al., 2026a), and multimodal-agent architectures and storage (Xie et al., 2025; Mokaria et al., 2026), benchmarks (Xie et al., 2025), and applications (Xie et al., 2025; Mokaria et al., 2026).
In contrast, we shift the unit of analysis from memory components to the operational lifecycle: how multimodal experience becomes persistent memory, how representation constrains subsequent retrieval, revision, and verification, and where adaptation occurs as experience accumulates.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the background, formal scope, and multimodal memory lifecycle. Section 3 studies memory formation and representation, from source-preserving and modality-native memory to explicit textual and structured representations, latent and parametric memory, and hybrid source-linked designs. Section 4 examines memory management across T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory. Section 5 analyzes how representation choices constrain memory management and synthesizes corpus-level patterns across the two axes. Section 6 examines the systems mechanisms that realize these logical memory designs under resource and coordination constraints. Section 7 examines evaluation benchmarks and applications, while Section 8 discusses open challenges and future directions. Section 9 concludes the paper.

title: VLX-Go: Robust Embodied Tracking through Multi-Stage Learning and On-Policy Refinement
authors: Kyusong Lee,Heting Ying,Tiancheng Zhao
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present VLX-Go, a vision–language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision–language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
introduction:
Embodied navigation requires a robot to translate visual observations and language into motion through its surroundings. Predicting a short sequence of robot-centric waypoints offers a direct interface between multimodal perception and local control. We study this interface in embodied visual tracking (EVT), where a robot identifies a language-specified person or object and follows it through a changing scene. The robot must preserve target identity through occlusion and distractors while maintaining a useful following distance. This setting is relevant to service robots, guidance, and human–robot collaboration, and provides the empirical focus of this report.

Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple setting: the robot has fewer competing candidates to distinguish. A successful single-person demonstration therefore leaves an important deployment challenge unresolved. In shared spaces, other people can enter the camera view, cross the target’s path, or resemble the target. Distractor tracking (DT) tests this challenge directly. Benchmark results reported by TrackVLA [1] show a substantial drop from single-target tracking (STT) to DT across methods: for example, Uni-NaVid falls from 25.70% to 11.30% success, while TrackVLA falls from 85.10% to 57.60%. The size of this gap varies, but it motivates our emphasis on improving DT as a practical requirement for person-following robots.

Traditional EVT systems typically decompose the problem into detection, association, tracking, and planning. Such pipelines are interpretable, but errors compound: a target-identity mistake corrupts the tracking state, which in turn misleads the planner. Recent vision–language–action (VLA) approaches instead learn a shared representation for visual recognition, language grounding, temporal reasoning, and action prediction. This direction builds on embodied language grounding [2, 3], direct vision–language action prediction [4], and open generalist robot policies [5, 6]. Uni-NaVid [7] studies a unified video-conditioned navigation formulation, while TrackVLA [1] specializes VLA learning for EVT and demonstrates strong performance on EVT-Bench. TrackVLA++ [8] further introduces explicit spatial reasoning and long-horizon target memory.

A short-horizon waypoint representation makes the connection between multimodal understanding and local control explicit. Waypoints express the intended motion in the robot’s coordinate frame, while a low-level controller handles execution. For target following, the prediction must combine the language-specified identity with both the current spatial configuration and recent motion. This motivates a policy that brings visual history and language into a shared representation before decoding a local trajectory.

VLX-Go formulates local motion generation as vision–language-conditioned short-horizon waypoint prediction. It uses complementary frozen DINOv3 [9] and SigLIP [10] encoders, a multiscale history representation, a pretrained transformer backbone [11], and a waypoint regression head. This design pairs a transformer backbone with an explicit spatial output: eight future robot-centric waypoints that can be passed to a low-level controller.

Our working hypothesis is that effective target following among distractors benefits from aligning visual features with language before learning tracking-specific motion. This follows the staged learning principle used by OmChat [12] and LLaVA [13], which aligns visual features with a pretrained language backbone before visual instruction tuning. We adopt this principle for embodied tracking through multimodal alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization. Stage 1 trains only the vision–language adapter. Stage 2 jointly trains the transformer backbone and adapter using both the Stage 1 alignment data and additional VQA data. Stage 3 then starts from the Stage 2 base checkpoint and applies SFT on tracking data. Finally, we fine-tune on on-policy data aggregated with DAgger [14], filtering privileged oracle labels using target framing, proximity, and recent tracking history. The main benchmark results evaluate the resulting tracking model across all three tasks.

Starting from a baseline model [15] performance 41.54% DT success; the multi-stage policy improves the success rate to 55.80%. This substantial observed gain motivates the staged recipe, while leaving the contribution of each stage to be isolated. We then investigate on-policy refinement with DAgger as a preliminary extension: oracle supervision on policy-visited states raises DT success by another 2.42 percentage points to 58.22%. Its combination of higher DT success and fewer collisions is promising for further study of tracking in shared spaces.

In summary, this report contributes:

A vision–language waypoint policy. VLX-Go combines frozen DINOv3 and SigLIP features, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight decoder for short-horizon robot-centric waypoints.

Three-stage training followed by DAgger. Adapter alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking SFT connect general multimodal learning to waypoint prediction. We describe the 19,532-episode oracle collection and its conversion into training examples, and a DAgger stage that filters privileged oracle labels.

Evaluation across tracking conditions. VLX-Go reaches success rates of 58.22% and 60.93% on DT and AT, the highest listed SR on these tasks. Results emphasize episode success and collision avoidance, with comparisons of the three-stage and DAgger policies across all three tasks. Interaction diagnostics provide additional context for further development.

title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
authors: Hochul Hwang,Jahir Sadik Monon,Soowan Yang,Shiven Umeshbhai Patel,Anh Nhat Hong Nguyen,Kien Nguyen,Keshav Garg,Dylan Gage,Duretti Hordofaa,Anshu Anjna,Eshed Ohn-Bar,Donghyun Kim
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are severely underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity, limiting the perception reliability that BLV navigation requires.
We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 36K curated open-source images with 5.5K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 500 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection.
Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios.
Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps that have limited progress in this domain. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.
introduction:
Over 36 million people worldwide are blind, a number projected to more than double in the next 30 years [1]. In response, researchers have developed a wide range of assistive technologies, including smart white canes [2, 3], wearable computer-vision systems [4], and guide dog robot platforms [5, 6, 7], all of which rely on robust perception to alert users to hazards, identify navigational landmarks, and support route-following. In practice, however, prior work with BLV end-users shows that perception failures remain a major barrier to adoption, as missed detections and false positives interrupt navigation and erode user trust [8, 9, 10, 11].

At the core of this problem is a data bottleneck: the accessibility-critical object categories that matter most for BLV navigation—such as Accessible Pedestrian Signals (APS), handrails, and door-activation buttons—are either entirely absent, coarsely defined, or severely underrepresented in large-scale vision datasets such as ADE20K [12], COCO [13], and Cityscapes [14], which predominantly focus on standard categories like vehicles and buildings. As demonstrated in Section 4, many state-of-the-art open-source segmentation models [15, 16, 17] omit accessibility-critical classes from their vocabularies, and several open-vocabulary models exhibit substantial performance degradation in zero-shot settings [18].

Targeted efforts have emerged to address this data scarcity, but their impact remains limited because most operate within narrowly defined, domain-specific scopes that constrain broader downstream deployment. A large body of work has investigated obstacle detection for sidewalk navigation of BLV individuals [19, 20, 21, 22], with an emphasis on localization and recognition of static and dynamic obstacles that obstruct safe and continuous walking. Other datasets, such as SurDis [23], target more specialized hazards, particularly surface discontinuities such as steps and drop-offs. GuideTWSI [24] focuses narrowly on tactile walking surface indicators. More recently, the literature has expanded to include VLM-based scene understanding [25] and description [26, 27]. However, despite these advances, none of these efforts provide datasets that meaningfully support dense detection or segmentation across broad BLV-relevant classes. Islam et al. [28] introduce a taxonomy of 90 BLV-critical object categories with image-level presence labels, rather than the dense pixel-level annotations required for segmentation. As a result, existing real-world datasets remain limited in scale, semantic coverage, and intra-class diversity.

Beyond these structural limitations, a fundamental viewpoint mismatch persists between existing data and deployed assistive perception platforms. Most vision datasets are curated from human-eye-level or vehicle-mounted perspectives, whereas assistive platforms—such as chest-worn wearables [29], cane-mounted cameras [30], and quadruped robots [31, 5, 32, 33]—perceive the world from fundamentally different egocentric viewpoints. This mismatch between training distributions and embodied sensor inputs is further compounded by limited intra-class diversity and insufficient coverage of environmental variations, resulting in poor zero-shot segmentation performance [34, 11].

To bridge these gaps, we develop NavAble, a dataset and a generator tailored to perception for BLV-assistive navigation. NavAble is guided by two principles: first, reliable navigation demands large-scale real-world coverage of fine-grained accessibility-critical object categories selected through prior BLV-related human studies [32, 35]; second, robust deployment requires a controllable synthetic data generator capable of producing viewpoint-specific data that reflects the geometry, sensing perspective, and environmental variations encountered by assistive platforms in practice. This paper makes two contributions and reports four empirical findings.

Technical Contributions:

NavAble Dataset. A large-scale dataset of 41.5K densely annotated real-world images spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, comprising 5.5K newly collected egocentric images and 36K curated open-source images aggregated and re-standardized from fragmented class-specific repositories. To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest collection of high-fidelity pixel-level annotations targeting BLV-assistive perception.

NavAble Generator. title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
authors: Henry Che,Xuanchi Ren,Sanja Fidler,Shenlong Wang,Laura Leal-Taixé,Shengyu Huang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.
introduction:
Sensor simulation is critical for developing autonomous systems. Robots and self-driving vehicles must operate safely across a long tail of environments, trajectories, and interactions that cannot be collected exhaustively in the real world. Recent reconstruction-based systems such as NVIDIA Omniverse NuRec (NVIDIA, 2024) transform captured driving logs into interactive simulation environments, while generative simulators such as OmniDreams (Basant et al., 2026) synthesize controllable observations beyond the captured data. Together, they highlight two complementary capabilities: preserving an observed world while changing the sensor trajectory, and creating new worlds beyond recorded experience. LiDAR is especially important in this setting because it provides direct geometric measurements under challenging illumination, yet its sparse, viewpoint-dependent returns are difficult to simulate faithfully. A practical LiDAR simulator should offer both capabilities while producing accurate observations, remaining temporally coherent under sensor motion, and running fast enough for interactive use.

Neural LiDAR simulation has largely developed along the same divide. Reconstruction-based methods fit an explicit neural scene representation to a captured log and render LiDAR from novel sensor poses (Wu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a). Their persistent 3D representations provide strong geometric consistency and precise viewpoint control, making them well suited to scene resimulation. However, fitting each scene can require hours of optimization, and the resulting simulator remains tied to a manually collected log. These methods can vary the sensor trajectory within a scene, but do not readily scale to a diverse distribution of new environments.

Generative methods instead amortize scene modeling across data and learn a distribution from which novel LiDAR scenes can be sampled (Zyrianov et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025b; Liang et al., 2026). This formulation promises diversity and scale, but realizing that promise depends on a suitable representation. Operating directly on unordered point sets is inefficient and prevents straightforward reuse of mature image and video generation infrastructure. Range images provide a structured, sensor-native alternative that preserves LiDAR scanning topology, but high-resolution range sequences are expensive to model directly with pixel-space diffusion (Zyrianov et al., 2022; Nakashima and Kurazume, 2024; Nakashima et al., 2025). Meanwhile, tokenizers developed for RGB video are poorly matched to range images, and existing LiDAR tokenizers generally target a single scanning pattern (Ran et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2024). LiDAR generation therefore still lacks a compact latent interface that scales across both time and sensors. As a result, existing generators tend to specialize in one sensor configuration, produce only short sequences, or require many denoising steps. The field thus lacks a unified simulator that combines the distributional coverage of generative models with the scene fidelity, persistence, and control of reconstruction-based methods.

We address this gap with LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model that brings generative and reconstruction-based simulation into one conditional framework. Its foundation is a universal, fully attention-based LiDAR tokenizer designed specifically for range images. Local spatial neighborhood attention captures sparse geometric structure, while factorized temporal attention exchanges information across sweeps without reducing the native temporal resolution. This design accommodates different scan patterns within a shared representation, allowing one tokenizer checkpoint to reconstruct data from 32-, 64-, and 128-beam sensors and generalize to an unseen scanning pattern. It also provides a common latent space in which heterogeneous LiDAR datasets can contribute to the same world model.

On this shared latent space, we train a bidirectional diffusion teacher with a unified interface for a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map and actor layout, a persistent spatial cache (PSC), and, optionally, text. Rather than assigning each task a separate architecture or prediction head, we sample these conditions independently during training and use their composition to specify the inference regime. With no observed LiDAR geometry, the model generates new worlds from scene-level conditions; an observed LiDAR prefix turns the same model into a point-cloud forecaster; and a PSC built from observed sweeps anchors the model to a particular world for generalizable LiDAR resimulation under a new sensor trajectory without per-scene optimization. Generation, forecasting, and resimulation are therefore different ways of querying the same learned world, distinguished by the available evidence rather than by model parameters.

To make this unified model practical for interactive simulation, we distill the bidirectional teacher into a four-step block-autoregressive causal student. A rolling temporal K/V cache retains recent dynamics, while a world-aligned PSC preserves scene geometry beyond the finite temporal window, enabling persistent and temporally coherent long-horizon rollouts. The resulting causal checkpoint retains the shared conditioning interface and performs all three tasks at or above the native 10-Hz LiDAR rate. Across their respective evaluation protocols, LidarVerse outperforms task-specific baselines on most reported metrics. Together, these results establish a unified sensor-simulation paradigm in which changing the conditions, rather than the architecture, moves one model between generative simulation and reconstruction-grounded resimulation. To summarize, our main contributions are:

Universal LiDAR tokenization. We introduce a fully attention-based tokenizer that preserves native temporal resolution, improves geometric reconstruction and generative modeling, and supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam sensor configurations within one checkpoint.

Universal LiDAR tokenization. We introduce a fully attention-based tokenizer that preserves native temporal resolution, improves geometric reconstruction and generative modeling, and supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam sensor configurations within one checkpoint.

Unified LiDAR sensor simulation. We bridge generative and reconstruction-based simulation within one conditional world model. By varying the available conditions, a shared checkpoint performs LiDAR generation, point-cloud forecasting, and generalizable LiDAR resimulation without task-specific heads or per-scene optimization.

Real-time, persistent world modeling. We distill the bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal student and introduce a rolling PSC for consistent long-horizon generation. The resulting model operates in real time and achieves state-of-the-art results across the three evaluated task protocols.

2. Unified LiDAR sensor simulation. We bridge generative and reconstruction-based simulation within one conditional world model. By varying the available conditions, a shared checkpoint performs LiDAR generation, point-cloud forecasting, and generalizable LiDAR resimulation without task-specific heads or per-scene optimization.

3. Real-time, persistent world modeling. We distill the bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal student and introduce a rolling PSC for consistent long-horizon generation. The resulting model operates in real time and achieves state-of-the-art results across the three evaluated task protocols.

title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU
authors: Kemeng Huang,Bowen Ren,Xinyu Lu,Minchen Li,Taku komura
abstract:
Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and continuous collision detection (CCD). However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex degrees of freedom (DoFs). We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable rest-shape design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak
speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0×150.0\times with full-space FEM
and 4133.3×4133.3\times with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.
introduction:
Gradient-based design, system identification, and control often optimize one object’s parameters for their effect on another object. A hanger’s shape determines whether a garment remains supported. An initial velocity determines where another body moves after collision, and a robot command changes the motion of a grasped deformable object. In each case, the gradient must follow forces transmitted through contact and the subsequent motion. Computing these derivatives efficiently is particularly challenging when a scene combines deformable objects with detailed, nearly rigid components: the representation must resolve the interactions without making every stiff component expensive to differentiate.

Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Differentiable projective-dynamics methods, including DiffPD and DiffCloth (Du et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022), accelerate repeated solves through local-global iterations and matrix prefactorization. Representing nearly rigid components as stiff deformable meshes nevertheless retains vertex-level motion DoFs, increasing simulation and differentiation costs even when only near-rigid motion is required (Lai et al., 2026). ADD (Geilinger et al., 2020) provides fully implicit, two-way coupled rigid and deformable dynamics with analytic adjoints, but uses penalty-based normal contact, which does not strictly prevent interpenetration. DiffIPC (Huang et al., 2024c) differentiates fully implicit FEM dynamics with friction, using IPC barriers and continuous collision detection to maintain non-penetration. Its full-space representation, however, carries the motion DoFs of every stiff component into the backward solve, making repeated evaluations costly in its CPU implementation. The resulting opportunity is to combine contact-coupled differentiation with compact motion coordinates and efficient GPU execution.

We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated framework for differentiating
coupled FEM-affine IPC simulations
(Figure 2). Building on the forward
formulation of StiffGIPC (Huang et al., 2025a), we derive frame-wise
adjoints directly in the mixed motion coordinates. Full-space FEM
retains the freedom needed for local deformation, while each affine
body contributes only twelve motion DoFs regardless of its surface
resolution. Contact and joint derivatives couple interacting bodies
within each frame. Inertia and friction make the time integration equations depend
on earlier states.
The backward systems therefore remain compact while preserving cross-object coupling and the temporal dependencies required for coupled inverse problems.

Compact motion coordinates alone do not provide shape or control gradients. Changing an affine rest surface changes its mass, the positions at which contact is evaluated, and the maps that convert point-space forces to affine coordinates. Under friction, the same rest change also moves the previous-frame points used to define sliding and the lagged contact quantities. We differentiate these dependencies explicitly, together with initial states and revolute or prismatic joint controls, and accumulate them in
parallel without enlarging the adjoint system. To retain the advantage of compact systems, conditional CUDA Graphs are employed to keep preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) iterations and convergence checks on the GPU, thereby reducing the overhead of repeated kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization. A PyTorch interface connects these
physical gradients to user-defined parameter maps and losses.

In summary, our contributions are:

Coupled FEM-affine adjoints for differentiable IPC.
We derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordinates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.

Coupled FEM-affine adjoints for differentiable IPC.
We derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordinates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.

Affine-body derivatives for shape design and articulated control.
We derive gradients for affine rest shapes, initial states, and joint controls, including shape-dependent inertia and frictional contact.

A reusable GPU optimization pipeline.
We develop a GPU-parallel adjoint and gradient-accumulation pipeline with conditional CUDA Graphs and a PyTorch interface for design, system identification, and control.

Fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC.
We present the first fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC framework for coupled nearly rigid and deformable bodies, with substantial speedups demonstrated across contact-rich inverse problems.

Our evaluation examines the benefits of GPU execution and compact motion representations across contact-rich inverse problems. For comparison with DiffIPC, we retain full-space FEM in both systems and use relatively low-resolution benchmarks to keep evaluation times manageable for the CPU-based baseline. Even at these resolutions, DiffGIPC achieves 12.312.3–34.1×34.1\times speedups in complete backward evaluation and 10.610.6–60.9×60.9\times speedups in combined forward and backward evaluation, covering initial motion, rest shape, material, and friction optimization. A separate resolution study examines how performance scales with geometric detail and the additional benefit of affine coordinates. Further experiments demonstrate cloth design, affine shape optimization, stable placement, and articulated control. The source code of our framework will be released.

We derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordinates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.

2. Affine-body derivatives for shape design and articulated control.
We derive gradients for affine rest shapes, initial states, and joint controls, including shape-dependent inertia and frictional contact.

3. A reusable GPU optimization pipeline.
We develop a GPU-parallel adjoint and gradient-accumulation pipeline with conditional CUDA Graphs and a PyTorch interface for design, system identification, and control.

4. Fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC.
We present the first fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC framework for coupled nearly rigid and deformable bodies, with substantial speedups demonstrated across contact-rich inverse problems.

title: All-St3R SLAM: Real-time RGB Dynamic SLAM with Pixel-wise Motion Masking
authors: Yewon Kim,Paul Hongsuck Seo,Sang Chul Ahn
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026. Project Page:this https URL
abstract:
SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a core technology in autonomous systems that enables them to estimate their own position and build a map of unknown environments simultaneously.
SLAM systems in dynamic environments are of great practical importance. However, existing dynamic SLAM approaches still have several limitations
like over-removal and high computational costs.
To address these limitations, we propose a real-time RGB Dynamic SLAM framework that precisely removes moving objects at the pixel level without relying on predefined labels or segmentation models. Our system combines pixel motion predicted by ego-motion using DUSt3R with point tracking from All-Tracker, removing only actually moving pixels by analyzing discrepancies between the two motion sources.
Unlike object-level masking methods, our approach eliminates only currently moving regions, allowing temporarily static parts to be utilized for tracking.
Operating at approximately 10 FPS, the system achieves real-time performance on standard 30 FPS video streams by subsampling every 3 frames. Relying solely on RGB inputs, this significantly improves upon state-of-the-art dense dynamic SLAM approaches (0.5–3 FPS), presenting a highly practical solution. introduction:
For embodied AI systems, such as service robots, autonomous drones, and mobile manipulators, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has become a fundamental perception module in real-world applications [1, 2].
However, real-world environments often contain moving objects, motivating the development of SLAM systems that can operate robustly even in dynamic environments.

Recent dynamic SLAM research has proposed two main strategies:
(1) joint tracking of camera and dynamic objects, and (2) dynamic removal. Although tracking-based methods [3, 4] provide comprehensive scene-level understanding, they are often too computationally expensive.
Consequently, the removal strategy—masking dynamic regions—has become the standard practical approach.

Existing removal-based approaches, however, face significant trade-offs. Early Geometric methods [5] are lightweight but remain sparse, while object-level and hybrid approaches [6, 7, 8] rely on heavy segmentation or detection priors. These methods not only suffer from over-removal (e.g., discarding parked cars) and limited generalization to unseen categories, but also introduce significant computational overhead, restricting real-time deployment.

Thus, we propose a dense, geometry-driven dynamic RGB SLAM system capable of per-pixel motion masking that achieves real-time performance without relying on heavy object-level segmentation or detection.
We integrate dense 3D matching from DUSt3R [9] with lightweight pairwise point tracking adapted from All-Tracker [10].
As illustrated in Fig. 1, dynamic regions are identified by comparing the pixel motion predicted by ego-motion with the observed point tracking motion. Our system offers several crucial advantages:

Dynamic removal without segmentation or detection models:
We detect dynamic regions purely from geometric discrepancy without relying on object-level segmentation or detection networks. This label-free formulation generalizes to unseen objects and preserves static pixels within partially moving objects, significantly reducing over-removal.

Dynamic removal without segmentation or detection models:
We detect dynamic regions purely from geometric discrepancy without relying on object-level segmentation or detection networks. This label-free formulation generalizes to unseen objects and preserves static pixels within partially moving objects, significantly reducing over-removal.

Robust tracking via progressive dynamic masking:
Unlike single-step removal strategies that risk discarding useful correspondences, our method progressively accumulates motion inconsistencies across frames. This strategy enables preserving maximal tracking correspondences, leading to robust tracking in dynamic scenes.

Real-time RGB-only framework:
By adapting All-Tracker to a pairwise two-frame inference setting, we eliminate sequential overhead without sacrificing tracking quality. Combined with lightweight geometric filtering, our system operates at approximately 10 FPS. By subsampling every 3 frames, this throughput enables real-time performance on standard 30 FPS video streams.

Our approach prioritizes real-time performance and high tracking accuracy using solely monocular RGB inputs.
